title: Allocation
text:
The options on allocation tab depend on whether an adaptive or non-adaptive design has been selected on the ‘Study > Study Info’ tab, and if adaptive whether subjects are recruited sequentially or in cohorts.
If the design is non-adaptive then the only allocation option is blocked with fixed allocation ratios.
If the design is adaptive with Continuous or Deterministic recruitment, then there are 4 allocation options.
If the design is adaptive with cohort recruitment then there are 3 allocation options, all of which can be combined with early stopping:

title: Allocation
text:
Randomization Ratio and Blocking
In the Randomization Ratio and Blocking section of the Allocation tab the user inputs the components of randomization blocks that enroll from the onset of the study and until any arm is dropped. These blocks work like the Fixed Allocation tab blocks.
Once an arm is dropped the “Upon arm drop:” option in the Setup section of the allocation tab will determine how randomization proceeds.

title: Allocation
text:
Arm Dropping Criteria
The user may select any combination of Bayesian “Per Dose” QOIs: Posterior Probabilities or Predictive Probabilities, or a Target Dose QOI. For each criteria selected (at least one must be selected), the user supplies a direction of comparison and probability threshold. If at any interim, any arm meets the specified arm dropping criteria, then that arm becomes a candidate for dropping. After all candidates are identified for dropping, the Setup rules determine which, if any, of the candidates will be dropped.

title: Allocation
text:
Setup
A variety of rules are specified in the Setup section of the Allocation tab.

Max number of arms that can be dropped during the study
The maximum number of arms that can be dropped – this can be set to from 0 to the number of active arms, the Control and Active Comparator are never dropped. This figure is the ‘maximum number of arms that can be dropped over the duration of the trial’. At any interim any number between 0 and the ‘maximum number of arms can be dropped as long as this limit is not exceeded on the overall number of arms that would have been dropped.
If the maximum number of arms that can be dropped is set to the number of study drug arms, then if all arms are dropped this is recorded as an “early termination for futility”.


Prune from lowest/highest dose
Arm dropping can be restricted to ‘pruning from the lowest dose’ and/or ‘pruning from the highest dose’. If ‘prune from the lowest dose’ is selected, then until the lowest dose meets the arm dropping criteria the second lowest dose cannot be dropped and so on. At an interim when the lowest dose does meet the arm dropping criteria, and the second dose does too, then the second dose can be dropped as well (and third and fourth …), it does not have to wait until the next interim. Pruning from the highest dose does the same thing, except that no dose can be dropped unless every larger dose will also be dropped.
If no pruning is selected or pruning from both ends is selected, then the user must select to prioritize the higher or lower dose to cover the instance when more doses are candidates for dropping than are allowed to drop by the maximum threshold. If “Prioritize dropping the lowest dose” is selected then when forced to choose between two or more doses to drop, the one with the lowest effective dose strength will be dropped.


Upon arm drop
Finally, specify what is to be done with the unused subjects that would have been allocated to an arm that has now been dropped. There are three options:

Maintain study size, maintain combined block size of treatments

Subjects that would have been allocated to arms that have been dropped are now randomized between all the remaining active treatment arms (excluding control and active comparator) using their original allocation ratios. For example, if the allocation ratio was 2:1:1:1 between Control and D1, D2 and D3, then after dropping D1 the block size remains size 5 (2 to Control and 1 to each of D2 and D3) with the \(5^{th}\) slot being allocated 1:1 between the remaining two study arms D2 & D3. Thus, the overall proportion of subjects on Control (and Active Comparator) is maintained.

Maintain study size, reduce combined block size of treatments

Subjects that would have been allocated to any arms that have been dropped are randomized between all remaining arms (including control) using a reduced total block size. Thus, if the allocation ratio was 2:1:1 between Control and D1 and D2, then after dropping D1 the block size drops to total size three: 2 to Control and 1 to D2.

Decrease the study size, reduce combined block size of treatments

Subjects that would have been allocated to any arms that have been dropped are no longer recruited, and the total sample size of the study is reduced; the remaining subjects are recruited using a reduced block. If interims are specified by number of subjects recruited, these interim sizes are reduced proportionally. As an example of this, if an arm that gets 20% of the randomization is dropped when there are 100 subjects enrolled, then if the next interim is scheduled at 200 subjects enrolled, it will actually be performed at 180 subjects enrolled.

title: Allocation
text:
Early Stopping Only
If allocation is to be fixed the “Early Stopping Only” option should be selected. Then on this tab the fixed allocation ratios and block size are specified – for the first cohort and then for all subsequent cohorts. In each case the user specifies the number of each arm to allocate in each cohort and the sum must equal the size of the cohort.






Figure 7: Cohort allocation tab with early stopping, but no adaptive allocation.

title: Allocation
text:
Adaptive Allocation
If allocation is to be adaptive the “Adaptive Allocation” option should be selected and then under “Subsequent Cohort Allocation” the “Allocate cohort by sampling from allocation vector” should be selected. Then on this tab

The fixed allocation ratios and block size are specified for the first cohort. The user specifies the number of each arm to allocate and the sum must equal the size of the cohort.
The user then specifies

The fixed allocation to control
The QOIs to be used to calculate the allocation ratios for the remaining subjects in the cohort as for adaptive allocation (see Adaptive Allocation above).








Figure 8: Cohort allocation tab adaptive allocation.




Adaptively allocate to best dose
If allocation is to be adaptive, but at each cohort just Control and the “best dose” are to be allocated to, the “Adaptive Allocation” option should be selected and then under “Subsequent Cohort Allocation” the “Allocate cohort to single treatment (plus control)” should be selected. Then on this tab

The fixed allocation ratios and block size are specified for the first cohort. The user specifies the number of each arm to allocate and the sum must equal the size of the cohort.
The user then specifies

The fixed allocation to control
The QOIs to be used to calculate the allocation weighting to calculate for the non-Control arms, (see Adaptive Allocation above) and all the subjects not allocated to control will be allocated to this arm.








Figure 9: Cohort allocation tab with adaptive allocation allocating to only the best dose.

title: Design Overview
text:
The FACTS core engine allows for the design and simulation of fixed and adaptive clinical trials, especially focused on, but not limited to, Bayesian designs with multiple active arms.

Sub-tabs of the Design Tab
Trials designed in the core engines are comprised of a number of elements:

The dose response model: the user must specify how the doses are related to each other in the primary analysis, though there is a simple ‘no model’ option that estimates the mean treatment effect of each arm independently. A fixed trial uses the dose response model for the final Bayesian analysis of the data; an adaptive trial uses the same model both for the final analysis and at the interim updates. For time-to-event endpoints, there is an additional tab for estimating the control arm hazard rate called hazard model.
The longitudinal model or predictor model: whether the trial is adaptive or fixed, the user may select whether to use a longitudinal model for continuous or dichotomous primary endpoints or a predictor model when using a time-to-event primary endpoint. In a fixed trial the longitudinal model can be used to multiply impute final values for subjects that have dropped out. In an adaptive trial it is also used at the interim updates to multiply impute final values for subjects who have been recruited but do not yet have final values. In a fixed trial with no subject dropouts using a longitudinal model would have no effect on the outcome, analysis, or conduct of the trial.
Allocation rules: in a fixed trial the user just specifies the proportion of subjects to be recruited to each arm, and the same can be done in an adaptive trial (i.e. an adaptive trial does not have to adapt the allocation), but an adaptive trial has a range of options that the user can use to adapt how subjects are allocated to the different treatment arms as the trial progresses.
Early stopping rules: in an adaptive trial the user can select the criteria and specify the thresholds at which trial should be stopped at any interim where the conditions are satisfied. Early stopping is optional, and even in an adaptive design the user can opt to always recruit the maximum permitted number of subjects. In a fixed trial there are no interim analyses and hence no opportunity to stop early.
Final evaluation criteria: the same Bayesian evaluation criteria are available whether the trial is fixed or adaptive. The user selects which criteria to use and what thresholds will constitute success or failure. The success and failure criteria do not have to be complements of eachother, and any analysis that doesn’t completely satisfy either the success or futility criteria is called, “inconclusive.”
Frequentist analysis: frequentist p-values can be calculated comparing each dose to the control arm (or a fixed value if there is no control). P-values can be used as decision making quantities at interim updates or final analyses. p-value cannot benefit from the dose reponse models or longitudinal models, which are specific to the Bayesian model in FACTS.







TipDesign tabs for multiple endpoint designs



The tab layout for multiple endpoint designs is slightly different when compared to the single endpoint engines. The multiple endpoint engine must allow for separate Dose Response, Frequentist Analysis, and Longitudinal specifications for each endpoint.
To allow for this, there is a “Response Models” tab as a first level sub-tab of the Design tab. There is 1 sub-tab below Response Models for each endpoint. Within the endpoint tab there will be a Dose Response, Frequentist Analysis, and Longitudinal tab (if applicable).




Evaluation of Bayesian Posterior Estimates
At every interim and final analysis there is a Bayesian model fit to the data observed up to that point in the trial. The Bayesian model contains a dose response model and, often, a longitudinal model. In the absence of a longitudinal model, the posterior is calculated as:
\[p(\omega|Y) \propto \prod_{i = 1}^{n}{p(y_{i}|\phi)p(\phi)}\]
where \(\phi\) is the set of parameters of the selected response model, \(p(\phi)\) is the prior for those parameters, \(y_i\) is the final response for each subject and \(n\) is the number of subjects with complete data.
With a longitudinal model, this becomes:
\[p(\omega|Y) \propto \prod_{i = 1}^{n}{p(y_{i}|\phi)p(\phi)\prod_{i = 1}^{n}{\prod_{j = 1}^{L}{p(y_{ij}|\psi)p(\psi)}}}\]
where \(\psi\) is the set of parameters of the selected longitudinal model, \(p(\psi)\) is the prior for those parameters, \(y_{ij}\) is the response for each subject \(i\) at each visit \(j\) and \(L\) is the number of visits.
The posterior is evaluated using  MCMC Markov Chain Monte Carlo  with individual parameters updated by Metropolis Hastings (or Gibbs sampling where possible), using only the \(y_i\) and \(y_{ij}\) data available at the time of the update.
The likelihood and priors for each of the dose response models are provided in the description of the Dose Response tab, and the likelihood and priors for the multiple imputation models are provided in the description of the Longitudinal Models tab.

title: Success/Futility Criteria
text:
The Success/Futility Criteria tab is where users specify the decision rules for determining study success or failure. The Final Analysis criteria always exist, and should, in general, be specified for every simulated trial. If simulating an adaptive trial, then interim analysis decision rules are also specified here.

Decisions in FACTS Core
There are \(7\) possible decisions that can be made in a FACTS Core design, each with a numeric identifier that FACTS uses in the .csv output to denote decisions. The Outcome column contains the decision made, and the number 1-7 map to decisions as follows:

1. Early Success

Early Success is achieved if and only if the trial meets the success condition at an interim analysis, and does not meet the futility criteria at the final analysis. The final analysis criteria must not be met whether or not subjects were selected to follow-up after an early success decision.

2. Late Success

Late Success is achieved if and only if the trial enrolls to the maximum sample size, collects full follow-up, and then meets the final analysis success criteria.

3. Late Futility

Late Futility is achieved if and only if the trial enrolls to the maximum sample size, collects full follow-up, and then meets the final analysis futility criteria. Late futility is not automatically the complement of late success; the futility rule must be specified as the complement of the success rule to make it true.

4. Early Futility

Early Futility is achieved if and only if the trial meets the futility condition at an interim analysis, and does not meet the success criteria at the final analysis. The final analysis criteria must not be met whether or not subjects were selected to follow-up after an early success decision.

5. Success to Futility Flip-Flop

Success to Futility Flip-Flop is achieved if and only if the trial meets the success condition at an interim analysis, but meets the futility condition at the final analysis. Success to Futility Flip-Flops can be achieved whether or not subjects are followed up after the early success decision.

6. Futility to Success Flip-Flop

Futility to success flip-flop is achieved if and only if the trial meets the futility condition at an interim analysis, but meets the success condition at the final analysis. Futility to Fuccess Flip-Flops can be achieved whether or not subjects are followed up after the early futility decision.

7. Inconclusive

Inconclusive is achieved if and only if the trial enrolls to the maximum sample size, collects full follow-up, and then does not meet the final success or final futility criteria.


Every simulated trial will result in exactly one of these decisions. Non-adaptive trials will result in either Late Success, Late Futility, or Inconclusive. An adaptive trial that does not stop at an interim analysis will result in Late Success, Late Futility, or Inconclusive. An adaptive trial that stops enrolling for early success at an interim analysis will end up as an Early Success or a Success to Futility flip-flop. An adaptive trial that stops enrolling for early futility will result in Early Futility or Futility to Success flip-flop.


Final Evaluation
On the Final Evaluation tab, the user can specify rules for judging the study for final futility or final success at its end.
The left column of the Final Evaluation tab contains the specification of the trial final futility rule, and the right column contains the specification of the final success rule.
To add a decision rule, click the “Add…” button within the appropriate column, select a decision quantity QOI, a comparison inequality sign, and a threshold. Final success and final futility criteria can each have multiple components to them, and the selection at the bottom of the column called “Combine criteria using:” dictates if success or futility should be declared if every single criteria is met (AND) or if any criteria is met (OR).
The success and futility rules need not be complementary - there can be trials that do not meet either criteria at the final analysis. These trials would be considered inconclusive. It is allowable, although generally not recommended, to specify overlapping success and futility rules. If a trial were to satisfy both the success and futility criteria at the final analysis it would be considered a final futility.
The Final Evaluation Criteria are always applied at the time of the final analysis, even if the study stops early for success or futility, and whether or not “Continue follow-up if study stopped for success” or “Continue follow-up if study stopped for futility” are selected. As a result, setting final analysis criteria that are easier to satisfy than interim analysis criteria may result in the labelling of trials that meet the interim analysis criteria but do not satisfy the final analysis criteria as flip-flops.






Figure 1: The final evaluation tab within the success futility tab.





Interim Analysis Criteria
On the success/futility criteria of a design with “Enable adaptive features” checked on the Study > Study Info page, the user can specify rules for judging the study for futility or success at an interim and at the final evaluation. If the trial has no interims there will be just a tab for the Final Evaluation criteria. If the trial has interim analyses, then there can be tabs that define different early success/futility criteria at the different interims.
At the top of the main tab is a control to allow tabs to be created for different interims. In a newly created adaptive design, FACTS will create a tab for interim 1.
If early success/futility criteria are specified for an interim, then they will be taken to apply to all subsequent interims until the next one for which criteria are supplied, then those criteria will apply until the next interim for which criteria are applied and so on. There will be no stopping for success or futility until the first interim for which early stopping criteria have been defined.
It is possible to specify overlapping early success and early futility criteria at an interim, but it is not possible to stop for both success and futility at the same time. The FACTS design engines will stop the trial but the user should not rely on one or other outcome taking precedence. It is not considered good practice to have success and futility rules that could both be true, so FACTS does not  guarantee a “tie break” rule As of FACTS 7.1 early futility will be the result if both early success and early futility criteria are met. .
In the output files there are columns labeled “Success ” and “Futile ” indicating whether any decision criteria became true, and “Success Combined” and “Futile Combined” indicating if all the criteria for a success or futility determination have been met. If both sets of criteria are met simultaneously, FACTS will only flag one of “Success Combined” and “Futile Combined” as being met, corresponding to how the outcome of the trial has been flagged.






Figure 2: An interim evaluation tab within the success futility tab. The selected interim evaluation tab controls the interim analysis decisions at the 3rd interim analysis and all later interims.



Having created a tab to define the early success/futility criteria at an interim, the user has options to delete the tab or to copy criteria that have already been entered on another tab before editing them.
The user specifies:

Whether early stopping for futility or success is to be allowed by selecting the “Futility criteria” or “Success criteria”
The stopping rules are specified, by selecting the QOI to be tested, the direction of the comparison and the threshold value for the criteria to be met, as in the Final Evaluation tab above.
The user can specify whether, if multiple criteria have been specified, they all need to be meet (Criteria combined using “AND”) or only any one of them needs to be met (Criteria combined using “OR”). These are specified independently for stopping for success and for futility.
If stopping is allowed, the user specifies what the minimum amount of information (using the information type specified on the Interims tab). This can be specified both in overall terms and information on specific doses. If multiple minimum-information criteria are specified they must all be met for the QOI criteria to be evaluated.

title: Execution Tab
Execution Tab
text:
If “Deterministic” accrual has been specified on the Study > Study Info tab, then on the Accrual tab, rather that specifying an accrual profile from which subject recruitment times are simulated, the user loads a file of specific accrual dates for every subject.






Figure 2: Execution > Deterministic Accrual tab.



The user specifies a “.dat” file to load that contains the  subject accrual dates in weeks This value is in weeks from FACTS 7.0 onwards, previously it was in days.  from the start of the trial.
The required file format is a text file with comma separate values. One row per subject, with 3 fields on each row:

the subject ID, (an integer)
the ID of the region where the subject was recruited (an integer)
and the subjects randomization date (in weeks from the start of the trial – this is a ‘real’ number allowing fractions of a week to be specified)

The file must contain sufficient entries to allow the maximum number of subjects specified on the Study > Study Info tab to be recruited.
After successfully loading a file, the FACTS GUI shows a plot of the resulting weekly accrual rate

This document describes how to use the FACTS Dose Escalation design engine to analyze a supplied data set. It describes how to run the design engine so that it analyzes the current trial data and outputs the recommended dose for the next cohort.

text:
3.1 bCRM.exe
The outputs from a simulation can be used to run the design engine in ‘simulator’ and ‘allocator’ modes. The simulator mode is run as a simple check of the installation.

Create a new, empty directory to carry out the installation verification.
Open Windows Explorer and navigate to the location of a FACTS project using the Dose Escalation design engine that has some simulation results. If you do not have such a directory, run FACTS and follow the Dose Escalation tutorial for a simple toxicity example up to the point that the first simulations have been run, and use the directory you have created.

Only a single simulation is required.
In the projects ‘data’ directory, there is a directory called ‘Results’, and within that there is a directory for every scenario simulated:
Figure 1 - FACTS project folder structure

From one of those directories, copy the init.bcrm file and paste it into the installation verification directory.
Open a command prompt window (Choose Start > All Programs > Accessories > Command Prompt) and change the current working directory so that it is the installation verification directory.
Enter the command: bcrm.exe s 1

This assumes a copy of the design engine has been placed in the directory, alternatively the design engine can be invoked from the directory where you extracted it, for instance:

C:\Program Files\Berry Consultants\FACTS 7.1.0\bin\bcrm.exe s 1

This command should cause a single simulation to be run and if it runs successfully it will create the following files in the installation verification directory:
cohorts001.csv
doses.csv
rvseed.upd
simulations.csv
summary.csv

title: Dose Escalation Design Trial Execution
text:
4.1 Input files
init.bcrm Parameter input file containing all design parameters for the trial execution
subject.csv Comma separated data file containing subject response data for the trial
subject2.csv Only required for 2 group designs, similar to subject.csv but for second group
lastMTD.txt Only required for designs with both toxicity and efficacy and only after the first cohort has been randomized; used to store dose index of last MTD allocation between executions. NB The value is a zero based index,
lastMTD2.txt As for lastMTD.txt but for the second group.
state33.txt Only required in 3+3
To be able to perform a run with the dose escalation design engine, a subject.csv file is required in addition to the init.bcrm file. The init.bcrm file should come from a FACTS simulation directory where the design for the trial was simulated. It does not matter what the scenarios were that were being simulated, these parameters will be ignored because there is actual data to be used. Typically, the Monte Carlo parameters “mcmc-trans” (the MCMC burnin), and “mcmc-maxiter” (number of MCMC samples) should be adjusted when executing an actual trial. Smaller default values are used during trial design to limit simulation times, but should be increased for improved statistics during trial execution. Monte Carlo parameters do not apply to 3+3 designs.
The MCMC parameters can be modified on the Simulations tab on the dialog that is displayed when “MCMC Settings” is clicked.
For efficacy only trials where extra subjects are being allocated to the maximum and minimum doses, init.bcrm must be edited to ensure that append is set to 1, i.e. it contains the line:

append 1

This will ensure that each randomization uses the random seeds updated by the previous run and so allocation to the maximum and minimum doses are truly random. When append=0, the rv-seed parameters from the init.bcrm parameter file are used as the starting point for each execution.


N.B. – With the exception of “mcmc-trans”, “mcmc-maxiter” and “append”, no other parameters in the init.bcrm file should be modified during execution of the design engine. Some parameter validation from the FACTS GUI is not repeated in the design engine, and changing parameters could produce misleading results.
The subject.csv file is a comma separated text file, which for purely historical reasons has (for our purposes) a number of redundant fields. The values in columns 2-6 should be left blank.















#Patient ID,
Patient Initials,
Year,
Month,
Day,
Time,
Cohort,
Dose,
Tox,
Eff





1, , , , , , 1, 1, 0, 0
2, , , , , , 2, 2, 0, 0
3, , , , , , 3, 3, 0, 0
4, , , , , , 4, 4, 1, 0
5, , , , , , 5, 3, 0, 0
6, , , , , , 5, 3, 0, 0
7, , , , , , 5, 3, 0, 0
8, , , , , , 6, 4, 0, 0
9, , , , , , 6, 4, 0, 0
10, , , , , , 6, 4, 0, 0
11, , , , , , 7, 4, 0, 0
12, , , , , , 7, 4, 0, 0
13, , , , , , 7, 4, 0, 0
(The file above has had a ‘tab’ inserted before each value to aid readability. This is not required in the actual file. It is recommended that Excel be used to create the file, saving it as ‘csv’.)
N.B. The “Dose” is the index of the treatment arm (see the Study > Treatment Arms tab) allocated to each subject, except in N-CRM where “Dose” is the Dose Strength which replaces “Dose Index” – (again see the Study > Treatment Arm tab).
Efficacy and toxicity data is not used for all design types. When one of these response columns is not used, the values for that column may all be set to 0, but still must be supplied. Responses used for each design are:
3+3 Tox only
CRM (Toxicity) Tox only
N-CRM Tox. If using ordinal toxicity, the value must be the category (i.e. 1, 2, 3 or 4) rather than the normal 0 or 1.
If efficacy is included, it must also be set.
bCRM Tox & Eff
CRM (Efficacy) Eff only
Ordinal Tox only. NB Tox must contain the toxicity category (i.e. 1, 2, 3 or 4) rather than the 0 or 1 used by the other versions.
The ‘subject2.csv’ file has identical formatting and supplies the response data for the second group.

4.1.1 lastMTD.txt and lastMTD2.txt
Finally, in addition to ‘subject.csv’, a ‘lastMTD.txt’ file is required when running a bCRM trial. This file is needed when fitting toxicity and efficacy because the last cohort may have been allocated to the MED and therefore cannot be used in determining the maximum allowed dose for MTD. The file will be created automatically when the engine is run in ’allocator’ mode with an empty subject.csv file at the start of a trial. From then on, the file must be present and must contain a valid dose index. The file is not necessary and will not be created when running toxicity or efficacy only trials. To create the file manually, right-click in the execution directory and select ’New > Text Document’. Rename the new file ‘lastMTD.txt’. Then edit the file to contain the zero based index of the last cohort targeted at the MTD. Thus if the doses are 10, 15, 20, 30, 50 and the last cohort allocated to MTD was at dose 20, the file should contain 2. However, in general this file should not be altered outside of engine execution.
lastMTD2.txt is identical to lastMTD.txt except that it is used for group 2. It is therefore only required in N-CRM with both efficacy and two groups enabled.


4.1.2 state33.txt
If running 3+3, state33.txt is used to keep track of what happened last.
If starting 3+3 with zero subjects, state33.txt will be created automatically. It only needs to be created manually, if starting part way through the trial. Once it exists, it will be updated automatically.
It contains a single number:

0=No cohorts yet (assumed if state33.txt is missing);
1=Normal allocation;
2=Last cohort was a confirmation cohort (i.e. the dose was repeated);
3=Last cohort was a validation cohort (i.e. it de-escalated)

The available command line options can be displayed by running the command:

Simulate mode – simulate the trial, with the optional argument specifying the number of simulations.

Print the version number.

Unused

Force the small cohort run-in to end

title: Dose Escalation Design Trial Execution
text:
4.3 The output files
dose.reco The recommended dose for the next cohort. When run in allocation mode, this file contains the randomized dose for the next cohort, output as the 0 based index of the dose. If an appropriate dose cannot be recommended or the trial should stop, the “Next dose” will be reported as –1.
doses.csv The dose to x-hat mapping.
alloc_out.txt Same output as dose.reco.
rvseed.upd Contains the random number seeds at the end of the run.
The random seeds work as a chain. The initial values are used to generate the next values, which are then used to generate another set, and so on. At the end of the execution, regardless of the value of append, the ending values of the seeds will be written to rvseed.upd. Because the values are updated after each run, this file should be backed up to a safe location following each allocation execution so that your actions can be repeated. Final seed values are also reported in the simulations.csv results file.
At the start of the run, if init.bcrm contains “append 1” and this file exists, it will be read by the program and the seeds used as the starting point for the next run.
If the file does not exist, or “append 0” is set, the rv_seeds in the init.bcrm parameter file will be used as the starting point for the next run.
simulations.csv This has the same format as the simulations file written by FACTS and contains a single row of data representing the current state of the trial.
lastMTD.txt This output file is generated only when both toxicity and efficacy are used and stores the (zero based) index of the last cohort targeted at the MTD.
lastMTD2.txt As lastMTD.txt but for group 2 if it is included.
state33.txt This output file is generated only when executing a 3+3 trial and is used to store a status flag between executions.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
This document describes the detailed functionality for running interim analyses designs simulated using FACTSTM (Fixed and Adaptive Clinical Trial Simulator) via the command line execution of the FACTS engines (we refer to this as the Trial Execution Mode). It describes the functionality for all four of the FACTS CorePlatform Trial engines and all for three Enrichment Design (ED) engines
The “Analysis” tab on the FACTS Graphical User Interface (GUI) provides a convenient graphical interface for invoking the trial execution directly from the GUI rather than from the command line. So this document also serves as a guide for using the “Analysis” tab in the GUI.
The design engines are simple command line programs that require no complex installation. They are supplied in a ‘Zip’ archive from which they should be extracted to an easy to locate directory.
For example:
C:\Program Files\BerryConsultants\FACTS 7.1.0\bin
This places them in a subdirectory (bBin’) in the standard FACTS install directory.
The following files are available (Note: the Enrichment Design (ED) engines were previously known as Adaptive Indication and Population Finder – hence the prefix “aipf_” on the executable files”).:

aipf_contin.exe - the ED engine for a continuous endpoint
aipf_dichot.exe the ED engine for a dichotomous endpoint
aipf_tte.exe the ED engine for a time-to-event endpoint
contin.exe the Core engine for a continuous endpoint
bCRM.exe the Dose Escalation engine (not used here)
combiF.exe the 2D Dose Escalation engine (not used here)
dichot.exe the Core engine for a dichotomous endpoint
multep.exe the Core engine for a multiple endpoints
pt_contin.exe the Plaftorm Trial engine for a continuous endpoint (not used here)
pt_dichot.exe the Platform Trial engine for a dichotomous endpoint (not used here)
tte.exe the Core engine for a time-to-event endpoint

To run the engines, open a command prompt window. Navigate to the directory where the various input files for the run are located and enter the command, for example:
C:\Program Files\BerryConsultants\FACTS 7.1.0\bin\contin.exe r n 10 > recommend_out.txt
For this example, two files are required:

a copy of the nuk1_e.param file from a simulation results directory of the FACTS design to be used; and
a patients data file (the formats of the patients data files are given below.

The engine will output a “weeks” file with the same columns as provided in simulations, giving the results of the analysis along with a results file and the requested number of randomisations (10 in the above example).


Execution updates for FACTS 6.2 only affect the Core and Staged Design engines. The details are in the FACTS Core and FACTS Staged Design sections below. Briefly the changes are:

The executable write on standard output a summary of the data that has been read in, to help check that FACTS has read the supplied data as intended and that there hasn’t been a data formatting problem.
Previously the engines were poor at coping with missing data entries – as none occur in simulation mode (where of course trial execution is perfect). FACTS Core and Staged Design are now better at coping with missing data.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
2.1 Input
The execution mode can be invoked from the command line by running the engine executable program with the appropriate option flags. The user will also have to provide a dataset with data on subjects enrolled in the trial at the time the analysis is required, and a parameter file describing the trial design and some additional inputs via command line options. The required input files and command-line options are as follows.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
2.2 The trial specification (‘param’) file
The trial specification parameters should be provided in a file named nuk1_e.param (C/ME), bin1_e.param (D) or tte1_e.param (TTE) in the directory in which the executable is run (or some other file name may be specified with the ‘f’ option). This is the file produced by the GUI in the design/simulation phase of the trial.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
2.3 Patient Data File
This format has changed from that in earlier versions of FACTS and is now identical to that of the patientsNNNNN.csv output files. Note that all columns should be present even if not used (e.g. baseline) in the particular design. It is recommended you supply the value -9999 in unused columns, this makes it clear to someone subsequently using the file that this is intended as an unused data column – the exception to this is the region id, here just supply the value “1”.

The subject data in a file named patients.dat should be provided in the directory in which the executable is run (or some other file name may be specified with the --execdata option).
It is a text file with comma separated fields. Empty lines and lines beginning with ‘#’ will be ignored.
Each subject’s data now appears on a single line with comma separated values. For continuous and dichotomous these are:

Subject ID: An integer value that is not used other than to identify a subject’s data records.
Region ID: The subject’s region ID (1…R). Unused in trial execution mode – just supply the value “1”.
Enrollment Date: A non-negative number of days.
Dose Index: Subject’s dose arm (1...D)
Last Visit #: Last observed visit. Zero to number of visits.
Dropout indicator: 1=dropped out, 0 otherwise
Baseline: Not used if no baseline (supply -9999)



For each scheduled visit:


Response at visit. Ignored if after Last Visit # (supply -9999). For dichotomous endpoints these are 0 or 1 (or -1 if restricted Markov). Note that in C/ME if the analysis is to be conducted on change from baseline and baseline is present, the Response column is expected to contain the original response and not difference from baseline.



The multiple endpoint format is identical except that columns are needed for each endpoint:

Subject ID
Region ID
Enrollment Date
Dose Index
Last Visit #: Zero to number of overall visits.
Dropout indicator



Then for each endpoint:


Last visit observed for the endpoint: 0 to the number of visits used for the endpoint.
Baseline: Not used if no baseline (supply -9999)


For each visit used by the endpoint:


Response



The time to event format is simpler in that there are no visits, but there are predictor columns:

Subject ID
Region ID
Enrollment Date:
Dose:
Dropout indicator: 1=dropped out, 0 otherwise
Duration: Duration until last observation (outcome=0) or time of event (outcome=1)
Outcome: 0=no event observed, 1=event observed
Predictor value: For a dichotomous predictor 0 or 1. For a time to event predictor, as for duration. Unused if there is no predictor (supply -9999).
Pred Outcome: 1 if the predictor value/event has been observed. If the subject dropped out before the predictor value was recorded or if they are still being followed up but predictor is not yet available, then set PredictorOutcome= 0. Unused if there is no predictor (supply -9999).


The subject data provided must be compatible with the trial setup specified in the ‘param’ file.
Where fields are unused, a numeric value still needs to be supplied but the exact value supplied is immaterial (though It is recommended that the value supplied is an integer).
Previous versions of FACTS execution engines could not handle missing values prior to the final observed visit, and user imputation was required. As of version 6.2, this issue has been remedied. A patient’s last visit (as specified by the last visit column) must be a valid value. However, visits prior to the last visit may be missing with the following exceptions: the dichotomous stable-state model must have all non-missing values up to the last visit, and the baseline value for a continuous endpoint must be non-missing if the endpoint is specified as change from baseline or if the baseline-adjusted model is used.
The default code of “-9999” is still expected for missing values, though any character string that cannot be interpreted as a number (except #) will be interpreted as missing.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
2.4 Program Invocation
The engine executables can be run with the following command line parameters:

r : Required. Invokes the execution mode
n <NNN> : Specifies how many new subjects we need treatment arm allocations for. (This is only relevant when adaptive randomization is applicable; ignored otherwise).
f <param-filename> : Specify the ‘param’ file. Default is nuk1_e.param (C/ME), bin1_e.param (D) or tte1_e.param (TTE).
--execdata <subject-data-filename> : Default is patients.dat
--interim <I> : where I is the interim number, an integer number should be supplied, there is no check that the value supplied is an integer, and the design engine behaviour is undefined if that is not the case.
--current-week <W> : where <W> is the current time in weeks (this parameter is required and should be correct with respect to the data submitted; if the specified date and the data supplied are not in alignment, the design engine’s behaviour is undefined).
--seed <N> : If this is specified, then N will be used as the random number generator (RNG) seed for this interim/final analysis. Otherwise, the seeds specified in the param file will be used.



--final : If this flag is specified, then a ‘final’ analysis and evaluation is performed (as opposed to interim evaluations of stopping criteria, etc. Takes precedence over --interim). Note that if neither an –interim or –final flag is suppled, then a final analysis is performed.
--armsdropped <B,B,B,B,B> : This needs to specified for interim analyses in arm-dropping settings or forced arm selection settings where some arms have been dropped at earlier interims (the engine needs to be told about this since it has no way of remembering previous states). For example if you have a trial with 6 arms, and arms 2 and 3 were dropped on a previous interim (or similarly in a forced arm selection setting if you retain arms 1,4,5,6), then you would specify this as “--armsdropped 0,1,1,0,0,0” (no spaces in the comma-separated argument string). If this is omitted in an arm-dropping trial, then it is assumed that no arms have already been dropped at the time of invocation. Note that this specification has to be compatible with the param file specified.
--o <output-directory> : Specify the output directory to place all output files generated from the engine run.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
2.5 Output Files

weeks00000.csv : The analysis is reported in a ‘weeks’ file format. [With the understanding that the weeks file structure is retained for familiarity, although some of the columns such as time-related ones (e.g. arm drop time, interim analysis time) will be meaningless since the engine does not track time or past events.]
results.txt : A simple text file that reports a high level summary of the analysis. It states whether: (1) the accrual has stopped because the max subjects/events was reached, or implied since the engine was invoked for the final analysis; and (2) whether the current analysis satisfied the success/failure criterion.
alloc.txt : A text file with a single columns listing the treatment allocations for the next N subjects. This is only output when requested in cases when the trial has not stopped accrual, and only for trials with probabilistic adaptive allocation.
Standard out: not actually a file of course, unless you pipe the output into one. The output is a duplicate of execdatasummary.csv (see below).
execdatasummary.csv: This is a comma separated text file. For every data column expected for input, the feedback consists of a summary of the column along with a summary of the column broken out by treatment arm. For continuous-valued inputs, the number of records, minimum, median, mean, maximum, standard deviation, and number of missing values is given. For dichotomous or categorical variables, the table of counts is given, including the number of missing values. For the special case of dichotomized continuous variables, a summary is given for both the continuous and dichotomous version of the variables.


Note that not all columns in the execdatasummary.csv file are computed for each row – only the quantities that are deemed relevant. For example, minimum, median, etc. are not computed for number of records nor for dichotomous values, whereas ntrue and nfalse is computed only for dichotomous values. Up to 100 unique values and their frequency are printed for categorical or numerical variables, which is likely comprehensive for categorical variables but not truly continuous variables. If more than 100 unique values are present, only the first 100 observed in the file are printed, as the intent is just a check on inputs, not a comprehensive summary.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
3.1 Input
The execution mode can be invoked from the command line by running the engine executable program with the appropriate option flags. The user will also have to provide a dataset with data on subjects enrolled in the trial at the time the analysis is required, and a parameter file describing the trial design and some additional inputs via command line options. The required input files and command-line options are as follows. The Staged Design execution mode usage is largely similar to the Core Designs, except for a few stage-specific inputs and options.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
3.2 The trial specification (‘param’) file

3.2.1 Stage 1
The trial specification parameters should be provided in a file named nuk1_e.param (C/ME), bin1_e.param (D) or tte1_e.param (TTE) in the directory in which the executable is run (or some other file name may be specified with the ‘f’ option). This is the file produced by the GUI in the design/simulation phase of the trial.


3.2.2 Stage 2
The trial specification parameters should be provided in a file named nuk2_e.param (C/ME), bin2_e.param (D) or tte2_e.param (TTE) in the directory in which the executable is run (or some other file name may be specified with the ‘f’ option). This is the file produced by the GUI in the design/simulation phase of the trial.
In addition to the trial specification parameters, the analysis engine needs some additional parameters that provide information on some Stage 1 outcomes and data summaries. This information should be provided in a file with a similar structure to the ‘*.param’ files mentioned above. The file name is s2_aux.param by default (but can be specified using the “—s2-aux-paramfile” option on the command line option). One such sample parameter file for TTE Staged Designs is given below to illustrate the format.
In the second stage of Staged Design, because of the relative complexity, in some circumstances, of determining whether minimum information requirements have been met, FACTS in TE mode used for the second stage of a Staged Design does not check if minimum information requirements have been met and hence it does not write out a “results.txt” file. The user must check themselves in the weeks00000.csv file if the decision conditions have been met and if the minimum information conditions have been satisfied.
--------- <s2_aux.param> -------------------
block_alloc = 2,0,0,0,0,0
block_size = 4
init_alloc = 1,1,0,0,0,1
max_events = 738
max_subjects = 661
stage1_lpfv = 29.976959561567821
start_time = 50
n_stage1_subjects_in_stage2 = 175
The parameters that have to be specified are:

Required parameters

max_subjects : This the maximum number of subjects that can be enrolled in Stage 2 (after accounting for the subjects enrolled in Stage 1).
max_events : (TTE only) This the maximum number of events that are allowed in Stage 2 (after accounting for the events in Stage 1).
start_time : The time in weeks when Stage 2 of the trial started.
stage1_lpfv : The time in weeks when the last Stage 1 patient enrolled.
init_alloc : A comma-separated list of 0/1s to indicate which of the complete set of arms were carried forward into Stage 2. E.g., If we had six arms in the trial and only arms 1, 2 and 6 were carried forward to Stage2 then it would be represented by init_alloc = 1,1,0,0,0,1.

Optional parameters (only needed if the treatment allocations for the next N subjects is required)

block_alloc : specifying which of the arms should be allocated via blocking and its allocation size within the block.
block_size : The block size. (Continuing the above example, with arms 1, 2 and 6 carried forward to Stage2, the above sample file illustrates the case where we wish to specify future allocation to be done with a block size of 4 with arm 1 allocated 2 slots per block and the remaining two slots being adaptively allocated to the two other allocatable arms in Stage 2.)


Note for TE mode, the aux file parameter “n_stage1_subjects_in_stage2” is not required.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
3.4 Program Invocation
The engine executables can be run with the following command line parameters:

r : Required. Invokes the execution mode
n <NNN> : Specifies how many new subjects we need treatment arm allocations for. (This is only relevant when adaptive randomization is applicable; ignored otherwise).
f <param-filename> : Specify the ‘param’ file. Default is nuk1_e.param (C/ME), bin1_e.param (D) or tte1_e.param (TTE).
--execdata <subject-data-filename> : Default is patients.dat
--stage <S> : where S is the stage number (1 or 2). Default is 1.
--interim <I> : where I is the interim number, an integer number should be supplied, there is no check that the value supplied is an integer, and the design engine behaviour is undefined if that is not the case.
--current-week <W> : where <W> is the current time in weeks (this parameter is required and should be correct with respect to the data submitted; if the specified date and the data supplied are not in alignment, the design engine’s behaviour is undefined).
--seed <N> : If this is specified, then N will be used as the random number generator (RNG) seed for this interim/final analysis. Otherwise, the seeds specified in the param file will be used.
--final : If this flag is specified, then a ‘final’ analysis and evaluation is performed (as opposed to interim evaluations of stopping criteria, etc.) If both and –interim and –final flag are specified, --final takes precedence. If one of --interim , --complete-data-analysis or —final flag is not supplied, then performing a final analysis is the default.
--armsdropped <B,B,B,B,B> : This needs to specified for interim analyses in arm-dropping settings or forced arm selection settings where some arms have been dropped at earlier interims (the engine needs to be told about this since it has no way of remembering previous states). For example if you have a trial with 6 arms, and arms 2 and 3 were dropped on a previous interim (or similarly in a forced arm selection setting if you retain arms 1,4,5,6), then you would specify this as “--armsdropped 0,1,1,0,0,0” (no spaces in the comma-separated argument string). If this is omitted in an arm-dropping trial, then it is assumed that no arms have already been dropped at the time of invocation. Note that this specification has to be compatible with the param file specified.
--complete-data-analysis (Stage 1 only) : If this flag is specified, then a ‘Complete Data Analysis’ is performed i.e., final analysis criteria are evaluated and no success/futility/arm-selection is assessed (Takes precedence over –interim and --final).
--arm-selection (Stage 1 only) : If this flag is specified, then an end-of-satge1 arm selection assessment is performed. It can only be performed with a --final analysis, so this flag can’t be combined with --interim or
--complete-data-analysis.
--s2-aux-paramfile <stage2-aux-param-filename> (Stage 2 only) : The filename of the Stage 2 auxiliary parameter file. Default is s2_aux.param
--o <output-directory> : Specify the output directory to place all output files generated from the engine run.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
3.5 Output Files

s1-weeks00000.csv or s2-weeks00000.csv : The analysis is reported in a ‘weeks’ file format. [With the understanding that the weeks file structure is retained for familiarity, although some of the columns such as time-related ones (e.g. arm drop time, interim analysis time) will be meaningless since the engine does not track time or past events. In s2-weeks00000.csv the fields “Comb”, “Information” and “Success/Futility Combined” are populated with -9999 as these are dependent on information from of Stage 1 that is not being passed to the engine when doing the Stage 2 analysis.]
results.txt : Output for Stage 1 only. A simple text file that reports a high level summary of the analysis. It states whether: (1) the accrual has stopped because the max subjects/events was reached, or implied since the engine was invoked for the final analysis; and (2) whether the current analysis satisfied the success/failure/graduation criterion. For Stage 2 TE can only provide analysis and QOI calculation, it cannot judge stopping rules as these may depend on information that is not available to it – hence it is left to the user to compare the calculated QOI values against the relevant thresholds and to check any information requirements and hence judge if any stopping criteria have been met.
alloc.txt : A text file with a single columns listing the treatment allocations for the next N subjects. This is only output when requested in cases when the trial has not stopped accrual, and only for trials with probabilistic adaptive allocation.
Standard out: not actually a file of course, unless you pipe the output into one. This is a summary of the data supplied. Containing:

The number of records per arm
The number of records per arm per region
The earliest and latest enrolment dates
The number of records per arm by the last observed visit
The number of dropouts per arm
a table per subject visit, describing at each visit the values per arm

the number of records,
the minimum value
the median value
the maximum value
the SD of the values
the number of missing values (at an interim this will include data missing simply because that subject who has not completed follow up).

execdatasummary.csv: This is a comma separated text file. For every data column expected for input, the feedback consists of a summary of the column along with a summary of the column broken out by treatment arm. For continuous-valued inputs, the number of records, minimum, median, mean, maximum, standard deviation, and number of missing values is given. For dichotomous or categorical variables, the table of counts is given, including the number of missing values. For the special case of dichotomized continuous variables, a summary is given for both the continuous and dichotomous version of the variables.


Note that not all columns in the execdatasummary.csv file are computed for each row – only the quantities that are deemed relevant. For example, minimum, median, etc. are not computed for number of records nor for dichotomous values, whereas ntrue and nfalse is computed only for dichotomous values. Up to 100 unique values and their frequency are printed for categorical or numerical variables, which is likely comprehensive for categorical variables but not truly continuous variables. If more than 100 unique values are present, only the first 100 observed in the file are printed, as the intent is just a check on inputs, not a comprehensive summary.


NumberOfRecords: total and per arm, the active column is ‘nvalid’ which reports how many valid records there are in total and per arm.
Region: total and per arm, the active columns are ‘nvalid’ which reports how many valid entries there are and nunique, which reports how many unique values there are (region ids), then the pairs ‘uvalueN’ and ‘nvalueN’ list the different values and how often they occur. (i.e. how many region 1s, how many region 2s, etc.) This field is intended to record the region in which the participant was recruited, but for analysis purposes it is ignored by FACTS.
LastVisit: total and per arm, the active columns are ‘nvalid’ which reports how many valid entries there are and nunique, which reports how many unique values there are (last visit ids), then the pairs ‘uvalueN’ and ‘nvalueN’ list the different values and how often they occur. (i.e. how many participants last visit was visit 1, how many visit 2, etc.).
Dropouts: total and per arm, the active columns are are ‘nvalid’ which reports how many valid entries there are and ntrue, which report how many of the values where “true” – i.e. how many dropouts have been reported.
Visit_X_Values: total and per arm per visit, potentially all columns are active:

nvalid: the number of valid records
min: the minimum response seen for this arm and visit
median: the median response seen for this arm and visit
mean: the mean response seen for this arm and visit
max: the maximum response seen for this arm and visit
sd: the standard deviation of the responses seen for this arm and visit
ntrue: (dichotomous response) the number of responders for this arm and visit
nfalse: (dichotomous response) the number of non-responders for this arm and visit
nmissing: the number of missing records (at an interim this may be due to subjects not yet having reached that visit yet, but it will also include dropouts)
nunique: the number of unique values seen
uvalueN, nvalueN: for up to the first 100 unique values, the value seen and the number of times it occurs. Where there is missing data, the value “-9999” will be reported.


The purpose of these two data summaries are to allow a quick check that there is nothing obviously amiss with the data file that has been supplied.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
4.1 Inputs
The execution mode can be invoked from the command line by running the engine executable program with the appropriate option flags. The user will also have to provide a dataset with data on subjects enrolled in the trial at the time the analysis is required, and a parameter file describing the trial design and some additional inputs via command line options. The required input files and command-line options are as follows.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
4.2 The trial specification (‘param’) file
The trial specification parameters should be provided in a file named nuk1_e.param in the directory in which the executable is run (or some other file name may be specified with the ‘f’ option). This is the file produced by the GUI in the design/simulation phase of the trial.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
4.3 Patient Data File
This format has changed from that in earlier versions of FACTS and is now identical to that of the patientsNNNNN.csv output files. Note that all columns should be present even if not used (apart from.baseline which is continuous only) in the particular design. It is recommended you supply the value -9999 in unused columns, this makes it clear to someone subsequently using the file that this is intended as an unused data column – the exception to this is the region id, here just supply the value “1”.

The subject data in a file named patients.dat should be provided in the directory in which the executable is run (or some other file name may be specified with the --execdata option).
It is a text file with comma separated fields. Empty lines and lines beginning with ‘#’ will be ignored.
Each subject’s data now appears on a single line with comma separated values. For continuous and dichotomous these are:

Subject ID: An integer value (unique to a subject) that is not used other than to identify a subject’s data records.
Region ID: The subject’s region ID (1…R). Unused in trial execution mode – just supply “1”.
Enrollment Date: A non-negative number of days.
Group : Subject’s Group (1..G)
Arm: Subject’s treatment arm (1=Trt, 0=Control)
Last Visit #: Last observed visit. Zero to number of visits.
Dropout indicator: 1=dropped out, 0 otherwise
Baseline (AIPF-C only): Only present if baseline is included



For each scheduled visit:


Response at visit. Ignored if after Last Visit # (supply -9999). For dichotomous endpoints these are 0 or 1 (or -1 if restricted Markov). Note that in C, if the analysis is to be conducted on change from baseline and baseline is present, the Response column is expected to contain the original response and not difference from baseline.



For time to event the columns are similar:

Subject ID
Region ID
Enrollment Date:
Group
Arm
Placeholder: this corresponds to the “dropout” column in continuous or dichotomous and not used in TTE, a dummy value is required, and the value of 0 should be supplied. .
Duration: Duration until last observation/censoring time (outcome=0) or time of event (outcome=1)
Outcome : 0=no event observed (yet) or 1=event observed.

The subject data provided must be compatible with the trial setup specified in the ‘param’ file.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
4.4 The State File
The user needs to provide an additional file with information on the current trial state. The following information needs to be provided in a file named “current_state.csv”. The file should have two comma separated columns providing the group stopping type (if stopped) and the group data completeness status. The following example for a case with four groups illustrates the structure required:
--------- <current_state.csv> -------------------
Grp1_stop_type, Grp1_all_in
Grp2_stop_type, Grp2_all_in
Grp3_stop_type, Grp3_all_in
Grp4_stop_type, Grp4_all_in
Study_stop_type, <dummy integer>
-----------------------------------------------------
GrpN_all_in is a 1/0 indicator indicating that everyone in a group has finished (dropout, had final visit, or no longer being followed up).
(Since we aren't asking for any 'times' as input, we need this to distinguish between the case when a group stops enrolling due to cap and later qualifies for early success when (1) Not all in vs (2) All in -- the outcomes are classified differently.)
GrpN_stop_type is:

Success=1, Futility=3, Cap=2,
OtherStop=4 (For a group it means group stops because study stopped early for success/futility. When applied to a study, it means all groups stopped (could be a combination of individual group stopping causes).
StudyCap=5 (When a group stops because the study cap is reached)
None=-9999

The final row in the file contains the corresponding information for the overall study.
At the completion of the execution of the program a file named ”new_state.csv” is output which contains the updated state information.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
4.5 Program Invocation
The AIPF engine executables can be run with the following command line parameters

r : Required. Invokes the execution mode
f <param-filename> : Specify the ‘param’ file. Default is nuk1_e.param
--execdata <subject-data-filename> : Default is patients.data
--interim <I> :where I is the interim number, an integer number should be supplied, there is no check that the value supplied is an integer, and the design engine behaviour is undefined if that is not the case
--current-week <W> : where <W> is the current time in weeks. (required if information is defined in terms of opportunity to complete and should be correct with respect to the data submitted; if the specified date and the data supplied are not in alignment, the design engine’s behaviour is undefined).
--seed N : If this is specified, then N will be used as the RNG seed for this interim/final analysis. Otherwise, the seeds specified in the param file will be used.
--final : If this flag is specified, then a ‘final’ analysis and evaluations (as opposed to interim evaluations of stopping criteria, etc. . Takes precedence over --interim).
-o <output-directory> : Specify the output directory to place all output files generated from the engine run.

title: FACTS Trial Execution
text:
4.6 Output Files

weeks00000.csv : The analysis is reported in a ‘weeks’ file format. [With the understanding that the weeks file structure is retained for familiarity, although some of the columns such as time-related ones (e.g. group stop time, interim analysis time) will be meaningless since the engine does not track time or past events.]
new_state.csv : An updated ‘state information’ file.

In the group info tab we get to select the values we are declaring for success and futility. These are “differences” from the historical rate of 15% that we are assuming. So, when we say that the target rate difference for success is 0.05 this means:

text:
4.3 Trial Execution
Under the execution we specify how to simulate key logistical aspects of the trial – how fast subjects are accrued and their probability of dropping out.

4.3.1 Accrual

The accrual rate and dropout rates don’t affect this design as they are non-adaptive.


4.3.2 Dropouts
No drop-outs are assumed in these examples.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Cancer)
text:
4.4 Design

4.4.1 Control Model

This is the section in which we place the historical rate for each group, and in this example we assume it is 15% (0.15). We are also modeling these as independent in this example. When we later allow borrowing this historical rate will come in to play as a centering aspect in the borrowing.


4.4.2 Treatment Model

We model the log-odds rate in each arm independently with a prior distribution that is extremely diffuse:
\[\theta_d \sim N\left(-1.73, 100^2\right).\]
This distribution is essentially no prior weight (mean at 0.15) because the standard deviation is so large. The model here is a standard logistic model:
\[\theta_d = \log\left(\frac{P_d}{1 - P_d}\right)\]
The across groups box refers to a model that ignores the groups. This is essentially pooling all the groups together in to one group and analyzing that common group. We have selected the same model for this group – essentially a weak prior.


4.4.3 Evaluation Criteria

The evaluation tab is quite complex!!! This is good and bad. There is a great deal of flexibility and power to this flexibility, but it is also fairly complex.

First, you are allowed to use posterior probabilities or predictive probabilities for phase III. Back on the Study:Group Info tab you can create the phase III criteria. We are not using that option in this simulation.
In this example I want to evaluate each group individually as to whether it is successful or not. Therefore in the “Group evaluation rule” I have specified “Group only”. You can have group success depend on what happens in other groups.
A note on the “Study CSD for success” or “Study CSD for futility”: these are the values of “Target rate difference” specified on the “Study:Group Info” tab. Thus they cannot be adjusted here. The probability threshold to label the individual group a success or futility are listed and are editable.
Lastly you get to determine an overall study conclusion. So, how do you label the study overall (success/inconclusive/futility) when a collection of the groups are labeled in possibly mixed ways? You can select a subset of these by clicking (or not) the very last column. In this example above we have selected each of the group to classify the study as a success or futility – and on the far left clicked “AND” on how to combine these. So, in the specs above all must be success to label the study as a success and ALL must be a futility in order to label the study thusly.
We will worry about “success” in this example and not futility. We’ll address that in other examples.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Cancer)
text:
4.5 Simulation
For the results of this design we have simulated 1000 trials:

In each case we have used the same seeds.
Recall we defined the trial success to depend on all the groups being a success (or futility). These probabilities are:

And the probability of success for each group is:

From this table above we have about a 3% type I error rate (for this null that is 5% below the cut-off). For the mathematical null – which is the “Equal Weak” profile, the type I error is about 16%. Recall there is no borrowing at all between the groups and thus the results are independent for each of the 5 groups. Notice the power for the Equal Moderate profile is about 66%. The results for Group #3 in Mixed Moderate is the exact same 0.646 (true rate of 30%, same as Equal Moderate). Even though the other groups have different rates, the results for this Group 3 are identical in Equal Moderate and Mixed Moderate.
We will later enhance this design by exploring borrowing in the next design.

Here is a look at the graph for the “Mixed Moderate” example. This shows a boxplot of the final probability of being greater than the success CSD of 0.15 + 0.05 = 0.20. The mean of each group is shown by the ‘dot’ – which is the value in the table on the top of the previous page.

title: Continuous Endpoint (Alzheimer’s)
text:
4.1 Study
Under the study tab we define the basic properties of the trial we are simulating

4.1.1 Study Info
Under the study info tab we define

Whether comparison will be against a control arm, or an Objective Control (or “Historical”) level of response.
Whether increase or decreasing scores indicate a subject is improving.
The design options we wish to use:

An adaptive or non-adaptive design
Frequentist Analysis (or only Bayesian)
Longitudinal modelling (and hence subject intermediate visits)
Simulation of subject baseline scores

How many groups there are in the analysis and whether we wish to cap enrolment into any group.


In this design we don’t apply group caps, just an overall study cap of 600 patients. We will use a longitudinal model for this study because of the relatively long lag (12 months) to observing the primary endpoint. We won’t be simulating baseline scores or a baseline related response.


4.1.2 Group Info
On the group info tab we can specify targets for the group response.

Here we set our target clinically significant difference for futility at 0.5 and set up the criteria for a future phase III trial. For predicting success in a future phase III trial, we assume a phase III trial with 350 patients per arm with the objective of declaring superiority versus control. The target clinically significant difference for success is not used in this trial, though at least a 1 point difference between treatment and control would be considered very good.


4.1.3 Visits
On this tab we define the number and timing of subject visits.

We assume three visits at 3, 6, and 12 months.

4.2.1 Group Response
Here we specify the mean change from baseline and the SD (“sigma”) of the endpoint for each arm in each group. This will form a group response “profile” that will form part of a simulation “scenario”. (Somewhat like a frequentist “hypothesis” but with more details).

These profiles range from ineffective to optimistically effective.
In the “Null” profile, the drug is completely ineffective in all three groups and in the “All Futile” profile, the drug is only slightly effective and the effect is less than the futility target in all groups.
In the “All in the Middle” case, the drug has an effect just above the futility target, but is only moderately effective. In the “Two Good” profile, the drug is at the futility target in one group, but effective in the other two groups. In the “All Good” profile, the drug has a strong effect in all groups.
There are two pathological cases “Nugget” and “Nugget2” where the drug is effective in only one group
The final true sigma in each profile is 5


4.2.2 Longitudinal response
In the longitudinal response

We must also specify a longitudinal profile for the change at each visit. We assume that 1/3 of the full treatment effect is observed at 3 months, and 2/3 at 12 months. The correlation between visits is 0.8 and 0.8 of the final sigma (5) is observed at the earlier two visits.

title: Continuous Endpoint (Alzheimer’s)
text:
4.3 Execution
Under the execution we specify how to simulate key logistical aspects of the trial – how fast subjects are accrued and their probability of dropping out.

4.3.1 Accrual

The groups are expected to be relatively similar in size – 40% of the population will be mild, 30% will be moderate, and 30% will be severe. There are no group maximum sample sizes, just an overall study maximum sample size, so the total numbers in each group will depend on their relative accrual.
All groups open accrual at the start of the study
We assume an accrual profile of 12 patients per month


4.3.2 Dropout

We assume 5% drop-out at each visit for this example

title: Continuous Endpoint (Alzheimer’s)
text:
4.4 Design

4.4.1 Control Model

We place a hierarchical model on the control groups with a weak prior of N(0, 12) for the mean of the hierarchical distribution (0 is the expected response on control and a 2 point difference is our best expected response) and a weak prior inverse gamma distribution with mean 0.5 and “weight” 1 on the variance of the hierarchical distribution. We expect this to lead to a modest shrinkage in the estimates of the response on the control arms when the means of the different groups are within 0.25-0.5 of each other.


4.4.2 Treatment Model

And we place a hierarchical model on the treatment arms. With a weak prior of N(0, 52) for the mean of the hierarchical distribution (0 is the expected response on control and a 2 point difference is our best expected response) and a weak prior inverse gamma distribution with mean 1 and “weight” 0.5 on the variance of the hierarchical distribution. We expect this to lead to a modest shrinkage in the estimates of the response on the treatment arms, but the effect should be weaker than the effect of the hierarchical model on the control arms.


4.4.3 Frequentist Analysis
Here we can set the alpha levels for the different p-values that will be calculated. We use a two-sided alpha of 0.05 for them all.



4.4.4 Longitudinal Model

For the longitudinal model, we use linear regression and specify a slightly different prior for each visit.
We model each arm (control & treatment) separately – but have common models for control and treatment across all the groups.


4.4.5 Allocation

We will allocate patients evenly between the control and treatment arms in each group, in blocks of 4.


4.4.6 Interims

Here we specify that interim looks will be begin when 200 patients have been enrolled and will be repeated every 3 months (13 weeks).
We will continue to follow groups stopped for success, but not those stopped for futility. If a group is stopped for success, they will continue treatment, but if a group is stopped for futility, they will stop treatment.


4.4.7 Stopping Criteria
Here we specify the criteria for stopping groups and the overall study early for futility or success.

We based early stopping for futility on the posterior probability that within each group the response on the treatment arm is better than the control arm by the CSD for futility (which was 0.5). We monitor each group for futility. If there is a less than 20% probability the group beats the futility target of 0.5, the group is stopped for futility. If all groups are stopped, the study will stop. We don’t allow a group to stop for futility until it has enrolled at least 100 subjects.
We base early stopping for success on the predictive probability of phase III success. We monitor each group and across all groups for early success. For a single group, if the predictive probability of phase III success is at least 70%, it will stop early for success. If, across all groups, there is at least an 80% predictive probability of phase III success, then the study will stop early for success. We don’t allow a group to stop for success until it has enrolled at lest 100 subjects, and we don’t allow the study to stop for success using the “across groups” analysis until the study has enrolled at least 100 subjects (but the first interim is not until 200 subjects have been enrolled, so that restriction is currently unnecessary).


4.4.8 Final Evaluation Criteria

Evaluation criteria at the end of the study are similar, but less stringent. Furthermore, all groups must meet the futility criteria for the study to be declared futile whereas only one group, or across groups, need be successful for the study to be declared a success.

title: Continuous Endpoint (Alzheimer’s)
text:
4.5 Simulation Results
We simulate each scenario 1000 times:

In each case we have used the same seeds.
The study level results are:

This reports the trial probability of success and futility overall. In the Null case, 52.6% of trials stop early for futility. In the All Futile case, 46.2% stop early for futility. All groups must be futile in order for the trial to be declared futile. With a futility target of 0.5, and a true effect of 0 with a standard deviation of 5, it is a conservative definition of futility
On the other hand, for success, only one group must meet the success criteria for a trial to be declared a success. In the All Good case, 97.6% stop early for success. With the moderate treatment effects in “All in the Middle”, early success is less likely, but 76.5% of trials overall (early or late) are successful. In the Nugget cases, one strong group means the probabilities of trial success (early or late) are fairly high.

This is a graph from the “2 Good” profile. This shows the shrinkage of the treatment effects between the groups. The group with the lower treatment effect is pulled up, and the group with the strongest treatment effect is pulled down. This also illustrates that the group with the strongest treatment effect has the smallest sample size, a result of this group stopping earlier for success.

Early stopping for each group is shown in this graph. We see the severe group stops early for success in 76% of the simulations. The mild group stopped early for success in 43% of simulations and stopped early for futility in 23% of simulations. Again, the mild group has true response of 0.5, which is right at the futility CSD. So the effect is not necessarily poor enough to stop for futility with high probability or strong enough to stop for success with high probability. Thus, this group continues to enroll additional patients.

This boxplot of the probability of being better than the control group by the futility CSD shows that the mild group has a mean of approximately 60% probability of being better than control by the futility CSD. The other two groups have quite a good probability of being better than the futility CSD.

3.1 Toxicity
This trial will target a toxicity interval, the dose with the highest probability that it has a DLT rate in the range 0.15 to 0.3. During the trial we will limit dosing to exclude doses that are assessed to have posterior probability of over 0.25 that their DLT rate is above 0.3. (Note we check this overdose control limit is not so extreme that it limits dose escalation when we would like to occur, later.)

3.2 Treatment Arms
We enter the 8 dose levels. They range from 500mg to 2250mg in steps of 250mg. We assign them dose strengths of 5 to 22.5 in steps of 2.5. The other dependency is in the spacing of the dose values, here we have entered a linearly spaced set of doses and so will use a linear transform when we specify how the effective dose strengths, the “x-hats”, are to be derived. if the doses strengths were exponentially spaced we would use the log of the dose ratio transform so that the resulting effective dose strengths are linearly spaced.
