title: CRM Open Enrollment
text:
3.5 Design

3.5.1 x-hats
As noted above (see “Treatment Arms”) we use the linear dose transformation “dose strength – reference dose”.
We also elect to use a reference dose of 0. Sometimes a reference dose in the middle of the dose range can give problems. If the prior on Ln(Beta) is very uninformative, observing no toxicities below the reference dose can yield higher expectations of toxicity above the reference dose compared to seeing a toxicity below the reference dose. This can be addressed with an informative prior on ln(Beta) – but this requires some careful tuning to ensure the fitting of the model across the range of scenarios is still good. Here we avoid the problem simply.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated




3.5.2 Toxicity Response
We will use a logistic model for the dose toxicity model. We place priors on the parameters for the logistic model. The priors are scaled to be consistent with the selection of refence dose and the x-hat values. This can be done by looking at the logits of the scenarios manually, or with reference to the “Derive prior” “Scenarios” option. Here this latter approach results in a prior of Alpha ~N(-4.1227, 2.07482), Ln(Beta) ~N(-1.6815, 0.60572) Rho=-0.8327. We have rounded these values to a single decimal place, replaced the SD for Ln(Beta) with a larger value (making the prior less informative) and set the prior for Rho to 0, also making the prior less informative.



A screenshot of a computer Description automatically generated




3.5.3 Prior Pseudo-subjects
Prior pseudo subjects are an explicit mechanism for making the prior more informative. We will apply some prior pseudo subject data in the next iteration of the design.



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated




3.5.4 Allocation rule
In the design tab, under “Allocation” we define the patient allocation to the dose levels and the dose escalation rules. We do not use a single patient/small cohort run-in. We will require DLT information from at least 1 cohort/3 patients on each dose level in order to escalate. No doses may be skipped, and more specifically, the dose may only be escalated one dose level from the dose most recently used. The starting dose will be the first dose level, 500mg.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated





A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated




3.5.5 Stopping Criteria
This trial will stop early for having identified the MTD if we have at least 3 cohorts/9 patients assigned to the MTD. Alternatively, we must observe at least 2 toxicities before the trial could stop early for safety.

Because the allocation under backfill is to lower doses, the overall proportion of subjects experiencing a DTL is slightly less. The average number of subjects allocated at or around the MTD is slightly higher, the selection of MTD is better.

text:
5.6 Per Sim Open Enrolment Allocation History
When we look at the dose escalation behavior within a single simulated trial, FACTS now shows the assignment of each patient entering the trial as an ’interim”. This allows us to see the current status of trial as each patient is enrolled in the continuous enrollment setting. In the example below, the dose has escalated to the 4th dose level then de-escalated to the 3rd dose. Early in the trial while waiting for subjects to complete, patient that becomes available is marked as “lost” with a yellow x at the bottom. Once the trial is allocating at 1000mg or above, backfill first at 750mg then 1000mg becomes possible and no patients are lost. The backfill patients are informative – one on 750 experiences a DLT, the subjects on 10000mg eventually contribute to the number of subjects on the MTD and allow the trial to stop earlier.

2.1 Response Model
If the probability of observing grade i or higher toxicity for a subject given dose j is pij
We will model the probability of toxicity across the range of doses:
\[\log\left(\frac{p_{ij}}{1 - p_{ij}}\right) = \alpha_i + \beta\widehat{x_{j}}\]
With α3 set to 3 and β given the prior distribution:
\[\beta \sim \exp(1)\]
And α2 and α4 given Normal prior distributions (mean 5, variance 4) and (mean 1 variance 4) respectively:
\[\alpha_2 \sim N(5,4),\ \alpha_4 \sim N(1,4)\]
Each dose j is given a ‘strength’ \(\widehat{x_{j}}\) by fitting the user supplied prior expectations of toxicity for each dose p03j to the above model with β set to 1. i.e. solving:
\[\log\left(\frac{p^{0}_{3j}}{1 - p^{0}_{3j}}\right) = \alpha_3 + \widehat{x_{j}}\]
for \(\widehat{x_{j}}\).

title: CRM (Ordinal)
text:
2.3 Expected performance
The probabilities of grade 3 or higher toxicity in scenarios #1 and #2 are the same. In scenario #1 the probabilities of grade 2 or higher are the same as for grade 3 toxicity and the probability of grade 4 toxicity is 0 – i.e. all that should be observed are grade 3 toxicities. In scenario #2 the probabilities of grade 2 or higher toxicity are the same as for grade 3 but shifted 2 doses to the left and the probabilities of grade 4 or higher are the same as for grade 3 but shifted 2 doses to the right. The operating characteristics of these scenarios can be compared to CRM toxicity tutorial scenario 1. If only grade 3 toxicity is observed (ordinal scenario #1) we would expect this to give very similar results to the non-ordinal case. If there is grade #2 toxicity with a similar but earlier dose-toxicity relationship, we might hope this improves our ability to determine the MTD.
In scenario #3 there is effectively no grade 3 or grade 4 toxicity, however there is significant grade 2 toxicity, this tests the effect of grade 2 toxicity then that alone is what is observed.
In scenario #4 there is only significant grade 3 toxicity at the highest two doses with significant grade 2 toxicity at the highest three doses. This can be compared to the CRM toxicity tutorial scenario 4.
In scenarios #5 and #6 there is detectable but tolerable levels of grade 3 toxicity at the highest two doses. In scenario 5 the probabilities of grade 2 and 4 toxicity are identical to those for grade 3, so only grade 3 toxicity should be seen. The performance in this case should be comparable to CRM toxicity tutorial scenario #6. In scenario #6 the difference is that there is early high probability of grade 2 toxicity, this should give results similar to scenario #3 above.

3.1 Study
Under the study tab we will enter the overall shape of the trial, the toxicity target, the efficacy target and the details of the doses available to test in the trial.

3.1.1 Study Info
On the Study Info tab, we:

Check the “Include Efficacy” check box,
Opt to recruit subjects in cohorts
Specify that the

maximum number of cohorts will be 10
the cohort size will be 3,
there will be no cohorts accrued until the results of the current cohort are known.

We leave the “execution rate” at the default of 2 weeks (though is likely to be un-realistic) as this is a strict cohort design, the estimation of time is not very interesting, time will be solely dependent on the time to recruit and follow up a cohort and the number of cohorts. In terms of the expected duration we will simply compare number of cohorts. One assumption of this simulation is that in the allocation to the MED phase we wait until we have both the toxicity and efficacy results from the current cohort before selecting the dose for the next.
There is just one “group” in this trial.
There is no cohort expansion.




3.1.2 Toxicity
To replicate the Braun example (and bCRM) we ignore some of N-CRM options, and select

Not to simulate ordinal toxicity
To target a single dose (not a toxicity band), targeting

The dose with toxicity nearest to a rate of 0.15

No overdose control limits are specified
But we do specify a target toxicity band, this not used in the simulations, but it is used by the FACTS GUI to interpret the results, it will tell us, for each scenario, how often the dose selected as MTD was in the underdosing, target, excess toxicity or unacceptable band. The target toxicity rate is 0.15, but none of the scenarios have a dose with exactly that rate and we only select doses present in the trial, we do not interpolate. The scenarios have doses with simulated rates 0.1 and 0.2, and we decide that selection of either would be an acceptable choice. To ensure that when FACTS judges whether the design has selected a dose with true rate of 0.1 or 0.2 it determines them to be in the target band we, set the band limits to 0.099 and 0.201.




3.1.3 Efficacy
On the efficacy tab we specify that

A target experiencing a toxicity can still count towards efficacy
The target efficacy rate is 95%
The targe MED dose is the one nearest the target rate.




3.1.4 Treatment Arms
On the Treatment Arms tab we create 18 doses and give them strengths from 1 to 9.5 in steps of 0.5.



3.1.5 Variants
The variants tab allows us to easily create different versions of the design with different maximum numbers of cohorts. We leave the tab at its default and do not create any variants.

3.2 Virtual Subject Response

3.2.1 Explicitly Defined > Toxicity
On this tab we specify the 3 toxicity profiles described above in section 2.1, calling them “MTD-dose_5”, “MTD_dose_11” and “MTD_dose_13” to reflect the dose in that profile with a toxicity rate closest to the target. Note though that in the profile no dose has a simulated rate of target rate (0.15) and the doses in the profile names actually all have simulated rates of 0.1 (and the next highest dose in all these profiles have a simulated rate of 0.2 which is actually just as close to the target and so just as valid a dose to select).



3.2.2 Explicitly Defined > Efficacy
On this tab, similarly to the toxicity tab, we specify the 3 efficacy profiles described above in section 2.1, calling them “MED-dose_6”, “MED_dose_9” and “MED_dose_12” to reflect the first dose in that profile with an efficacy rate closest to the target of 0.95.



3.2.3 Parametric
This tab allows toxicity and efficacy profiles to be defined using parametric models, we are not using any of these in this example.


3.2.4 External
This tab allows toxicity and efficacy responses to be specified by supplying a file of simulated patient responses, we are not using any of these in this example.

title: bCRM
text:
3.3 Design
The N-CRM with efficacy differs from the bCRM based on Thomas Braun’s paper in two respects

N-CRM uses the Bayesian Logistic Regression model with both parameters being estimated, the Braun paper uses the CRM method that uses the model but fixes the alpha parameter.
N-CRM with efficacy does not attempt to estimate the probability of a patient experiencing both toxicity and efficacy, but Braun does.


3.3.1 Design > X-hats
Here we specify the transformation of the dose strengths to the “effective dose strengths” to be used in the Bayesian Logistic Regression model. The specification consists of two parts:

Specification of a ‘reference dose’
Specification of the transformation which is either to use the log of the ratio of dose strengths to the reference dose or a simple linear transformation where the reference dose is subtracted from the dose strength.
We select to use the median dose strength as the reference dose, and the linear transformation – as the dose strengths we have entered changed linearly. The result is that the effective dose strengths, the ‘x-hats’ vary linearly.


These “x-hats” are quite different from the Braun paper, and those used in the bCRM implementation of this case study (see below). Indeed N-CRM constrains us to use the same x-hats for both the toxicity and the efficacy models, whereas in Braun and bCRM they are different. However we can get away with this in the N-CRM because we are going to fit the two-parameter model, where bCRM requires alpha to be fixed and only estimates the slope – which is why the x-hats then have to be different for the two outcomes, the toxicity response sets the x-hats so that the fixed point (where the x-hat value is 0, so the model has the fixed value of alpha) is above the dose range, and the efficacy response has the fixed point below the dose range.
As you will see from the simulation results the performance is not harmed by this.


3.3.2 Design > Toxicity Response
This example is unusual in that the upper limit of toxicity is less than 1, the profiles we will be simulating from (see section 2.1 above) plateau out at 0.5. So, the most important element of the toxicity model specified here is that we will re-scale the logistic so that it runs between 0 and 0.55. This means the usual derive prior tool cannot be used and we need to manually come up with the parameters of the bi-variate normal for alpha and beta. We aim to have a relatively uninformative prior.
Alpha is the expected toxicity at the reference dose we set the prior to N(-1.75, 22) in the log-odds space, that is a mean at around 0.15, which is 0.08 after re-scaling. The +/- 2SD range is 0.003 to 0.9, which is 0.002 to 0.497 after re-scaling. We will be simulating rates of 0.0175, 0.075 and 0.485 at the reference dose (the reference dose is half way between doses 9 and 10) so this seems reasonable.
Ln(Beta) is the slope, we simply set the prior to N(0,1), experience (and the sampled plots) show this to be a sufficiently uninformative prior that permits a wide range of curves to be fitted - permitting any dose to be the MTD with a toxicity rate of 0.15.
The correlation of the prior is set to 0 – we do not presume any linkage between the toxicity at the reference dose and the slope.



3.3.3 Design > Efficacy Response
Similar to the toxicity response, the efficacy responses we are simulating from (see 2.1 above) range from 0.5 to1. So we rescale the efficacy model to range between 0.4 and 1.
Alpha is the expected efficacy at the reference dose we set the prior to N(2.6, 1.52) in the log-odds space, that is a mean at around 0.93, which is 0.96 after re-scaling. The +/- 2SD range is 0.40 to 0.996, which is 0.64 to 0.998 after re-scaling. We will be simulating rates of 0.9675, 0.96 and 0.675 at the reference dose (the reference dose is half way between doses 9 and 10) so this seems reasonable.
Ln(Beta) is the slope, we simply set the prior to N(0,0.5), experience (and the sampled plots) show this to be a sufficiently uninformative prior that permits a wide range of curves to be fitted – permitting any dose to be the MED with an efficacy rate of 0.95 (though unlikely at above dose 15)
The correlation of the prior is set to 0 – we do not presume any linkage between the efficacy at the reference dose and the slope.



Graphical user interface Description automatically generated




3.3.4 Prior pseudo-subjects
No prior pseudo subjects are specified – either for toxicity or efficacy.


3.3.5 Allocation Rules
There is no run-in.
The starting dose is Dose 9.

We only require one cohort on a dose before we can escalate beyond it.
We allow escalation to be by up to 2 dose levels above the dose last tested.
We want the “MTD” search stage to be able to complete with 6 cohorts.



3.3.6 Stopping Criteria
To end the “search for the MTD” phase, we simply require that:

Two cohorts have been tested at the dose currently estimated to be the MTD,
We have enrolled at least one cohort (which of course must be true if there are two cohorts on the MTD)
If all doses appear to be too toxic, that we have tested at least two cohorts before stopping the trial.
OR that we have tested 6 cohorts, this means that the “search for the MTD” phase will end after 6 cohorts, even if we do not have 2 cohorts on the dose currently estimated to be the MTD.


To end the “search for MED” phase (and hence the trial) we simply require 2 cohorts on the dose currently estimated to be the MED.
If the MED lies above the MTD (so we can’t allocate to it) then we stop if there are 2 cohorts on the dose currently estimated to be the MTD.

title: bCRM
text:
3.4 Simulation Results
Running just 100 simulations for now we can get a flavour for how the design has worked.



Graphical user interface, text, application Description automatically generated


The graph in “Show Across Scenario Graphs” we can see how often each dose has been selected in each scenario:



Calendar Description automatically generated


The histogram helpfully coloured according to the true toxicity being simulated and which range it is in: “underdosing”, “target”, “excess”, “unacceptable”. Recall we set the target range to be from 0.099 to 0.21 so the doses with toxicity rates of 0.1 or 0.2 are included as “target”. We can see that these doses are typically the most selected, and that doses with “excess” toxicity are rarely selected and with “unacceptable” toxicity are never selected.
Running 1,000 simulations, and then on the “Across Scenarios Graphs” we can use “Select Scenarios/Variants” to look at just the MTD_dose_10, MTD_dose_13 and MTD_dose_5 graphs separately. These are a clearer:

3.4.1 MTD Graphs
When the MTD is at Dose 5 (or 6) we can see these two doses dominate the MTD selection. In the summary results there is a column “ppn MTD Target” that reports what proportion of the simulations selected a dose as MTD that had a true toxicity in the target range. The results for these three scenarios are: 0.687, 0.685 and 0.674.



Chart Description automatically generated with medium confidence


When the MTD is at Dose 10 (or 11) we can see these two doses dominate the MTD selection. In the summary results there is a column “ppn MTD Target” that reports what proportion of the simulations selected a dose as MTD that had a true toxicity in the target range. The results for these three scenarios are: 0.696, 0.680 and 0.651.



Chart Description automatically generated


When the MTD is at Dose 13 (or 14) we can see three doses dominate the MTD selection – doses 12, 13 and 14. In the summary results the column “ppn MTD Target” reports that proportion of the simulations selected a dose as MTD that had a true toxicity in the target range was: 0.464, 0.479 and 0.428. Because the true MTD is at a higher dose in these scenarios, the trial fails to find as well as in the other scenarios, with a tendency to pick the dose just below the true MTD just as often as either of the true MTD doses.



Chart, bar chart Description automatically generated




3.4.2  




3.4.3 OSD Graphs
The “Optimal Selected Dose” is the MED unless the MTD is below the MED, in which case it’s the MTD. These graphs colour the bars in the histogram by the combination of the 4 categories of the true toxicity of the dose in the scenario: “Under dosing”, “Target toxicity”, “Excess toxicity” and “Unacceptable toxicity” with the 2 categories of the true efficacy: “Ineffective” (below the target efficacy rate for the MED) and “Effective”.
In the scenarios where the MTD is dose 5 (or 6) then only when the MED is at dose 6 is there the possibility of an effective dose that is also in the toxicity target range otherwise inevitably the majority of the probability is that the selection of the OSD will be at an ineffective dose.



A picture containing chart Description automatically generated


In the scenarios where the true MTD is dose 10 (or 11) except when the MED is at dose 12, we see the majority of the probability is that the selected OSD dose will be either effective and safe or effective and tolerable. When the MED is at dose 12, we see results similar to above when the MTD is below the MED, a safe or tolerable but ineffective dose is selected because there is no safe or tolerable and effective dose in the scenario.
In the scenarios where the true MTD is dose 13 (or 14) we see the majority of the probability is that the selected OSD dose will be either effective and safe or effective and tolerable. When the MED is at dose 12, there is a modest risk (~30%) that an ineffective dose will be selected – we can see that this is the same as the risk of underestimating the MTD, and it is this that has caused the OSD to be too low.



Chart Description automatically generated

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.1 Trial tab – trial info



Graphical user interface, application Description automatically generated


Trial > Trial Info: The trial design is intended as an ongoing trial, with no definitive end. However, the simulation must be limited in some manner. For the purposes we are exploring here, we will restrict the simulations of the trial to the first 1250 participants. The maximum number of participants for any treatment arm is 100. The trial will allow at most 3 concurrent treatment arms to be enrolling. The final endpoint is observed 12 weeks from baseline.

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.2 Trial tab – Trial Arms - Definition

Trial > Trial Arms > Definition: Here, we could name the actual treatment arms, but since we are agnostic about the actual treatment arms, we leave the generic name. We have added 20 treatment arms to the trial (in addition to the control arm). Though we do not expect to enrol 20 arms (and in fact cannot in the non-adaptive case), this high number of treatments is included to ensure that the trial enrols all the way to 1250 participants without running out of treatments (even in the adaptive trials coming up).

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.3 Trial tab – Trial Arms - Arrivals

Trial > Trial Arms > Arrivals: For a platform trial simulation, it is required to establish when a treatment becomes available to enter the trial. In many platform trials, the limited availability of treatments over time can be a critical factor in operating characteristics. However, for this PTSD example, there are notionally more treatments available than can be handled by the trial. As such, we establish a simple arrival pattern. In this case, all treatments become available at exactly time 0 [by putting 0 in the earliest and latest possible arrival columns] and remain available for 520 weeks, which should be longer than the duration of the trial. Just because it is available to the trial does not mean that it is available to participants. On the Trial > Trial Info tab, the maximum number of concurrent treatments was set to 3. So the first 3 treatments will enter the trial while the others wait. As soon as a treatment arm stops enrolling, the next one on the waitlist will enter the trial. With this setup, we should always have exactly 3 treatments available in the trial (unless we run out of treatments).

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.4 Virtual Response tab – Treatment classification
For assessing operating characteristics, we need to classify treatment effects. Here, we will consider any average effect of ‑8 or lower compared to control to be a “good” effect, where we would expect to achieve success. Any treatment effect of 0 or higher compared to control is an “unacceptable” treatment effect that should be declared futile. There is a gray area in-between where the treatment is effective but perhaps not at a level that we expect to be detectable, so treatments with effects between 0 and -8 are considered “mediocre.” These effect-level classifications are used in FACTS summary output.



Graphical user interface, application, Word Description automatically generated

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.5 Virtual Response tab – Arm Responses

Virtual Response > Explicitly Defined > Arm Response: For this simulation, we simulate the control participants as having a mean change from baseline of 0, implying no placebo effect. Since we are treating all of the treatment arms as exchangeable, all other treatment arms have a mean change from baseline that is simulated, and each uses the same distribution (as established on the next tab). The treatment effect will be constant within each simulation but can vary from simulation to simulation. The standard deviation in the change from baseline score for a simulated participant (conditional on their mean) is 23.
For the purposes of this tutorial, we are only exploring two virtual response scenarios. In practice, we would generally set up many more scenarios to explore a wide range of possibilities (possibly including a control with a placebo effect or putting a distribution on the placebo effect).
Here, we use the same set-up for both scenarios, where all treatment arm effect sizes are drawn from the same distribution for the scenario. The two scenarios are constructed by using two different effect distributions. The “Rare but Good” scenario samples from “Dist 1”, while the “Rarer less Good” scenario samples from “Dist 2”, as described below.



Graphical user interface, application Description automatically generated

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.6 Virtual Response tab – Treatment Distribution

Virtual Response > Explicitly Defined > Treatment Distribution: On this tab, we establish the distribution that will be used to simulate the true treatment responses. We are choosing to define the distribution in terms of an effect size (a difference from the control) rather than a response. [Since we are using a control mean of 0, the two would be equivalent. However, should we choose later to explore a non-zero placebo effect, we would likely prefer to have this distribution set up as an effect, to be an “above and beyond” placebo effect.]
For “Dist 1”, used in the “Rare but Good” scenario, the probability that a treatment is completely ineffective (equivalent to control) is set to 0.75. If it is not equivalent to control, the mean effect size is drawn from a normal distribution with mean -10 and standard deviation of 3. Under this distribution, about 75% of non-equivalent-to-control treatments will have a treatment effect in the “good” range (less than ­‑8), but 25% will be in the mediocre range (‑8 to 0). This distribution also gives a modest chance of effect sizes well into the “good” range.

For “Dist 2”, used in the “Rarer less Good” scenario, there is a higher probability of no effect: 0.8, and when it is effective, the effect size is more modest than the “Rare but Good” scenario, with a mean of -9 and a standard deviation of 2.

Virtual Response > Dropout Rate: A dropout rate of 10% is expected to be the same for all arms.

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.7 Accrual tab

Accrual: A constant enrolment rate of 4 participants/week is used for this simulation.

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.8 Quantities of Interest tab




Graphical user interface Description automatically generated


Quantities of Interest: For the non-adaptive design, a single quantity of interest is established for inference, the posterior probability of superiority over control. In this case, since a lower score is better, a mean less than the control indicates superiority.

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.9 Design tab – Control Response

Design > Control Response: A relatively low-information prior – N(0, 362) – is used for the control mean.

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.10 Design tab – Treatment Response

Design > Treatment Response: The same, relatively low-information prior – N(0, 362) – is used for each treatment mean. The prior for the observation standard deviation is set to have a central value of 23 with a weight of 1 (equivalent of one observation). While there are dropouts in this design, there is no longitudinal information being simulated, and thus there is no need to set the way that dropouts are handled. The selection of “Bayesian multiple imputation from post baseline” will be ignored since there are no post-baseline visits for dropouts.

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.11 Design tab - Allocation

Design > Allocation: A fixed allocation scheme is used of 1:1:1:1 for treatment:treatment:treatment:control, in block sizes of 12. The treatment arrivals for this design are set up so that there will always be exactly three treatments in the trial. However, under the circumstance (that could possibly appear in the adaptive versions of this design) that the trial runs out of treatment arms, it is possible to have fewer than 3 for a short period of time. Allocation is 1:1 treatment:control in blocks of 6 if only a single treatment arm is available, and 1:1:1 treatment:treatment:control in blocks of 9 if only two treatment arms are available.

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.12 Design tab – Success/Futility Criteria

 
Design > Success/Futility Criteria > All Treatments: For the non-adaptive version of the trial, only final evaluations of futility and success are established. Success is declared if the probability of superiority is greater than 0.975, and futility if it is below 0.975. [It is possible though rare to achieve exactly 0.975, since this quantity is computed as a proportion of MCMC samples, in which case the result would be inconclusive.] This rule applies to all treatment arms.

Design > Success/Futility Criteria > Treatment X: In this trial, we are specifying no additional criteria for any of the individual arms.

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.13 Simulation tab

Simulation: Here, we ran 5000 simulations in order to keep sampling error low for operating characteristics. Once complete, the primary operating characteristics of interest can be found by scrolling across the columns shown (or by viewing in the Show Other Columns … Highlights window).
Note: Platform simulations can be relatively time-consuming, so you may wish to run a smaller number of simulations for quicker comparisons (say 500 or 1000).

title: Continuous Endpoint (PTSD)
text:
2.14 Operating Characteristics and Exploration
Tables 1 and 2 show operating characteristics for the two simulated scenarios. For the purposes of this simulation, we are primarily interested in characteristics of the trial rather than the characteristics of individual treatment arms. For this non-adaptive scenario, the same number of treatments are analyzed each time, since the set-up slightly over-enrols in order to guarantee exactly 9 analyses. (In practice, if the non-adaptive design were of essential interest, we would have restricted the number of treatment arms to 9, but for the purposes of comparing to other designs, we are stopping the simulation at 1250 patients in each case.) This design provides good true positive rates – 92.6% and 88.1% of “good” treatment arms are being declared successful, while a 2.5% rate of false positives is observed – “unacceptable arms” being declared successful. As expected, the “Rarer less Good” scenario has a lower true positive rate, as the effect sizes being simulated tend to be closer to the “good” effect size threshold of -8.

Some characteristics of the trial can be explored in the graphs available within FACTS. These are accessible through the View Graphs button on the Simulations tab. Several of the graphs are oriented toward looking at the behavior of a particular arm. Since this design considers all arms exchangeable, these by treatment arm graphs may be of little interest. However, a generally useful graph for checking that the overall platform design is operating as expected, in terms of treatments entering and leaving the trial, is the “Per Sim: Arm and Participant Arrival” graph.



Chart Description automatically generated


In this graph, we can see that there are always 3 treatment arms enrolling at any given time (the thick lines). And that all treatments are ready and waiting to enter the trial from the start (the dashed line). Outcomes and associated desired outcomes (based on effect size) are also displayed if the user is interested in seeing the detailed result of any particular simulation.
FACTS provides a plot of Outcome by Treatment, shown here for the Good but Rare scenario.

This plot primarily demonstrates the scenario set-up. Since the treatment arms are exchangeable, this plot is effectively showing the proportion of simulations that an arm was simulated as a zero treatment effect. More interesting for this scenario is to restrict attention to treatment arms with a simulated “good” treatment effect, by selecting “Good” from the Controls > Trt. Classification drop-down menu.



Graphical user interface Description automatically generated with medium confidence


Here, we can see that the early arms in the trial have reduced power, due to the smaller number of controls available for comparison. This behavior is expected and is a reason that platform trials sometimes consider different sample sizes or stopping rules for early arms.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Lung Cancer)
section: 3.1 The Expected Event Rate & Conventional Sample Size
text:
3.1 The Expected Event Rate & Conventional Sample Size
The overall probability of survival in this patient population is 90% after the first 18 weeks of treatment, 70% after the first year and 37.5% after 2 years.
For a one-sided significance of 0.05, assuming the accrual is over 3 years, with a two year follow up and 21 month median survival time, to detect a hazard ratio of 0.833 with 80% power, a conventional sample size calculation gives a required total sample size of 1059 subjects (Schoenfeld’s formula).

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Lung Cancer)
text:
3.2 Study
Start FACTS, double click on: Core Design – Time to Event.

Using the menu option “File > Save As”, save this design as “Fixed-2-arm” in a convenient location (e.g. in a folder called FACTS\TTE--example in your ‘My Documents’ folder).

3.2.1 Study Info
The Study tab captures basic information about the trial. Set the following parameters:

Select: Non-Adaptive design
Do not select Include Predictor Type
Set Maximum number of subjects: 1060
We do not have a limit on number of events, so Set Maximum number of events: 1060
Specify Max follow-up per subject (wks): 104 weeks (2 years).
Set: Events indicate: Failure




3.2.2 Visits

Do not select “Restrict Event Times to Visits”




A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated




3.2.3 Treatment Arms
Set the following parameters:

A control arm is always included in TTE designs, because the analysis uses a hazard ratio.
Add just 1 study dose with a level of 1 (the level is actually immaterial).

The Dose Name may be changed by double-clicking on the relevant cell in the table. This name is simply a label for the treatment arms.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Lung Cancer)
text:
3.3 Virtual Subject Response – Explicitly Defined

3.3.1 Control Hazard Rate
The Virtual Subject Response (VSR) tab describes how subject-level data will be generated for the simulations. For time-to-event endpoint, the VSR includes two components – the hazard rate for the control arm, and the hazard ratio for the treatment arm. Event times will be simulated according to a piecewise-exponential model.
For now just one scenario is specified for the control hazard rate, others should be added reflecting the uncertainty in the true underlying rate, in order to provide a sensitivity analysis.
Create one control profile by clicking the Add button. The Profile can be named by double-clicking on the default name, e.g. “CHaz 1” and renaming.

Create segment breakpoints at 18, 30, 42, 54, 79 and 1041 weeks giving an initial segment of 18 weeks (6 * 3 week treatment cycles), 3 * 12 week observations and 2 * 25 week observations.
Set the event rate per unit time (weeks) to 0.005 for the first segment (0-18), 0.0075 for the 3 * 12 week segments, and 0.01 for the 2 * 25 week segments.



Use the Graph drop down box to see the cumulative probability of having an event (progression) or not having an event (progression-free survival).




3.3.2 Dose Response
Dose response is defined as the overall hazard ratio for each dose relative to control. (For more complex dose response models, you may wish to generate the data for a patient population externally and load it as a file). In this trial there is only one study dose, thus the response scenarios are defined by a single number.
Four different possible dose response scenarios will be simulated, where the hazard ratio is 1 (the ‘null case’), 0.9, 0.8 and 0.7 respectively. These are scenarios that represent a drug that is no different from the current standard of care, a weak performing drug, a good drug and an excellent drug.
Create 4 scenarios:

Null: where the hazard ratio is 1
Weak: where the hazard ratio is 0.9
Good: where the hazard ratio is 0.8
Excellent: where the hazard ratio is 0.7

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Lung Cancer)
text:
3.4 Execution

3.4.1 Accrual
Add an accrual scenario by clicking the Add button on the far left, then add 1 region by clicking the Add button above the table. Set the peak accrual rate to 6.5 subjects per week, to give an overall recruitment period of ~3 years.
The names of the accrual profile and the region may be renamed by double-clicking on them.



3.4.2 Dropout Rate
No results are expected to be missing at random, select “No Dropouts”.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Lung Cancer)
text:
3.5 Quantities of Interest
The Quantities of Interest (QOIs) are criteria on which decisions, interim or final analyses, will be made. Numerous QOIs are available and you may select multiple quantities for evaluation. A basic set of QOIs is provided by default. Additional QOIs may be added by clicking the Add row in the table. A QOI can be removed by clicking the X on the right side of the cell. Each QOI may be edited by clicking on it, which opens a pop-up box.
The trial will be judged a success if at the end of the trial:

The study arm has a posterior probability of at least 60% that the hazard ratio compared to Control is less than 0.9 (this 60% threshold was established by simulation to limit the proportion of successes when simulating the null case to < 0.05).

Otherwise the trial will be judged to be futile.
Set the following parameters:

At the bottom of the page, set the Clinically significant hazard ratio delta (CSHRD): 0.1 (i.e. hazard ratio 0.9 or less)
For Posterior Probabilities:

Pr(HR_d-1<-0.1) is already added.
Make sure Condition: <
Select Delta -0.1
The above should have been automatically filled in because we already specified the CSHRD

We are not interested in any Predictive Probabilities, so we delete these options to reduce output. However, it is acceptable to have them calculated even if it is not part of the design.
For Probability of being Target, we keep Target Type: Max. Although, specifying a target is not necessary because there is only one dose and a control.
For Decision Quantities (Scalars):

QOI: Pr(HR_d-1<-0.1)
Evaluation Dose: Dose 1

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Lung Cancer)
text:
3.6 Design
The statistical model must specify priors for the control hazard rate, and the hazard ratio. The hazard rate is expected to vary over time: from 0.005 per week during treatment, to 0.0075 for the rest of the first year, and then 0.01 for the second year.
For a time-to-event endpoint we model event rates over a set of segments s є {1, ..., S}. The hazard rate of the control arm in each segment is λs. For the treatment arm a proportional hazards model is assumed. The model hazard rate for dose d, and segment s, hsd. is:
\[h_{sd} = \lambda_s e^{\theta_d},\]
So θd is the log hazard ratio:
\[\theta_d = \log\left(h_{sd} / \lambda_s\right)\]
where d is the dose and θ0=0. The prior distribution for the control arm hazard rate in segment s, λs is
\[\lambda_s \sim \text{Gamma}\left(\lambda_n, \lambda_n \lambda_\mu\right)\]
where λμ is the prior mean of λ, and λn is a subject equivalent weight. As there is only one study arm, the log hazard ratio of the treatment arm is simply modeled as independent and normally distributed with a prior of:
\[\theta_d \sim N\left(\mu_{0d}, \nu_{0d}^2\right)\]

3.6.1 Hazard Model
This tab captures the prior distribution for the control hazard rate. Set the following parameters:

Select Hazard Model: Use piecewise exponential model
Create the same segment breakpoints as for the control hazard rate: 18, 30, 42, 54 and 79 weeks. Note: it is not required for the same segments to be used for the model and for data generation.
Presuming there is a lot of useful data on hazard rates for SCLC, we set priors that mirror the simulated hazard rate from the Virtual Subject Response tab, and give them a prior weight of 10 (equivalent to observing 10 events over the appropriate exposure period – i.e. equivalent to 1-2,000 weeks of data).




3.6.2 Dose Response
This tab captures the prior distribution on the log hazard ratio. Set the following parameters:

Select: Independent Dose Mode, no model (i.e. pair-wise comparison)
For the prior distributions for the normal distribution of the log-hazard ratio use a mean of 0 and Std Dev of 5. This is a weak prior. Too small a Std Dev will tend to affect the estimate of the hazard rate, it is difficult to judge ‘too small’ by analysis, but easy to see it in simulations where other effects (response modeling, early stopping, adaptive allocation) are disabled.




3.6.3 Frequentist Analysis
Change the required alpha for the frequentist analysis to 0.05 one-sided and leave “Output frequentist files” checked. The results of these frequentist tests will be monitored in the output files, but are not used for decision-making in the simulations.



3.6.4 Allocation
Because we selected Non-Adaptive on the Study Info screen, only fixed allocation is available. This initial design will use a fixed allocation of 1:1.
Set the following parameters:

Set the allocation ratio as 1:1 for Control, and the study arm.




3.6.5 Success/Futility Criteria
The trial will be judged a success if at the end of the trial:

the study arm has a posterior probability of at least 60% that the hazard ratio compared to Control is less than 0.9, (this threshold was established by simulation to limit the proportion of successes when simulating the null case to < 0.05).

Otherwise the trial will be judged to be futile.
Set the following parameters

Futility Evaluation:

QOI: Pr(HR_d-1<-0.1); d=Dose 1
Condition: <
Threshold: 0.60

Success Evaluation:

QOI: Pr(HR_d-1<-0.1); d=Dose 1
Condition: >
Threshold: 0.60

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Lung Cancer)
text:
3.7 Simulation
In order to get an initial check on the design set up, set the number of simulations to run to 10, then press Simulate. This allows us to make a quick assessment of whether the design is behaving as expected: that the Null scenario ends up mainly futile and the Excellent scenario mainly successful.
If the results look reasonable, increase the number of simulations to run to 1000, (re-check all the scenario combinations) and then press Simulate again. This is a design that is very fast to simulate, even running 10,000 simulations for each scenario takes less than an hour on a laptop. If you have access to a computer grid, and your FACTS installation has been correctly configured to use it, you may use the grid’s parallel computing capabilities to improve computation speed. To do so, select “on Grid.”

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Lung Cancer)
text:
3.8 Results
Looking at the operating characteristics for each scenario:

The probabilities of success and futility are as we require: a false positive rate of 0.05 or less on the null scenario, a power of > 80% for the good scenario and a power of 40% on the ‘weak’ scenario where the simulated hazard ratio is exactly the Clinically Significant Hazard Ration (CSHR) and our success criteria are a 60% posterior probability that we achieved it.
Compare these results to the frequentist results (click on “Show Other Columns” and select “Frequentist Results”). The Bayesian analysis gives a little more power – e.g. for the ‘good’ scenario, where power of the above design is 90%, the proportion of simulations significant by most of the frequentist measures (Log-Rank test, Wilcox, Hazard Ratio) is 86%. For the other scenarios too (except the Null) the power of the Bayesian analysis is somewhat greater (probably because it does not assume a constant hazard rate, and in this example, we have simulated an increasing hazard rate over time).

4.2 Design

4.2.1 Allocation
We will use fixed allocation but perform regular analysis in order to determine whether to stop the trial. To specify this:

Select the “Fixed Allocation” option
Specify 1:1 randomization






4.2.2 Interims
Set the following parameters:

Set Subject Information Defined By: Events
Set Specify Interims By:

Time – every 16 weeks (or very 4 months) – given the length of accrual (~ 3 years) and follow up (~ 2 years)
First interim at 50 events.

For Subject Follow-up Options un-check both Continue follow-up if study stopped for success and Continue follow-up if study stopped for futility, the trial can stop when we have sufficient events to determine success or futility (in practice further follow up could take place but we wish the simulations to report the time to decision via the reported “duration” quantity).




A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated




4.2.3 Simulation
We now simulate the trial. Each simulation will run to the end and evaluate each interim, we will use these simulated values at the interims to set the early stopping thresholds. In order that that the values at each interim are written out for each simulation, we need to set the “Number of Weeks files to output” – in this case to 1,000 to match the number of simulations we will run.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


The number of Weeks files is 1,000.
There is no early stopping for success or futility as we have not yet specified stopping criteria & thresholds. In order to set these we will in this example, look to make decisions on the same criteria that we are using to make the final decision:

Pr(HR_d-1<-0.1); d=Dose 1

We wish to set success early stopping thresholds so there is minimal additional false positive results in the “Null” scenario, and minimal additional false negative results in the “Good” scenario. We can get a good initial value to use (we may need to refine with a little trial and error) using the “Interim-2-arm” simulation results and the graphs “Explore: Early Success Criteria” from the “Null” scenario and “Explore: Early Futility Criteria” from the “Good” scenario.



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


From the “Explore: Early Success Criteria” from the “Null” scenario we can see that a threshold of 0.98 will give a minimal (< 1%) chance of the trial stopping early for success if there is in truth no treatment effect (HR=1). The solid bright green 0.98 line is just visible above the black “no early stopping” line.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


From the “Explore: Early Futility Criteria” from the “Good” scenario we can see that a threshold of 0.05 will give a minimal (< 1%) chance of the trial stopping early for futility if there is in truth a good treatment effect (HR=0.8). The solid bright red 0.05 line is just visible above the black “no early stopping” line.


4.2.4 Success/Futility Criteria
In order to decide whether to stop early, we will evaluate the same criteria used for the final analysis but use these much more conservative thresholds that we identified above. We will allow stopping for either success or futility. But early stopping will not be enabled until we have a desired amount of information. In this case we do not want to allow the trial to stop enrollment early until at least 50 total events have been observed, including 20 on the treatment arm.


4.2.5 Interim 1 Criteria
On this tab we specify the interim analyses early stopping criteria. In this example we keep the same criteria across all interims. If we wanted to have different criteria for different interims, we would select Create new interim criteria at interim and specify the interim where criteria changes.
Set the following parameters:

Select Futility Criteria

Add a QOI:

Select Pr(HR_d-1<-0.1); d=Dose 1
Select a Condition of <
Enter a threshold of 0.05




Specify Minimum number of Events before trial can stop for futility: 50 (note this is “belt and braces” we have already specified that the first interim is to occur at 50 events so this criteria should always be true)
Specify Pr(Max) as the evaluation dose, and that we require to have observed a minimum of 20 events on that arm before stopping.

Select Success Criteria

Add a QOI:

Select Pr(HR_d-1<-0.1); d=Dose 1
Select a Condition of >
Enter a threshold of 0.98




Specify Minimum number of Events before trial can stop for success: 50 (again this is belt and braces)
Specify Pr(Max) as the evaluation dose, and that we require to have observed a minimum of 20 events on that arm before stopping.





A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


The Final Evaluation remains the same as the fixed design.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Lung Cancer)
text:
4.3 Simulation
Running the simulation is the same as for the fixed design (we no longer require 1,000 weeks files).
Results can be compared between the designs in terms of

Type 1 and type 2 errors: note that you will need to add together early success, late success, and futility to success flip flop for type 1 error in the Null scenario, and early futility, late futility, and success to futility flip flop for type 2 error in the other scenarios. The Type I error in this situation is 0.051 (0.006+0.045+0.0), which is greater than 0.05 but is within the simulation error, greater numbers of simulations will be required to see if a small increase in the final success threshold is necessary to keep the type-1 error below 0.05.2
The mean trial size ranges from 765-978, but we can’t assume that the distribution of the expected trial sizes will be uniform. For instance a scatter plot of the trial sizes for the ‘Good’ scenario shows a small group simulations stopping early for futility, then a regular stream stopping for success from about 400 subject onwards, and of course a large spike at the study cap.





A screenshot of a map Description automatically generated




In this design we do not need to check for the risk of a ‘flip-flop’ (a trial that stopped early contradicting its reason for stopping early in the final analysis after full follow-up) as we have unchecked the “follow-up after early stopping” options..





A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated



Note that whilst still controlling the type-1 error (0.006+0.045=0.051), and without loss of power in the ‘Good’ (0.417+0.473=0.890) and ‘Excellent’ scenarios (0.921+0.077=0.998), there is the possibility of significant savings in time and cost – with fewer subjects being required on average and a 57% chance of stopping early in the Null scenario and 42% chance of stopping early in the ‘Good’ scenario and 92% chance of stopping early in the ‘Excellent’ scenario.
This results in a reduction in expected mean sample size from 1060 to 870 in the Null, 950 in the Good and 770 in the Excellent scenarios, and reduction in expected mean duration from 267 weeks to 183 weeks (Null), 210 weeks (Good) and 130 weeks (Excellent). Note that as many of the interims will occur during the 104 week follow up after the last subject has been recruited some early stopping will only save time and not sample size.

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
3.1 Start
Start FACTS 8.0 or later. Under the Trial Types menu to the left, select “Phase 2 and Phase 3”. Then click the “New” button at the bottom of the Start from Scratch list to select a new Ordinal design.

Using the menu option “File > Save As”, save this design as “OrdinalTutorial1” in a convenient location.

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
3.2 Study

3.2.1 Study \(\rightarrow\) Study Info
On the Study \(\rightarrow\) Study Info tab, select the following options:

Under Design Options, select Enable adaptive features
Still under Design Options, select Cumulative logistic for the ordinal endpoint modeling option.
Under Trial information, select Continuously for random arrival of subjects
Set the Max number of subjects to be 600
Check “Lower endpoint value index is improvement” because the most desirable value of the endpoint is value 1, and the worst is value 7.
Under Ordinal Endpoint Values, click the +Add button seven times to add seven values. Then click inside the cells of the table to enter the names of the endpoint values (Perfect through Dead) and assign utility values (10 through 0).
Enter 13 for the Time to Final endpoint (approximately 90 days).




3.2.2 Study \(\rightarrow\) Study Arms
On the Study Arms tab:

Include a control treatment arm. (As of FACTS 8.0, including a control arm is required.)
Enter the doses with dose strengths 1, 2, 4, and 10, by entering these values one at a time and clicking “Add arm” four times so that Dose 1 through Dose 4 are added. If desired, the arms can be given different names by clicking inside the Arm Name column and entering the preferred names.


We will not be using the Variants tab.

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
3.3 Virtual Subject Response
On the Virtual Subject Response tab, we define the probabilities of the endpoint values for simulated patients.
We will define eleven treatment effect scenarios: three null scenarios, four scenarios where the doses have increasing effectiveness, and four scenarios where all doses are equally effective and better than control. We will use the proportional odds model assumption, although FACTS Ordinal will also allow you to enter arbitrary values for the probabilities that do not necessarily satisfy the proportional odds assumption, by unchecking Use Proportional Odds.
Our historical data on control arm patients in the population similar to those we intend to enroll in the trial suggest 5% Perfect, 10% Good, 20% Fine, 20% Fair, 10% Poor, 25% Dependent, 10% Dead. We will assume that the control arm patients have these probabilities in our “Base” scenarios with various treatment effects (odds ratios). Numbers proportional to these probabilities can be entered in the “Outcome Data: Relative Proportions” table; we will enter 1, 2, 4, 4, 2, 5, 2. Since lower values of the ordinal endpoint are preferred, an Odds Ratio relative to control less than 1 corresponds to a beneficial treatment, since it implies smaller probabilities of larger values. Our scenarios include the following considerations, and these are summarized in Table 2.

Null scenarios, where all four doses are equivalent to control
Efficacious (Eff) scenarios, where the four doses have odds ratios relative to control of 0.95, 0.85, 0.7, 0.65
Scenarios where the control arm patients are systematically healthier than in the Base scenarios (“Healthier”), and other scenarios where they are “Less Healthy”
Flat scenarios, one where all experimental arms have odds ratios of 0.6, another with 0.65, another with 0.7, and another with 0.8.
A tweak to the Eff scenario where the largest dose has an odds ratio of 0.6.

It is believed that a treatment with an odds ratio of 0.75 or smaller relative to control is a good enough treatment to develop further. Such treatments should be identified with “Should Succeed”.
To add the null scenario, select the Virtual Subject Response, Explicitly Defined, Arm Response tab and click the “+ Add” button. Rename the Profile from “Resp 1” to “NullBase” by clicking and then typing “NullBase” in the Profiles dialog. In the Relative Proportions table, enter the values 1, 2, 4, 4, 2, 5, 2 as shown in Table 2 for this scenario, and enter 1, 1, 1, 1 for the odds ratios for Doses 1 through 4. Then follow the same procedure for the other scenarios, entering the data given in Table 2. Click the Should Succeed checkbox for the doses with odds ratios less than 0.75 (shown in bold in the table).

text:
3.4 Execution \(\mathbf{\rightarrow}\) Accrual
Move to the Execution: Accrual tab, and add an accrual scenario by clicking the Add button on the far left. Set the peak accrual rate to 6 participants per week. We intend accrual for the trial to last for about two years (104 weeks), so roughly 600 patients can be accrued in that time.
The names of the accrual profile and the region may be renamed by double-clicking on them.

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
3.5 Execution \(\mathbf{\rightarrow}\) Dropout Rate
On the Dropout Rate tab, click +Add to add a dropout scenario with no dropouts. If desired, a FACTS user can also specify different dropout rates for different arms.

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
3.6 Quantities of Interest
FACTS has considerable flexibility in allowing the user to define Quantities of Interest (QOIs) to drive adaptations in the trial and decisions at the end of the trial. A basic set of QOIs is provided by default. Additional QOIs may be added by clicking the Add row in the table. A QOI can be removed by clicking the X on the right side of the cell. Each QOI may be edited by clicking on it, which opens a pop-up box.
In this trial we will use the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test for the primary efficacy analysis. We will use predictive probabilities of significant results on this test to make decisions of early stopping for expected success. Response-adaptive randomization probabilities will be based on the Bayesian posterior probability that an arm has an odds ratio relative to control of 0.75 or better (smaller). Futility decisions will also be based on the probability of an odds ratio less than 0.75.
On the Quantities of Interest tab, first select 0.25 as the clinically significant difference (CSD) in the bottom Standard Evaluation Variables panel. This selection will allow us to compare odds ratios to 0.75: note that the top left Posterior Probabilities quantity of interest has changed to Pr(OR_d – 1<= -0.25) i.e. the probability that the d’th odds ratio is at least 0.25 smaller than 1, i.e. the probability that the d’th odds ratio is less than 0.75.

To enable the Wilcoxon(-Mann-Whitney) test, click on “Add…” in the p-values (Trt. vs Control) section (lower left). The Add Frequentist p-value dialog will appear. We will handle missing values by ignoring them. With no dropouts, this will not matter in the final analysis, which will be conducted after all enrolled patients have completed 13 weeks of follow-up. Select “Wilcoxon” as the Test Type.



A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect.


Next, we will enable predictive probabilities of the Wilcoxon test based on the current sample size after all patients complete follow-up. Under Predictive Probabilities, click on Add… and enter:

Type: Bayesian. (Conditional power capability will be added in a future release).
Phase: Current Trial. (Alternatively, one may predict the outcome of a separate two-arm phase-III-like trial).
Handle missingness using: Ignore. (One may also choose to impute missing data with the worst ordinal outcome. In a future release we will add the capability of predicting a final ordinal endpoint with an earlier observation of that same endpoint).
Test Type: Wilcoxon (We will discuss the other options below).
Sample Size: Current Enrollment. (The other option is the final sample size of the trial, here 600, but this option is only available in trials without response-adaptive randomization).
One-sided Alpha: 0.025.


We will also define an Operational Quantity of interest, a feature new as of FACTS 8.0. We want to insist that we are not stopping early for success based on optimism about an arm unless that arm has at least 50 patients enrolled. This will not be a very stringent requirement: it would prevent early stopping at the 200 patient analysis. At the 300 patient analysis, we intend 100 control patients and 200 experimental arm patients spread across the 4 experimental arms, so an experimental arm could have fewer than 50 patients if it had been underperforming relative to other arms at the 200 patient analysis. Click on Add… in the Operational Quantities area:

Now that we have defined the four quantities of interest that we will need, the next step is to promote them to be decision quantities that can be used in trial decisions. We will click on “Add…” in the Decision Quantities (Scalars) area (bottom right). First we will use Wilcoxon p-value corresponding to the arm with the Greatest Pr(Max), i.e. the arm that is the most likely to have the smallest odds ratio:

Next we will use the predictive probability of a significant Wilcoxon test, again for the arm that is most likely to have the smallest odds ratio. If this predictive probability is large enough, the trial will stop for expected success in anticipation of a significant final efficacy analysis.

We will use the largest Bayesian posterior probability that an arm has an odds ratio of 0.75 or better. If this probability is small, i.e. if all arms have small posterior probabilities of small enough odds ratios, the trial will stop for futility.

Finally we will use the number of patients enrolled for the Pr(Max) arm (arm with the highest probability of an odds ratio less than 0.75):

When the Quantities of Interest have been entered, the page should look like this:

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
3.7 Design

3.7.1 Dirichlet Model
We will use a noninformative Dirichlet prior distribution for the control probabilities. FACTS Ordinal’s default is to use exponents of 0.8 divided by the number of ordinal values, as recommended by Berger, Bernardo, and Sun in Bayesian Analysis 2015. One may use informative priors, for example by choosing the prior exponents to be data from a previous study.



3.7.2 Dose-Response Model
We will use a normal dynamic linear model, with the control arm included in the model. FACTS Ordinal includes many of the FACTS Core dose-response models, and it applies those models to the log odds ratios of the arms relative to control. By definition, the control arm has a log odds ratio of zero, so the normal dynamic linear model curve goes through the point (dose 0, log odds ratio 0). We will use a prior distribution for the smoothing parameter with center 0.2 and weight 4.



3.7.3 Allocation
We are going to use response-adaptive allocation, with the randomization probability for control fixed at 1/3, and with the experimental arms fighting over the remaining 2/3, based on their probabilities of an odds ratio less than 0.75.
On the Design: Allocation tab, check the Adaptive Allocation box. This will open up a table for defining randomization blocks and fixing the control probability. Enter 4, 2, 2, 2, 2 for the Pre First Interim Allocation Ratios, click on the Control’s “Fix Alloc.” box, and enter 4 for its Post First Interim Alloc. per Block. Also enter 12 as the Post First Interim block size. In this way, 4 out of every 12 subjects will be randomized to control, both prior to the first interim and after subsequent interims.
Now under Adaptive Allocation Targets, click Add, and select the Pr(OR_d – 1 <= -0.25) QOI. Weight for Probability and use Relative Weight 1, although these last two selections will have no effect because we are using only one adaptive allocation target.

If this allocation target gives an arm an allocation probability between 0 and 0.04, we will round it down to zero and renormalize the other experimental arm probabilities to make up the difference. Now the Allocation tab should be filled out like this:



3.7.4 Interims
In this trial that will randomize a maximum of 600 patients, we will conduct the first trial update when 200 subjects have been randomized, and every 100 patients thereafter.
On the Design:Interims tab, select “Subjects Enrolled” to define the measure of Subject Information: i.e. we will conduct analyses based on number of patients enrolled in the trial. Information can also be defined based on participants with Complete Data. (Opportunity to Complete is another option that can apply, and be different from Complete Data, when there are dropouts.) Select “Information” as the method for Specifying Interims, then click the +Add button four times to add four interim analysis, and enter 200, 300, 400, and 500 in the Subjects Enrolled column in the table.
Under “Subject Follow-Up Options After Early Decision”, check “Continue follow-up if study stops for early success” and uncheck “Continue follow-up if study stops for early futility.” If the trial stops early because of positive data, we will wait until final data are available before making a final efficacy claim, but if the trial stops for futility, we will not claim efficacy even if there is a dramatic turn-around while follow-up is being completed (binding futility).



3.7.5 Success/Futility Criteria
The Design:Success/Futility Criteria tab has a new design as of FACTS 8.0 to allow users to define more flexible criteria based on AND/OR logic. Previously, a criterion could only be defined to be satisfied if all of a set of simple criteria were satisfied (AND), or if at least one of the simple criteria was satisfied (OR). Now FACTS supports more complex combinations of criteria. For example, success can be declared if a posterior probability is greater than 0.95 and the sample size is less than 100, OR if the posterior probability is greater than 0.90 and the sample size is more than 100.
At any of the interim analyses, we will stop for futility if no dose has a sufficiently large (10%) probability of a treatment effect at least as good as an Odds Ratio of 0.75. We will stop for expected success if the Bayesian predictive probability of a significant Wilcoxon test conducted on the currently enrolled patients when they finish follow-up, is at least 90% for the arm that is the most likely to have the most favorable odds ratio, AND if the arm most likely to have the most favorable odds ratio has at least 50 patients randomized.
On the Design \(\mathbf{\rightarrow}\) Success/Futility Criteria tab, select the checkbox next to Enable advanced features. To define the futility rule, check the Early Futility Criteria checkbox, and click the +Add Criterion button. Then choose the following options from the drop-down menus in the popup dialog box as shown in the screenshot below:

For QOI, select “Pr(OR_d – 1 <= -0.25); d = Max probability over all doses
For Condition, select “<=”
For Threshold, enter “0.1”.


Next, to define the early success stopping rule, select the “Early Success Criteria” checkbox and click on the +Add Criterion button below it. In the pop-up dialog box, choose:

Pr(Succ. Current Trial): Ignore; Wilcoxon; Current Enrollment α=0.025; d=Greatest Pr(Max) for QOI;
> for Condition;
And enter 0.90 for Threshold.


Now, to insist that we only stop for expected success when the arm prompting the stop (the arm with the highest probability of having the most favorable odds ratio) has at least 50 patients enrolled, select/highlight the AND below “X Delete AND/OR Group” by clicking it, and click on +Add Criterion. Fill in the entries in the pop-up with:

QOI: select Num. Enrolled; d=Greatest Pr(Max)
Condition: >
Threshold:49.5. Since FACTS uses strict inequalities for > in stopping criteria, we need to enter a number strictly less than 50 if we want 50 to be the exact minimum allowed.


We will use the same stopping rules for all 4 interim analyses, although note that FACTS allows users to have different rules for each. For example, to introduce different stopping rules at interim 3, enter ‘3’ in the “Create new criteria at interim:” box and click “Create”.
The final analysis will be a Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test conducted at the 0.025 level and comparing the arm with the highest probability of having the most favorable odds ratio. We will define final futility so that it is the complement of final success, i.e. there will be no inconclusive final results.
Still on the Design \(\mathbf{\rightarrow}\) Success/Futility Criteria tab, select the “Final Evaluation” tab now that we are done with the Interim 1 tab. Under Late Futility Criteria, click on +Add Criterion and enter:

QOI: p-value; Ignore; Wilcoxon; d=Greatest Pr(Max)
Condition: >
Threshold: 0.025.

The trial’s final result is futility if the Wilcoxon p-value is more than 0.025 for the most likely best arm.

Under Late Success Criteria, click on +Add Criterion and enter:

QOI: p-value; Ignore; Wilcoxon; d=Greatest Pr(Max)
Condition: <=
Threshold: 0.025.

The trial’s final result will be a success in exactly the conditions where it is not a futility, namely when the most likely best arm has a Wilcoxon p-value less than 0.025.

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
3.8 Simulation
We are now ready to simulate the trial. Normally we recommend running a small number of simulations per scenario first to get fast feedback, and this is a time-consuming design to simulate, but we will skip to running 1000 simulations. Set the number of simulations to 1000, click “Select All” then press Simulate. When the simulations are complete, FACTS pops up a graphics window summarizing results across scenarios.

This Outcome graph shows the simulation-based estimates of the probabilities of each trial outcome in each scenario. The two green colors depict early and late success, so the combined heights of the two green sections give quick indications of the design’s power and Type I error. The three null scenarios are on the right of the graph and they have the smallest probability of trial success, clearly less than 10%. The “Flat Eff 60” scenario, where all four experimental arms have odds ratios of 0.6, has the highest power as expected, followed by the other scenario with a single 0.6 arm (Eff60Base).
More precise data about the operating characteristics are available in the table on the Simulation tab.

The “Ppn Overall Success” column reports the simulated power and Type I error estimates. The null scenarios have 7-8% success probability, which is a considerable amount of Type I error inflation relative to the 2.5% nominal level at which the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney tests were performed. It is not surprising that our design has inflated Type I error, because we allow it to choose the best performing of four experimental arms, and we allow early stopping for expected success which increases the risk of reacting to a temporary random high. This is an arbitrary example of a design, and whether a designer needs to rigorously reduce their Type I error depends on the application. Also, we recommend more than 1000 simulations to accurately estimate Type I error.
We also see that the standard efficacy scenario with treatment effects for the four arms that improve to an odds ratio of 0.65 are achieving approximately 70% power. If all four arms have odds ratios of 0.65, then the power is about 80%. With an odds ratio of 0.60, nearly 90% power is achieved when all four arms are that good, and about 80% when the effect sizes are 0.95, 0.85, 0.7, and 0.6. Of course the power numbers would be reduced if measures were taken to reduce Type I error such as reducing the level of the Wilcoxon test from 0.025. To convert this design into an adequate and well-controlled trial with 80% or 90% power, one would need to increase the sample size and/or target larger effect sizes.
By scrolling to the right in the table, we also see that early futility probabilities in the null scenario are only 35-39%, and often we would want more frequent futility. Recall that we require all four experimental arms to have less than a 10% probability of a hazard ratio less than 0.75. We could modify this rule to have more frequent futility. In many designs, we like to use the predictive probability of a significant final analysis assuming the maximum sample size, but this is not available in FACTS 8.0 for this design because we are using response-adaptive randomization and therefore cannot precisely predict the final sample sizes on each arm.
Returning to the graphs supplied by FACTS, consider the Selected Arms graph from the Across Scenario Graphs. Note that in all scenarios, the larger doses are more likely to be selected. This is as one would hope for the sloping efficacy scenarios. It is what one would expect for the flat (including the null) scenarios as well, because the prior distribution, a normal dynamic linear model that includes the control in the model, implies higher prior uncertainty about the treatment effect for the arms more distant from the control. If one wishes more even balance between the selected arms, one can use a different prior distribution family such as a hierarchical model.

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
4.3 Quantities of Interest
On the Quantities of Interest tab, as we were warned, the posterior probability QOIs were converted from comparisons of odds ratios to comparisons of expected utilities. Toward the bottom, enter 0.5 as the Clinically significant difference (CSD); this is a difference on the expected utility scale. (It turns out that an odds ratio of 0.78 compared to control is enough to increase expected utility by 0.5 if the control population has our usual probabilities). The Posterior Probability QOI in the upper left changes to incorporate the new CSD. Now we need to promote the new QOI to be a Decision Quantity so that we can use it in response-adaptive randomization and futility. Click on Add…in the table of Decision Quantities (Scalars) to call up the pop-up, choose Pr(EU_d – EU_(Control) > 0.5) and Max probability over all doses, then click Add.

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
4.4 Design: Dirichlet Model
Defining the statistical model in the Dirichlet case is straightforward, although it may be tedious to fill in desired values in the table. Where the cumulative logistic modeling framework required a Dirichlet prior distribution for the probabilities of the ordinal values for the control arm, here we specify one Dirichlet prior distribution for each arm. By default, FACTS uses prior exponents of 0.8 divided by the number of possible ordinal values. In our design we will just use the defaults.

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
4.5 Design: Allocation
Since we were previously using cumulative logistic odds ratios for adaptive allocation, that Adaptive Allocation Target will have disappeared and we will need to replace it with one based on expected utility. On the Design:Allocation tab, click to Add and Adaptive Allocation Target, and choose Pr(EU_d – EU_(Control) > 0.5). Arms will receive allocation probability to the extent that they have high posterior probabilities of increasing expected utility by at least 0.5 units relative to control.

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
4.6 Design: Success/Futility Criteria
We were also previously using the posterior probability of a benefit in log odds ratio to decide whether to stop for futility, and this is no longer available with Dirichlet modeling, so we need to replace this criterion as well. Under Design: Success/Futility Criteria, on the Interim 1 tab, under Early Futility Criteria, click on +Add Criterion. In the pop-up window, choose:

QOI: Pr(EU_d – EU_(Control) > 0.5); d=Max probability over all doses
Condtion: <=
Threshold: 0.10

title: Ordinal Endpoint
text:
4.7 Simulation
And now we can return to the Simulation tab and simulate the new design. Select All scenarios, and click on Simulate. After 1000 simulations of each scenario we get results like those shown below. The new Nonproportional scenario has low power of 21.4%: it is appropriate that its power is low because the experimental arms are not clearly beneficial, with higher probabilities of very good values but also higher probability of death. The expected utilities for the experimental arms are not much different from the control arm.
When compared to the previous design with cumulative logistic modeling, this design appears to have slightly higher power but that includes higher Type I error. In the null scenarios, the Dirichlet-based design has considerably higher expected sample size (around 548 compared to around 500) and lower probability of early futility (16-19% compared to 36-39%). These differences are to be expected: the Dirichlet design treats all arms independently, while the cumulative logistic design exploits a longitudinal model to smooth the treatment effects. In this way, the cumulative logistic design can more easily determine that all four experimental arms have low probabilities of substantial benefits compared to control, and more easily stop for futility. Also, the dose-response model will dampen down random highs in one of the four arms and reduce Type I error compared to the Dirichlet model with independent arms. In practice, the Dirichlet design would most likely be modified to have more frequent early futility, and both designs would be tweaked to have operating characteristics commensurate with the goals of the planned trial.
