text:
4.1 Study

4.1.1 Study Info
The Study tab captures basic information about the trial. Set the following parameters:

Select the Non-adaptive option: since this tutorial is focused on the modeling options, adaptive features will not be used.
Clear the “Use longitudinal model” check box. No intermediate outcomes are observed for patients.
Set the time to final endpoint to 26 weeks.
Set the accrual to “Continuously.”
Set the maximum number of subjects to 200.
Select “Response indicates positive outcome.”




4.1.2 Treatment Arms
Set the following parameters:

Select the box “Include a control treatment arm.”
Select the box “Use 2D treatment arm model.” This selection adds two panels to the screen to allow the set up of dosing according to two factors. Only when this selection is chosen will the 2D dose response model options be available.
Add 3 column factor levels with effective column strengths of 0.5, 1, and 1.5 to represent the atmospheric pressure options. Note that the Control is already chosen with an effective strength of 0, though it corresponds to an ATA of 1.0. Thus, we are selecting effective column strengths based on the ATA difference from control.

Change the column names to “Ctrl (ATA 1.0),” “ATA 1.5,” “ATA 2.0,” and “ATA 2.5.”

Add 2 row factor levels with effective row strengths of 0 and 1, to represent the without and with NBH options

Change the row names to “No NBH” and “With NBH.”


At this point, the screen should look like the following. Look at the right panel of the screen, labeled “Dose Combinations.” All combinations of column and row factors are listed in the left column of that panel.


One by one, click the “Use” box next to each dose combination in the left column of the Dose Combinations panel. After use click on Use for the dose combination, the Effective Dose Strength column becomes visible. Edit the effective dose strengths so that: Ctl (ATA 1.0); No NBH = 0, ATA 1.5; No NBH = 2.6, ATA 2.0; No NBH = 4.17, ATA 2.5; No NBH = 5.92, Ctl (ATA 1.0); With NBH = 5.4, ATA 1.5; With NBH = 6.4, ATA 2.0; With NBH =7.76, and ATA 2.5; With NBH = 9.52.
Note: since the “Include a control arm” is selected at the top of this tab, the treatment arm with an effective column strength of 0 and the lowest allowed value for the column strength is considered the control arm. In this case, that is the Ctl (ATA 1.0); No NBH arm.
Note: after the effective dose strengths are entered. The right column of the Dose Combinations panel shows the ordering of the doses that are used in the trial (not all column and row factor combinations need be selected), ordered according to the effective dose strength. Graphs will be plotted with this ordering for the doses, and quantities of interest that depend on order (i.e., MED and EDq) utilize this ordering.
Note: when a dose combination is selected for use, its default effective dose strength is the sum of the effective column strength for the column factor and effective row strength for the row factor. These are intended only as starting values and should be edited to match the expected combination strength. Ties in effective dose strength are not allowed, so each combination must be given a unique strength value.

text:
4.3 External Files
There are no externally generated data for this example.

title: Two-Dimensional Dosing (Dichotomous)
text:
4.4 Execution

4.4.1 Accrual
Since no adaptive features are being used, accrual rate only contributes to trial duration for the purposes of this tutorial. Add one profile with an average accrual of 10/week.



4.4.2 Dropout Rate
Select “No Dropouts”.

title: Two-Dimensional Dosing (Dichotomous)
text:
4.5 Quantities of Interest
The Quantities of Interest (QOIs) are the criteria on which decisions, interim or final analyses, will be made. Numerous QOIs are available and you may select multiple quantities for evaluation. A basic set of QOIs is provided by default. Additional QOIs may be added by clicking the Add row in the table. A QOI can be removed by clicking the X on the right side of the cell. Each QOI may be edited by clicking on it, which opens a pop-up box.
The primary goal of this trial is to find the most effective treatment arm to carry to Phase III, and to trigger the initiation of the Phase III trial only with sufficient evidence to potential success.
The treatment arm that has the highest probability of being the maximally effective treatment arm, Pr(Max), is the arm at which potential Phase III success will be judged. Two decision QoIs based on that dose will be used to determine trial success:

Pr(P_d > P_(Ctrl (ATA 1.0); No NBH))
Pr(Succ. Future Trial; N=500; Sup. α=0.025; δ=0)

The former of these, the posterior probability of beating control, is available by default. There is a Pr(Succ. Future Trial) QoI set up by default as well, though it must be edited to match the Phase III sample size desired. Click on the Pr(Succ. Future Trial) predictive probability QoI. Set Phase to Future Trial, Test Type to Superiority, Subjects per Arm to 500, One-sided Alpha to 0.025, and Superiority Margin to 0.

In this trial, there is no need to establish the notions of a minimally effective dose (MED) nor a treatment arm that’s at least q% as good as the maximally effective dose (EDq). However, they will be explored briefly in this tutorial in order to demonstrate the effect of the 2D dosing structure on such quantities. Both of these quantities require an ordering to the dose strengths in order to be well-defined. The ordering used is the effective dose strength that is established in the Dose Combinations panel of the Study > Treatment Arms tab. This trial also has no meaningful definition for a clinically significant difference, but for the sake of constructing an example, a value of 0.14 is used to match the “should succeed” criterion established with the VSR. Setting the CSD to 0.14 on the bottom of the QoI tab will automatically update the default MED QoI. Click on the Pr(EDq relative to Ctrl (ATA 1.0) QoI, and change the quantile to 0.8.
Two decision QoIs are needed. Click on “Add…” under the Decision Quantities (Scalars) panel to add one. First select the posterior probability of beating control QoI and evaluate it at the Greatest Pr(Max) dose. Then add a second decision QoI by selecting the predictive probability for a future trial and evaluating it at the Greatest Pr(Max) dose.
 
The finished QoI tab looks like this:

title: Two-Dimensional Dosing (Dichotomous)
text:
4.6 Design

4.6.1 Dose Response
For the first version of the design, we will use one of 2D dose response models – the 2D Continuous Factorial model. This approach models the log-odds of response as an additive linear model, treating the column effective strength values as a continuous covariate and the row effective strength values as a continuous covariate. There is an option for an interaction term as well, but we will not use that option in this example.
We will need to assign prior distributions to the parameters of the dose response model. In practice, the construction of the priors should be assisted by subject matter experts. For purposes of this tutorial, relatively non-informative priors were used, with an attempt to match the spirit of the priors in the Gajewski paper. Since analysis will only be performed for a complete data set, the non-informative priors should have relatively minor effect on the final analysis, though expert-informed priors would likely perform better.
Select the ‘2D Continuous Factorial Model’ option.

Under Model Parameters, uncheck the box for “Include Interaction Term.”
For α0, enter a mean of -0.41 (which is the logit of a nominal response rate of 40%) and a SD of 1. This parameter corresponds to the dose response for an effective column strength of 0 and an effective row strength of 0, which for this example corresponds to the control treatment arm. However, in this trial, the control arm represents a natural environment with variability in natural conditions, so it will be modeled separately [see below].
For α1 and α2, enter a mean of 0.0 with a standard deviation of 1. This represents an a priori assumption of no treatment effect, but with a moderate amount of uncertainty. A positive value of α1 corresponds to an increase in the response rate as the effective column strength increases. A positive value of α2 corresponds to an increase in the response rate as the effective row strength increases.
Check the box “Model Control Separately.” Select Fixed Prior and enter a mean of -0.41 and an SD of 0.75. This represents the a priori knowledge of the response rate for the control arm.
The Handling of Missing Data Due to Dropouts selection will not matter, since no dropouts are being simulated.




4.6.2 Frequentist Analysis
We do not require a frequentist analysis, to save run-time we ensure that all the options for handling missingness are de-selected. In particular we ensure that the option to calculate Dunnetts adjusted p-values is de-selected (this has a particularly high runtime overhead and should only be selected if required).



4.6.3 Allocation
Set all the allocation ratio to 39 for the control arm (Ctrl (ATA 1.0); No NBH) and to 23 for the remaining treatment arms. The control arm thus has more information than any single treatment arm, though the treatment arms will share information through the dose response model.



4.6.4 Success/Futility Criteria
The success criteria will be defined by two criteria:

the dose most likely to be max response has a greater than P posterior probability that its response is better than Control. The value of P will be adjusted separately for each dose response model considered, to give 10% type I error under the null hypothesis. For the 2D Continuous Factorial model P=0.955.
and the dose most likely to be max response has a greater than 0.5 predictive probability of winning a future Phase III trial with N=500.

Set the following parameters for Success Criteria:
1st Criterion

Select the QOI: Pr(θ_d - θ_(Ctrl (Ata 1.0); No NBH)); d=Greatest Pr(Max)
Select a Condition of >
Enter a threshold of 0.955

2nd Criterion

Select the QOI: Pr(Succ. Future Trial): N=500; Sup. α=0.025; δ=0; d=Greatest Pr(Max)
Select a Condition of >
Enter a threshold of 0.5

Select: Combine criteria using: AND
We will define the futility criteria as the exact complement of these. Set the following parameters for Failure Criteria:
1st Criterion

Select the QOI: Pr(θ_d - θ_(Ctrl (Ata 1.0); No NBH)); d=Greatest Pr(Max)
Select a Condition of <
Enter a threshold of 0.955

2nd Criterion

Select the QOI: Pr(Succ. Future Trial): N=500; Sup. α=0.025; δ=0; d=Greatest Pr(Max)
Select a Condition of <
Enter a threshold of 0.5

Select: Combine criteria using: OR

title: Two-Dimensional Dosing (Dichotomous)
text:
4.7 Setting the dose selection criteria
As we have indicated on the Virtual Subject Response profiles which doses “should succeed”, FACTs will summarize for us how often one of these doses is actually selected. In order to do this correctly, we need to indicate to FACTS which Target QoI we will be using to select the dose to go forward. Here it is the Pr(Max) [which is FACTS default]. This is specified on the Study > Variants tab (even though we are not defining any variants).

title: Two-Dimensional Dosing (Dichotomous)
text:
4.8 Simulation
To get an initial check on the design set up, set the number of simulations to run to 100, Select All, the press Simulate.
If the results look reasonable, increase the number of simulations to run to 1000. Select All and then press Simulate again.
To achieve more precise estimates of the operating characteristics, we may need to run 10,000 or more simulations of a scenario. By default, FACTS simulations run locally on your computer, which for this simple fixed design is likely to take a few seconds to run 1000 simulations. If you have access to a computer grid and your FACTS installation has been correctly configured to use it, you may use the grid’s parallel computing capabilities to improve computation speed. To do so, select “on Grid.”


4.8.1 Results
The success/futility thresholds were adjusted to provide a type-1 error of approximately 10%, which can be seen from the Ppn Late Success column for the Null scenario. The power is high (>90%) for all scenarios except one, the overdose scenario. However, declaration of success in a trial is only good if the selected dose was a good selection. To explore this, we will look at some graphs of model fits and dose selection. On the Simulations tab, click on View Graph and select the Show Across Scenario Graphs Option.
The first across scenario graph shows the dose selection for each scenario. Note that a lot of information is being displayed in this graph, and you may need to adjust to a full screen view to be able to see details. There may be insufficient room for all of the treatment arm labels to show across the x-axis. The treatment arms are ordered in the same order as presented on the Virtual Subject Response tab. The scenarios will have been re-ordered alphabetically by scenario name.

The blue bars in these plots indicate a successful trial that selected of a good treatment arm – one that was listed as “Should Succeed” on the Virtual Subject Response tab. The red bars indicate a successful trial that selected a treatment arm that should not have succeeded. The light blue bars indicate the dose selection in unsuccessful trials.
For four of the scenarios, this design generally selected a good treatment arm. However, it is not always selecting the best treatment arm. Below is the same graph if we had defined “should succeed” as only the best arm rather than any arm with response rate > 0.55.

In particular, note that it never selects the correct arm for the Disc. Factorial setting. A careful examination shows that in fact the model only ever picks one of 4 treatment arms. This is due to the linearity assumption of the model. Since there is no interaction term in the model, the only doses that can be selected are doses that are on the corners of the 2D grid – either the highest or lowest on column strength and row strength.
To see how well the model does on average for the various scenarios, select the Response graph.

This graph overlays the mean fitted response from the model along with the true values for the scenarios. For the Cont. Factorial scenario and the Null scenario, the fits line up very well with the response, since the true values correspond to scenarios where the VSR truth corresponds exactly to the 2D continuous factorial model, for appropriately chosen parameters. There are two scenarios where no model parameters are good at approximating the true VSR – the Disc. Factorial where the column strength (ATA) is not linear (nor monotonic) and the Overdose scenario which deviates greatly from the linearity/monotonicity assumption. For the Overdose scenario, the model tends to fit a negative value for both α1 and α2, due to the extremely poor response rate for the highest combination doses. As such, it tends to select the lowest dose: ATA 1.5; No NBH as the Pr(Max), when in truth that treatment arm has lower response than control. Over 30% of the time, the trial is being declared successful and selecting this arm. If this scenario is a realistic scenario, this may indicate a substantive problem with using this model for this design.
We can take a closer look at the Disc. Factorial scenario by selecting its row on the Simulations tab, then selecting View Graph > Show Per Scenario Graphs. Click on the Response and Target Selection Graph. For the target of Pr(Max), we see a more detailed view of what was shown above in the across scenarios graph.

An option to help see the two-dimensional structure of the fits is to click on the checkbox “Show row factors as separate series.” With this option, each level of the row factor is plotted with connected lines across the column factors. In the plot below, the linear structure of the continuous factorial model is much easier to see when separated out by row.

It does not make sense in the context of this example to use an EDq target rather than the Pr(Max), as toxicity from overdosing is not a concern – the dichotomous response already accounts for overdosing response. But for the sake of demonstrating the quantity in the context of 2D dosing, we will examine the ED80 selection for this scenario.

The ED80 dose is the lowest dose that achieves at least 80% of the response of the best treatment arm. Here, lowest refers to the effective dose strength defined for the dose combinations. The graph shows the treatment arms in increasing order of the effective combination dose. Had we used the ED80 as the dose selection option, we then have a chance to choose arms other than the 4 that the Pr(Max) chooses. In this example, while the continuous factorial model tends to make the ATA 2.5; With NBH arm the best dose, but occasionally, the fitted α1 term is small enough to indicate that the ATA 2.0; With NBH arm is nearly as good, and since it is lower in combination dose strength, it is chosen as the ED80. And sometimes, when ATA 2.5; No NBH is selected as the Pr(Max) arm, the Ctrl (ATA 1.0); With NBH arm is selected as the ED80, since in terms of combination effective dose strength, it is a lower effective dose than ATA 2.5; No NBH.

title: Two-Dimensional Dosing (Dichotomous)
text:

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
4.5 Quantities of Interest
The Quantities of Interest (QOIs) are the criteria on which decisions, interim or final analyses, will be made. Numerous QOIs are available and you may select multiple quantities for evaluation. A basic set of QOIs is provided by default. Additional QOIs may be added by clicking the Add row in the table. A QOI can be removed by clicking the X on the right side of the cell. Each QOI may be edited by clicking on it, which opens a pop-up box.
Recall that one of the aims of the trial is to select an effective dose, but not a dose that is higher in strength than necessary. We will attempt to achieve this by selecting the dose that has 90% of the maximum treatment effect – the ED90.
Thus the trial will be judged a success if at the end of the trial if:

the dose most likely to be ED90 has a greater than 90% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Control by at least 0.1 (the clinically significant difference).
and the dose most likely to be ED90 has a greater than 90% posterior probability that its mean improvement better than the Active Comparator.

We set the default Clinically Significant Difference to 0.1. This is then applied to the default QoI that tests dose response against Control with a CSD and it is used for the delta in the definition of the MED target QOI.
We will be using the target QoI: Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=0.9), this is present by default.
These two default QoIs can be deleted:

Pr(θ_d > θ_(Control))
Pr(Succ. Future Trial)

We now to create two “Decision” QoI’s. The Posterior Probability QoI’s are evaluated for each arm, (as would be any predictive probability or p-value QoIs, to use these in a decision we need to pick one, to do this we use a Target QoI. Thus, to enable us to implement the two success criteria above we define two decision QoIs:

Both using the dose with the greatest probability of being the ED90, one using its posterior probability of beating Control by the CSD, the other using it posterior probability of beating the Active Comparator.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
4.6 Design

4.6.1 On Setting Priors
On setting priors – as a rule it is recommended that the user specifies weakly informative priors rather than non-informative ones. There are a number of reasons for this:

In a few circumstances non-informative priors can end up being informative.
What values make a prior non-informative vary depending on the range of the value being estimated, a measure with a SD of 1000 requires quite a different value for a prior to be non-informative than one with an SD of 1.
Measures that are log-odds or log hazard ratios can have parameters that are then exponentiated and used as parameters to other distributions as a maximum these values should have range of (-10,10) and (-5,5). Greater than this and numeric overflows can occur.
Using a “non-informative” prior can sometimes be used as an excuse for not thinking about the prior. Not thinking about a prior is never a good idea.
There are some priors, particularly for the variance parameters of hierarchical models where (as we use inverse Gamma distributions for the priors, weakly informative priors are preferred to uninformative ones [Gelman 2006, “Prior distributions for variance parameters in hierarchical models” Bayesian Analysis Vol 1 Number 3]
When simulating clinical trial designs there is a balance to be struck between the MCMC sample length used in the within-trial analyses and the number of simulations run. Weakly informative priors can help the MCMC to converge and allow us to use shorter sample lengths.

For many priors the weakly informative is easily judged where the priors directly correspond to values that we are simulating. Others are not so easily judged, for these we used “non-informative” priors ran some simulations and looked at the means and SDs of the posterior estimates of the parameters over all the scenarios and then based a weakly informative prior on these. You will see these priors below being described as having an “initial un-informative” prior and then a weakly informative one. Care must be taken with this approach to not over specify a prior based on the selection of scenarios, and it must be borne in mind that the scenarios may not capture the full potential variability in what the “truth value in nature” might actually be.


4.6.2 Dose Response
For the fixed design we do not want a dose response model; that is, we model each arm independently. Select the ‘Independent Dose Model’ option, this option does not do dose response modeling.

Select the same prior for all doses and set the prior mean to 0 (the expected response on the control arm – so the prior is conservative) and the standard deviation of the prior to 1 (5 times the expected SD of the response – so the prior is very weak) .
For the Active Comparator, set the prior mean to 0.1 (the expected response of the Active Comparator) and the standard deviation to 1 (5 times the expected SD of the response – so the prior is very weak).
Set the prior mean for sigma to 0.2 (the expected SD of the response) and the number of observations weight for the prior to 1 (so the prior is weak, equivalent to a singe subject’s responses and the impact of the prior on the final posterior will be negligible). Note that the inverse-gamma distribution is parameterized in terms of mean and weight. If you prefer to see the standard alpha and beta parameters, click the Settings menu at the top of the screen. Select Options and a pop-up window appears. Navigate to the tab for Gamma Distribution Parameters, and toggle the radio button to Show Alpha and Beta.




4.6.3 Frequentist Analysis
We do not require a frequentist analysis, to save run-time we ensure that all the options for handling missingness are de-selected. In particular we ensure that the option to calculate Dunnetts adjusted p-values is de-selected (this has a particularly high runtime overhead and should only be selected if required).



4.6.4 Allocation
Set all the allocation ratios to 1 for all doses. (We could marginally increase the power of the trial by allocating more to the Control and Active Comparator – the rule of thumb is that if there are N treatment arms then the highest power occurs at an allocation ratio of √N:1:1:… with 3 arms study arms this can be approximated by 5:3:3:3:5. However this means we’d allocate less than half the study subjects to the study arms reducing the other data that we might wish to analyze post trial).



4.6.5 Success/Futility Criteria
As stated above, the trial will be judged a success if at the end of the trial:

the dose most likely to be ED90 has a greater than 90% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Control plus the clinically significant difference of 0.1.
and the dose most likely to be ED90 has a greater than 90% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Active Comparator.

Set the following parameters for Success Criteria:
1st Criteria
Click the Add row, then:

Select the QOI: Pr(θ_d - θ_(Control)>0.1); d=Greatest Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=0.9)
Select a Condition of >
Enter a threshold of 0.90

2nd Criteria
Cick the Add row, then:

Select the QOI: Pr(θ_d > θ_(AC)); d=Greatest Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=0.9)
Select a Condition of >
Enter a threshold of 0.90

Select: Combine criteria using: AND
We could define the futility criteria as the exact compliment of these, but instead we’ll use more stringent futility criteria and leave a possible band of “inconclusive” outcome.
We will define the trial as futile if:

the dose most likely to be ED90 has a less than 50% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Control plus the clinically significant difference of 0.1.
OR the dose most likely to be ED90 has a less than 50% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Active Comparator.

Set the following parameters for Futility Criteria:
1st Criteria
Click the Add row, then:

Select the QOI: Pr(θ_d - θ_(Control)>0.1); d=Greatest Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=0.9)
Select a Condition of <
Enter a threshold of 0.50

2nd Criteria
Click the Add row, then:

Select the QOI: Pr(θ_d > θ_(AC)); d=Greatest Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=0.9)
Select a Condition of <
Enter a threshold of 0.50

Select: Combine criteria using: OR

Thus, either criteria need to be met for the trial to be deemed a failure, and both criteria need to be met for the trial to be declared a success. Anything in between and we will deem the trial is inconclusive.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
4.7 Setting the dose selection criteria
As we have indicated on the Virtual Subject Response profiles which doses “should succeed”, FACTs will summarize for us how often one of these doses is actually selected. In order to do this correctly, we need to indicate to FACTS which Target QoI we will be using to select the dose to go forward. Here it is the ED90. This is specified on the Study > Variants tab (even though we are not defining any variants).

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
4.8 Simulation
To get an initial check on the design set up, set the number of simulations to run to 100, Select All, then press Simulate.
If the results look reasonable, increase the number of simulations to run to 1000. Select All and then press Simulate again.
To achieve more precise estimates of the operating characteristics, we will need to run 1,000 or 10,000 (or more) simulations of a scenario. By default, FACTS simulations run locally on your computer, which for this simple fixed design is likely to take ~10 seconds to run 100 simulations, and running 1,000s will take proportionately longer. If you have access to a computer grid and your FACTS installation has been correctly configured to use it, you may use the grid’s parallel computing capabilities to improve computation speed. To do so, select “on Grid.”




4.8.1 Results
Results can be compared between the designs in terms of

Type 1 and type 2 errors.
Correct selection of the ED90
Trial size.

The type-1 and type-2 errors seem well controlled:

On the ineffective, flat scenario there are no type 1 errors (trials that end up successful): out of the 100 simulated trials, there are 0 successes, and the Ppn Late Futility=1. Note, however, that more simulations would be required to precisely estimate this small proportion.
On the effective scenarios, how many trials are successful (power). Here the power is very high, the Ppn Late Success is 0.98 for both the early and late scenarios. Again more simulations would be required to estimate the power accurately but even with just 100 sims given that success rate we’d be confident the design has good power.

How well do we select the correct dose? As we checked the “Should Succeed” boxes on the Virtual Subject Response tab, and specified the dose selection QoI on the Variant tab, the simulation result columns “Ppn Correct Arm” and “Ppn Incorrect Arm” will tell us how often the dose we would have liked to be selected, was selected. These columns are far over on the right of the results columns.



We can also see the distribution of the ED90 selection numerically and graphically.
The results are availably numerically by clicking on “Show Other Columns” and selecting “Probabilities”, on the new table of results displayed, scroll to find the columns for the proportion (Ppn) of simulations a dose is the ED90 relative to Control. Here we see that for the flat scenarios the probabilities are similar because the doses are similar. For the “early” scenario, our preferred dose, Dose 10, is only selected as the ED90 at about 35% of the time. For the “late”scenario, our preferred dose, Dose 16, is selected with near certainty.



Graphically these can be seen by clicking on “View Graph”, selecting “Show per Scenario Graphs”, then selecting the “Response and Target Selection” graph, and set the “Quantity” displayed to the ED90 QoI.

Thus, though the design has good overall power, it is doing a poor job of dose selection, with a high probability of selecting the highest dose, even when there is reasonable dose response at the middle dose.
It may be possible to improve this design by modifying the selection criteria (the target QoI), but for brevity we’ll do that in the context of the more complex design.

5.3 Quantities of Interest
We will need to evaluate how well a range of target QoIs perform at selecting the correct doses.

For example, need to add to the Probability of being Target window:

Target Type: MED
Response Relation: Relative to:

Control

For each of these new target QoI’s we want to add decision QoIs that use them to select from the Pr(θ_d - θ_(Control) > 0.1) posterior probabilities and the Pr(θ_d > θ_(AC)) posterior probabilities.

This results in a large number of Decision QoIs

But apart from generating a lot of data columns in the output files there is no appreciable cost to this, and upon running the simulations, we will be able to evaluate a lot of target QoI options.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
5.4 Dose Response Model
If the response for the ith subject given dose d at week 8 is Y8i:
\[Y_{8i} \sim N\left(\theta_d, \sigma^2\right) \text{ for } d = 0,1,\ldots,17\]
We will model the mean response using a sigmoid (Emax) model:
\[\theta_d = a_1 + \left(\frac{\left(a_2 - a_1\right) v_d^{a_4}}{v_d^{a_4} + a_3^{a_4}}\right) \text{ for } d = 0,\ldots,16\]
Where a1 is the response at the lowest modeled dose, a2 some maximal response that is approached asymptotically, a3 is the dose level at which half the increase from a1 to a2 is observed, and a4 is a parameter defining the slope.
Bearing in mind this interpretation of the parameters, the priors for the model parameters are set to:
\[a_1 \sim N(0,1),\ a_2 \sim N(0.1,1)\]
\(a_{3}\sim N^{+}(8,8)\),
\[a_4 \sim N^{+}\left(10,10\right)\]
The priors for a1 and a2 (the min and the max of the sigmoid) are set to weak priors (SD=1) centered on the expected response of the Control and Active Comparator respectively.
The prior for a3 (the ED50 dose) is centered on the middle of the dose range (0-16) with SD=<half the dose range> so that the bulk of the prior mass lies within the dose range. If the prior for this parameter is set too broadly relative to the dose range being explored, then there can be a tendency for the posterior to contain a significant mass outside the dose range.
The prior for a4 is allowed to take a wide range of values relative to the expected change in response relative to the dose values to allow steep gradients at high doses to be within the prior.
And prior for the response on the Active Comparator (which is excluded from the model):
\[\theta_{AC} \sim N\left(0.10,1\right)\]
This is the same prior for the AC as used in the initial design.
And prior for the error variance:
\[\sigma_\mu = 0.2,\ \sigma_n = 1\]
This is the same prior for the estimate of the SD of the response as used in the initial design.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
5.5 Design
To add the dose response model, we make changes to the Design, Dose Response tab.

5.5.1 Dose Response
Set the following parameters:

Select the Sigmoidal model
For the prior distributions for the 4 parameters a1-a4 set

Λ1 = 0, λ1 = 1
Λ2 = 0.1, λ2 = 1
Λ3 = 8, λ3 = 8
Λ4 = 10, λ4 = 10

Control is NOT modeled separately; it is part of the dose response curve. We assume it is a dose of 0.
For the Comparator, the prior mean Is 0.1, the Std Dev of the prior mean is 1
Sigma prior mean = 0.2, and prior weight in terms of number of observations = 1.




5.5.2 Frequentist Analysis
Frequentist analysis is left disabled with no “handle missingness” options enabled.


5.5.3 Fitting a Longitudinal Model
The relationship between a subject’s final response and their intermediate responses is modeled using a simple linear regression model. During the course of the trial we fit three separate model instances, one for control treated patients, one for those on Active Comparator and one for all those on a dose of the study drug.
Using m to indicate the model (m=1,2,3: Control, Study Drug, Active Comparator) and t to indicate the visits before the final (t = weeks 1-7), we assume that the expected response at the final visit is linearly related to the response at visit t:
\[Y_8 \sim N\left(\alpha_{mt} + \beta_{mt} Y_t, \lambda_t^2\right) \quad m = 1,2,3;\ t = 1,\ldots,7\]
\[\alpha_{mt} \sim N(0,1) \quad m = 1,2,3;\ t = 1,\ldots,7\]
\[\beta_{mt} \sim N\left(0,1\right) \quad m = 1,2,3;\ t = 1,\ldots,7\]
\[\lambda_{mt}\ \sim IG(0.2,1)m = 1,2,3;t = 1,\ldots,7\]
\[IG\ parameters\ are\ mean\ and\ weight\ \]
Set the following parameters:

Select the Model: Linear Regression
Select to model Control and Active Comparator separately
Set the prior mean for the alphas (the fixed change from the response at the visit to final response) αμ = 0, with an SD = 1 (the prior centered on no change, but with an SD 5 times the expected response, so a very weak prior).
Set the prior mean for the Betas (the proportionate change in the response at the visit to the final response) βμ = 0 with an SD = 1, (the prior centered on no change, but with an SD 5 times the expected response, so a very weak prior).
Set the prior for the Lambdas (the residual error) to a mean = 0.2, and weight in terms of equivalent number of observations = 1 (the prior for the estimate of the SD of the final response).




5.5.4 Allocation
We will initially allocate 20 subjects each onto Control, dose 5, 10, 16 and Active Comparator. Then adaptive allocate to the doses closest to being the MED (delta of 0.1) and the ED90.
On the allocation tab we select “Adaptive Allocation”.
To do this we put the allocation ratio at 1 for each of the 5 arms we want to allocate to initially, and 0 for the rest. (The fact that it’s the first 100 subjects that will follow this fixed assignment will be set on the next tab – “Interims”).
After the first interim allocation will be adaptive across the study doses biased towards those that are most likely to be the desired targets. We will also allocate adaptively to Control – after each interim this will set the proportion to allocate to Control to be equal to the study drug with the highest proportion of allocation. Thus at the end of the trial the allocation to Control and the target dose will be roughly equal. In FACTS currently there is no such option for the Active Comparator, so we fix the allocation to this at 1 in 10.
Our Adaptive Allocation Targets will be the MED and ED90. We will adjust the randomization probabilities every four weeks allocating to the study drug doses in proportion to the information gained about the MED and ED90, and allocating adaptively to Control and 10% to the Active Comparator. To fix allocation to AC at 10% we select Fix Alloc. and for Post First Interim Alloc. per Block enter 1 and we set the post first interim block size to 10, and 1/10 is 10%. Thus, for each block, 1 subject will be allocated to the AC, and the remainder of the block allocated adaptively.
Set additional parameters:

Add Adaptive Allocation Targets QOI: Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=0.9)

Weight For: Information

We chose to weight for information because it is less aggressive on the adjusting of the randomization probabilities compared to weighting for probability. Either may be used.

Relative weight: 1 because we want to target the ED90 and MED equally.

Add Adaptive Allocation Targets QOI: Pr(MED relative to Control: Delta=0.1)

Weight For: Information

We chose to weight for information because it is less aggressive on the adjusting of the randomization probabilities compared to weighting for probability. Either may be used.

Relative weight: 1 because we want to target the ED90 and MED equally.




As there are a lot of doses, set the Allocation probability set to zero for values less than: 0



Set Raise allocation to power: 1

If you choose a power less than 1 the adaptive randomization will be less aggressive. Different options could be examined.





5.5.5 Interims
On the Design-Interims tab we specify the timing and frequency of the interim analyses.
Select the following parameters:

Set the Subject Information Defined By to Subjects Enrolled
Set the Specify Interims By: to Time

Set the Time to every 4 weeks
Set First interim at 100 subjects

Ensure that “Follow-up if study stopped for futility” is de-selected – we won’t be specifying early success stopping so it is immaterial how the follow up if stopped for success is set.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
5.6 Success/Futility Criteria
Under Design-Success/Futility Criteria we specify the criteria for early stopping for futility as well as the final evaluation criteria.

5.6.1 Interim 1 Criteria
On this tab we specify the interim analyses criteria for early stopping of accrual. In this example we keep the same criteria across all interims. If we wanted to have different criteria for different interims we would select Create new interim criteria at interim and specify the interim where criteria changes.
Stop accrual early for futility if there are at least 100 subjects randomized and

the dose most likely to be ED90 has a less than 10% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Control plus 0.1, the clinically significant difference
OR the dose most likely to be ED90 has a less than 10% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Active Comparator.

Select the following parameters

Select Futility Criteria
Add a QOI:

Select Pr(θ_d - θ_(Control)>0.1); d=Greatest Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=0.9)
Select a Condition of <
Enter a threshold of 0.10




Add a second QOI:

Select the QOI: Pr(θ_d > θ_(AC)>0.05); d=Greatest Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=0.9)
Set Condition <
Set Threshold 0.10




Select Combine criteria using: OR. The trial will only stop if either criteria is met.
Set Minimum Information Required to be 100 total subjects enrolled (this is not strictly necessary as the first interim is not until 100 subjects are enrolled).
Set the Evaluation Dose to be Greatest Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=90)

Set the Minimum Number of Subjects Enrolled to be 20, this is the minimum number of subjects on the arm with the greatest probability of being the ED90.


We will not stop accrual early for success.



5.6.2 Final Evaluation
The Final Evaluation has not changed from the fixed design. The same criteria, restated below, will be used to determine success and futility.
The trial will be judged a success if at the end of the trial:

the dose most likely to be ED90 has a greater than 90% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Control plus 0.1, the clinically significant difference.
AND the dose most likely to be ED90 has a greater than 90% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Active Comparator.

We will define the trial as futile if:

the dose most likely to be ED90 has a less than 50% posterior probability that its mean improvement better than Control plus 0.1, the clinically significant difference.
OR the dose most likely to be ED90 has a less than 50% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Active Comparator.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
5.7 Simulation
Similar to the fixed design, we set the number of simulations to run to 100 for an initial check, Select All, the press Simulate.
If the results look reasonable (the design has been entered correctly), increase the number of simulations to run to 1,000 or more. Select All and then press Simulate again. The criteria for reasonable is the same as stated above in 4.7.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
5.8 Results
Review the following to see if the design is successful

On the ineffective scenario all the simulations should end early for futility.
On the effective scenarios that there are a sufficient number of successful trials (sufficient power). The power for the ‘early’ scenario is ~0.9 and the power for the ‘late’ scenario is ~0.95.
That the targets (ED90) are correctly identified given the data observed. For the ‘early scenario, the proportion of simulations with a correct selection of target arm is ~0.5 and for the ’late’ scenario is 0.95.



The dose response model fit should also be checked using the View Graph button. We can select Response and Target Selection, and then select quantity, here we chose ED90, to see the fit over all the simulations. In the “early” scenario, we observed that the dose-response model tends to smooth out the sharp edges of the curve. This graph also illustrates that dose 10 and 11 are selected most often as the ED90. For the ‘late’ scenario there is a slight smoothing of the sharp angle in the dose response, and dose 16 is selected as ED90 100% of the time.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
7.1 Quantities of Interest
We simply delete all the target QOIs except the two: Pr(MED relative to Control: Delta 0.1) and Pr(MED relative to Control: Delta 0.2).
FACTS automatically deletes the decision QoIs that used the other target QoIs, and removes them from the Adaptive Allocation and Success/Futility criteria.
We create the two decision QoIs of the posterior probability of beating Control by the CSD and of beating the AC at the MED with delta 0.2.
We also create two decision QoIs of the posterior probability of beating Control by the CSD and of beating the AC at the doses with the greatest values of the QoIs. We’ll see why we need these below.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
7.2 Design > Allocation
Having changed the target QoIs we need to update the Allocation rules to add in the Pr(MED relative to Control: Delta 0.2), to replace the now deleted Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=0.9) that we used before. Once again we weight for information and use a relative weight of 1.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
7.3 Design > Success/Futility Criteria
We also need to update the Success/Futilty rules to use the Pr(MED relative to Control: Delta 0.2) target in place of the now deleted Pr(EDq relative to Control: Quantile=0.9) target. BUT the selection of the MED is different from the selection of the ED. No matter what the data there is always an ED (whatever the quartile), but it is possible (especially when using a parametric response model) in a Null scenario that no dose meets the MED criteria – and there is a risk that randomly one dose will randomly have a very small probability. So when stopping for futility when targeting an MED it is best to test whether the dose with the maximum probability of beating Control or AC is below a threshold – not the probability at the MED.

7.3.1 Interim 1 Criteria
Once again we keep the same criteria across all interims.
We allow stopping early for futility if there are at least 140 subjects randomized (allowing stopping after only 100 enrolled causes a few random stops for futility in the ‘late’ scenario) and

The posterior probability of being better than Control plus 0.1, at the dose with the greatest probability, is less than 10%.
OR the posterior probability of being better than Active Comparator, at the dose with the greatest probability is less than 2.5%. (This probability tends to be lower than the probability of beating Control, and the threshold needs to be reduced to prevent early stopping for futility in the ‘early’ and ‘late’ scenarios.

Select the following parameters:

Select Futility Criteria
Add a QOI:

Select Pr(θ_d - θ_(Control)>0.1); d=Greatest probability over all doses
Select a Condition of <
Enter a threshold of 0.10




Add a second QOI:

Select the QOI: Pr(θ_d > θ_(AC)>0.05); d=Greatest probability over all doses
Set Condition <
Set Threshold 0.025




Select Combine criteria using: OR. The trial will only stop if either criteria is met.
Set Minimum Information Required to be 140 total subjects enrolled.

Unlike when targeting the ED we do not we do not set a minimum subjects to be on the Pr(MED relative to Control: Delta=0.2) – because as noted above, in the Null scenario its very likely there will be no MED dose identified, in which case the minimum subjects criteria would not be met.
We will not stop accrual early for success.

The Final Success/Futility criteria are as before but at the dose with the Greatest Pr(MED relative to Control: Delta 0.2). This may not be a great choice for the futility rule as noted above – but as in the Null scenario this design stops for futility close to 100% of the time, and in the other scenarios the MED is identified and we only look at the proportion of successful outcomes, this doesn’t really matter.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
7.4 Specifying the target dose
On the Study > Variants tab, it is necessary to set the definition of the selected dose to be the MED with a Delta of 0.2.

title: Continuous Endpoint (FEV)
text:
7.5 Simulation Results
This design (after 1,000 simulations) still avoids any type-1 error, and has power of > 0.85 and > 0.9 in the ‘early’ and ‘late’ scenarios respectively. Furthermore the probability of being successful AND selecting a dose (by selecting the MED with Delta 0.2) that “should succeed” is > 0.6 and > 0.85 in the ‘early’ and ‘late’ scenarios respectively. Whilst this is a slight drop in the ‘late’ scenario, it is a considerable improvement in the ‘early’ scenario, and the design has shown that it is possible to test a much larger set of doses to give a much higher chance of selecting the correct dose, while still controlling type-1 error.

text:
3.1 Study
Start FACTS, double click on: Core Design – Multiple Endpoint.

Using the menu option “File > Save”, save this design as “Core-ME-Chronic-Pain-Ex1” in a convenient location (e.g. in a folder called FACTS\ Core-ME-Chronic-Pain-Ex1 in your ‘My Documents’ folder).

3.1.1 Study Info
Set the following parameters:

This is a non-adaptive design
With a maximum of 250 subjects
Add a single visit at 6 weeks.




3.1.2 Treatment Arms
Set the following parameters:

Include a control arm
Auto generate 8 doses, starting at dose 1 with a spacing of 1.




3.1.3 Endpoints
We would like to select a dose that maximizes our chance of achieving a target minimum efficacy while minimizing our risk of lack of tolerability due to side-effects. In order to ensure a sufficient degree of efficacy we will not just test for superiority against the control arm, but against the control arm plus a clinically significant difference (CSD). Setting the CSD in the comparison used to show sufficient efficacy to the desired margin of 1.3 will make it hard to show efficacy except where the improvement in response is substantially better than 1.3.
In a similar manner to a ‘delta’ used in a non-inferiority test we need to pick as CSD somewhat less than1.3 in order to not exclude a dose with a true response of 1.3 but with randomly low data during the trial. To help us do this we will examine a range of CSDs, from 0.5 to 1.
To help us select a dose that has sufficient efficacy and acceptable tolerability, we construct a utility function. The utility function comprises a utility function for each endpoint that will map the estimate of the response on that endpoint to a common “utility” scale of our choosing and then a means of combining the utility of each of the two endpoints into an overall utility score.
Because we want a lack of tolerability rate of 20% or worse to equate to no-utility we choose to define the utility for this level of response on this endpoint as 0 and combine the utilities of the two endpoints by multiplying them. Keeping things simple we set the utility of a tolerability rate of less than 20% to be 1, (i.e. the belief is that a in-tolerable side-effect rate of over 20% would cause other drugs to be prescribed in preference, but as long as the rate was below that, the use of our drug would depend on its efficacy).
On the pain scale endpoint we specify that a response (compared to control) of 1.17 points or more, (a difference 10% below our target of 1.3), has a utility of 1, and that any dose with an expected efficacy of 0 or less has a utility of 0. Between 1.17 and 0 we will make the utility decrease quadratically from 1 to 0.
As the utility of each dose will be estimated by integrating over a large number of MCMC iterations the estimated utility in these ‘flat regions’ where the true utility is either 1 or 0 will be below 1 or above 0. Consider a dose where the mean estimate of the response on the intolerable side-effect scale is exactly 0.2, in roughly half the MCMC iterations it will have been less than 0.2 (and thus had a utility of 1) and in the other half it will have been above 0.2 (and thus have a utility of 0). Thus a dose with a mean estimate of response at “the step” between 1 and 0 will have a utility of 0.5 and doses with responses close to 0.2 will have utilities <0.5 and >0.5 and only gradually approach a utility of 0 or 1, only reaching them when the response rate so certainly below 0.2 or above 0.2 that in none of the MCMC samples was it the other side of the 0.2 threshold.
Thus when we include such a step in the utility of an endpoint we do not expect to see a step in the estimate of the utility, but rather a utility that is proportional to the probability that the tolerability of the dose will be above or below the acceptable threshold. This is acceptable because the utility is not an externally accepted measure that we are tying to estimate as part of the claim, the utility is for internal decision making purposes – namely to help us select a dose that combines a good certainty of being both sufficiently efficacious and sufficiently tolerable.
It would be interesting to explore the impact of changing the tolerability utility to use a linear decline from 1 to 0 over the range 0.1 to 0.2, this might also be more realistic.

3.1.3.1 Utility
We will use multiplied utilities.
Set the following parameters:

In the dropdown menu for Component utility combination method, select U1 * U2



3.1.3.2 Primary Endpoint
The primary endpoint, U1, is change from baseline in the average weekly pain score.
We set the following parameters:

We will not include baseline
We will not use longitudinal modelling in this design

In the interval from –infinity to –1.17, the utility is 1, so set Gamma to 1.
In the interval from –1.17 to 0 the utility falls off quadratically, set Alpha to 0.7305



(because 0.7305*(-1.17)2=1). And Set Gamma to 0


In the interval from 0 to infinity the utility is 0, set Gamma to 0.
Check Parameterize response relative to control




3.1.3.3 Endpoint 2
The second endpoint, U2, is a binary ‘tolerability’ endpoint, the toxic side effect endpoint.
Set the following parameters:

Set Type: Dichotomous
Set: Response indicates negative outcome



We will not use longitudinal modelling in this design

In the interval from 0 to 0.2, the utility is 1, set Gamma to 1.

text:
3.4 Quantities of Interest
We want to determine the probability of the mean pain response at the dose with the greatest utility compared to the Control dose, with the goal of this maximum utility dose being better on the pain score compared to the control by more than the Clinically Significant Difference. We examine a range of CSDs, from 0.5 to 1. Note that we are using the utility function to select the ‘best dose’, but not directly to judge success of the trial (and whether to run a subsequent trial). Success of the trial is based on best dose’s performance on the primary efficacy endpoint relative to placebo.
To do this we have 3 tabs where information can be selected – one for each endpoint and one for the overall utility.
We will need to specify

Quantities of Interest (QOI) on the pain scale – one for each of the CSD’s we wish to explore.
A QOI on the utility scale – specifying that we wish to identify as a ‘target’ dose the dose with the maximum utility.
Decision QOIs on the pain scale – the evaluation of each of the probabilities of being better than control by each of the CSD’s at the Dose with the maximum utility (UMax).
The tolerability endpoint is used as part of the calculation of utility and we do not need any QOI’s solely on this endpoint.


3.4.1 Pain, Tolerability, and Utility tabs
We want to determine the posterior probability of the difference of the maximum utility dose compared to control being greater less than -CSD, i.e. the maximum utility dose is better.
Set the following parameters:

We start by specifying our Target. Here our target will be the maximum Utility dose.

So first, we go the Utility tab, select the Probability of being Target: Pr(UMax). Our decisions will be made on the dose most likely to be the maximum utility dose. The other utility QOIs that FACTS created by default can be deleted (note at the bottom of the tab is button for restoring the default QOIs should we later decide we need them, or we can re-create them by manually specifying equivalents).

We go back to the Pain tab. and at the bottom of the page, ensure the trial type is set to Superiority then set the CSD to 0.8. Note, the CSD is NOT -0.8. We already specified that lower is subject improvement, thus FACTS understands that when comparing the difference between a dose and control we desire the result to be less than -0.8. However, we will examine multiple CSDs; specifying a single CSD here does not limit us to one CSD.
On the Pain tab, for Posterior Probabilities we are interested comparing the max utility dose to the control arm and seeing if it is better than a clinically significant difference (CSD). We select:

title: Multiple Endpoint (Pain + Drug Tolerability)
text:
3.5 Design

3.5.1 On Setting Priors
On setting priors – as a rule it is recommended that the user specifies weakly informative priors rather than non-informative ones. There are a number of reasons for this:

In a few circumstances non-informative priors can end up being informative.
What values make a prior non-informative vary depending on the range of the value being estimated, a measure with a SD of 1000 requires quite a different value for a prior to be non-informative than one with an SD of 1.
Measures that are log-odds or log hazard ratios can have parameters that are then exponentiated and used as parameters to other distributions as a maximum these values should have range of (-10,10) and (-5,5). Greater than this and numeric overflows can occur.
Using a “non-informative” prior can sometimes be used as an excuse for not thinking about the prior. Not thinking about a prior is never a good idea.
There are some priors, particularly for the variance parameters of hierarchical models where (as we use inverse Gamma distributions for the priors, weakly informative priors are preferred to uninformative ones [Gelman 2006, “Prior distributions for variance parameters in hierarchical models” Bayesian Analysis Vol 1 Number 3]
When simulating clinical trial designs there is a balance to be struck between the MCMC sample length used in the within-trial analyses and the number of simulations run. Weakly informative priors can help the MCMC to converge and allow us to use shorter sample lengths.

For many priors the weakly informative is easily judged where the priors directly correspond to values that we are simulating. Others are not so easily judged, for these we used “non-informative” priors, ran some simulations and looked at the means and SDs of the posterior estimates of the parameters over all the scenarios and then based a weakly informative prior on these. You will see these priors below being described as having an “initial un-informative” prior and then a weakly informative one. Care must be taken with this approach to not over specify a prior based on the selection of scenarios, and it must be borne in mind that the scenarios may not capture the full potential variability in what the “truth value in nature” might actually be.


3.5.2 Pain

3.5.2.1 Dose Response
We wish the design to be able to cope with non-monotonic dose response data for the primary endpoint, so we model the primary continuous endpoint using the Second Order NDLM.
We assume the dose strengths give a linear range of doses in terms of the expected change in dose effect, so they are given dose levels of 0, 1, 2, ..., 8 and control is included in the model as the first dose
If the response for the ith subject given dose d at week 6 is Y6i:
\[Y_{6i} \sim N\left(\theta_d, \sigma^2\right) \text{ for } d = 0,1,\ldots,8\]
We set the prior for the initial dose:
\[\theta_0 \sim N\left(0, 0.5^2\right)\]
The scenarios all use a control rate of 0, so a mean of 0 for the prior seems reasonable. An SD of 0.5 means that the +/- 2SD prior interval is (-1,+1) so any actual rate within that range should see little effect from this prior in the posterior estimate, whereas an observed rate outside that range will see some bias towards 0 in the posterior estimate. The SD of the endpoint is 2.12 (variance 4.5) so this prior (variance 0.25) is roughly equivalent to 18 observations with a sample mean of 0. As we will be simulating typically 50 subjects in control this will contribute some additional shrinkage to the final estimate of the response on control. It will contribute a considerably greater proportionate effect at early interims with a lot less actual data. Exploring how useful this is in this example is left the reader, it is very easily done by making a slight change to this example and re-running the simulations.
Prior for the First dose difference:
\[\theta_1 - \theta_0 \sim N\left(0, 2^2\right)\]
Here we use a weakly informative, conservative prior, the mean of the prior is that there is no change in response from the Control to the first dose. An SD of 2 means that the +/- 2SD prior interval is (-4,4). All our expected changes are well inside this range – the maximum difference of any dose from control is ~1.7 and the SD of the endpoint is 2.12.
The next two prior distributions use the Inverse Gamma distribution, these can be specified in FACTS using one of two parameterizations – either the “Alpha, Beta” parameterization which is the more normal parameterization for statisticians, or the “Central value and Weight” parameterization. It is easier with the latter form to discuss the likely impact of the prior so this is the form that will be used here. The FACTS “Settings” menu command can be used to select the form you use. See “Settings > Options > Gamma Distribution Parameters”.
The 2nd Order NDLM smoothing parameter \(\tau^{2}\) is similar to one of those variance parameters of a hierarchical distribution, and as the data being modeled is the change in dose response between doses the number of actual observations in this case to 7 and the prior can play an important role. If we have strong prior that this is a small value, the 2nd order NDLM will tend to a straight line (extreme smoothing) and if we have a strong prior that this is a large value, the 2nd order NDLM will tend to simple pairwise comparison (no smoothing). Thus if we weight the prior to a small value we can reduce type 1 error – as the Null case is a flat straight line, but at the expense of underestimating the dose response at doses where there are large changes in response from one dose to the next.
Initial simulations were run with prior mean and weight of 1 and 0.1. For this parameter this gave an average for the posterior mean of 0.43 with and SD over the simulations of 0.1 and an average SD of the posterior estimate over the simulations of 0.26. However on the Emax scenario we saw the smoothing cause a biased under estimate of the response on the first dose of -0.22. (~22%) so we strengthened the prior for tau at a slightly higher value choosing a mean of 0.6 and a weight of 5.
\[\tau^2 \sim IG\left(0.6, 5\right)\]
This marginally reduced the bias at the first dose in the Emax scenario to -0.19. This prior could be further refined by exploring the error and bias of the response estimates across the scenarios at different prior means and weights – particularly at the key doses.
For the nuisance parameter \(\sigma\) we specified a prior with a mean of 2 close to the scenario mean and weight of 5 – equivalent to 5 observed subjects - so in the posterior estimate, the prior will be quickly dominated by the observed data. With a well research endpoint it would be not usual to have a strong prior expectation for the value of this parameter.
\[\sigma^{2}\sim IG(2,5)\]
Set the following parameters:

Select Model: Second Order NDLM
For the initial dose set the prior mean to be 0 and standard deviation to be 0.5
For the first dose difference, set the prior mean to be 0 and standard deviation to be 2
For the “smoothing factor”, tau2 (τ2) set the prior mean to be 0.6 with weight of 5.
Set Error Parameters: Sigma prior mean to be 2, and with weight of 5
Control is not modeled separately




3.5.2.2 Frequentist Analysis
Since we have no dropouts, we leave just LOCF checked
The required alpha and the contrast coefficients can be set for the frequentist analysis. We leave them unchanged.



3.5.3 Tolerability

3.5.3.1 Dose Response
The second endpoint is strongly expected to be monotonic, so a 4-pararmeter sigmoid is used to model the log-odds of the probability of a lack of tolerability.
If the rate of intolerability response for the subjects on dose d is Pd:
\[P_{d} = \frac{e^{\theta_{d}}}{1 + e^{\theta_{d}}}\]
We will model the mean response:
\[\theta_d \sim a_1 + \frac{\left(a_2 - a_1\right) v_d^{a_4}}{v_d^{a_4} + a_3^{a_4}} \text{ for } d = 0,\ldots,8\]
Where a1 is the response at the lowest modeled dose, a2 some maximal response that is approached asymptotically, a3 is the dose level at which half the increase from a1 to a2 is observed, and a4 is a “hill” parameter defining the slope.
Bearing this in mind initially the priors for the model parameters of are set to:
\(a_1 \sim N\left(-2, 1^2\right)\), \(a_2 \sim N\left(0, 1^2\right)\)
\(a_3 \sim N^{+}\left(4, 3^2\right)\), \(a_4 \sim N^{+}\left(12, 100^2\right)\)
The mean of the prior for a1 corresponds to a probability of 0.12 and +/- 2 standard deviations gives a probability range from 0.02 to 0.5. As the mean tolerability rate on Control is 0.1 in all scenarios this is close to being correctly centered and is clearly only weakly informative.
The mean of the prior for a2 corresponds to a probability of 0.5 and +/- 2 standard deviations gives a probability range from 0.12 to 0.88. In the tolerability scenarios the lack of tolerability never reaches the plateau value that this parameter estimates. The scenarios only go as far as a rising lack of tolerability reaching a rate of 0.24.
The mean for the prior for a3 corresponds to the middle of the dose range and +/- 2 standard deviations gives a dose range from 0 to 10 – covering but not drastically exceeding the dose range being studied.
The mean for the prior for a4 corresponds to a reasonable slope (change in rate of 0.13 from d3 to d4) at the mean values for the other parameters, and the SD of 100 allows for a great deal of variation in the final value.
However after looking at the posterior estimates for these parameters from the initial run we saw that a3 and a4 were 6 and 77 respectively. As there are relatively few toxic event on each dose this endpoint was in some simulations being estimated poorly and so the priors for a3 and a4 were revised to
\(a_{3}\sim N^{+}\left( 6,2^{2} \right)\), \(a_{4}\sim N^{+}\left( 80,100^{2} \right)\)
Set the following parameters:

Select Model: Sigmoidal
For the prior distributions for the 4 alpha parameters set

Λ1 = -2, λ1 = 1 (log odds of: –4, -2, 0 correspond to probabilities of: 0.02, 0.12, 0.5 respectively)
Λ2 = 0, λ2 = 1 (log odds of: –2, 0, 2 correspond to probabilities of: 0.05, 0.5, 0.88 respectively)
Λ3 = 6, λ3 = 2 (spans the upper half of the dose range)
Λ4 = 80, λ4 = 100

Control is not modeled separately




3.5.3.2 Frequentist Analysis
Since we have no dropouts, we leave just LOCF checked.
The required alpha and the contrast coefficients can be set for the frequentist analysis. We leave them unchanged.



3.5.4 Allocation
Because we selected Non-Adaptive on the Study Info screen, only fixed allocation is available, specify a ratio of 2 on control and 1 on each study dose.
Set the following parameters:

Set the allocation ratio as 2 for Control, and 1 for every other arm.




3.5.5 Success/Futility Criteria
Here we only have a Final Evaluation tab; this initial design will not use any early stopping.
The trial will be judged a success if at the end of the trial:

the dose most likely to have the maximum utility dose has a posterior probability that its mean improvement minus the Control arm is better than 0.8, is greater than 75%.

The trial will be judged to be futile if at the end of the trial:

the dose most likely to have the maximum utility has a posterior probability that its mean improvement minus the Control arm is better than 0.8, is less than 25%.

Otherwise the trial will be judged to be inconclusive.
Note that we are using the utility function to select the ‘best dose’, but not directly to judge success of the trial (and whether to run a subsequent trial). Success is based on best dose’s performance on the primary efficacy endpoint relative to control.
Set the following parameters:

Futility Criteria:

QOI: Add “Pain: Pr(θ_d-θ_(Control)<-0.8); d=Utility; Greatest Pr(UMax)
Condition: <
Threshold: 0.25
Combine criteria using: Leave as default since we have specified only one QOI

Success Criteria:

QOI: Add “Pain: Pr(θ_d-θ_(Control)<-0.8); d=Utility; Greatest Pr(UMax)
Condition: >
Threshold: 0.75
Combine criteria using: Leave as default since we have specified only one QOI


Thus, if the probability of the mean response at the dose with the greatest utility being better than Control by more than the 0.8 is 75% or better the compound will be successful. If the probability that the mean response at dose with the greatest utility is better than Control by more than 0.8, is less than 25% the trial is a failure. For anything not meeting either of these criteria, the trial results are inconclusive. The thresholds for success and futility were determined by examining the results of simulations. The rationale for selection 0.8 as the desired amount of improvement over control was also determined by examining simulation results and the range of clinically meaning differences that were supplied. Additional details will be discussed in the Simulations section.

3.6 Simulation
Set the number of simulations to run to 10, Select all Scenarios, then press Simulate. This allows us to make a quick assessment of whether the design is behaving as expected: that the flat scenario’s end up mainly futile and the others mainly successful. With a fixed allocation in this design, the other scenarios will have lower probabilities of late success.
If the results look reasonable, increase the number of simulations to run to 100, (re-check the 5 scenario combinations we wish to run) and then press Simulate again. If the results still look promising run 1,000.

We can see that in the Emax case we select correctly a reasonable 0.9 of the simulations, but we fare less well in the other scenarios, with probabilities of 0.69, 0.64 and 0.45 in the Logistic, Umbrella and Linear scenarios respectively.
From the graphs available there is a particularly useful one for examining model fit of the utility for each of the given scenarios. The graph displays the true utility, the fitted utility, and the allocation for each arm. To view this graph, click on View Graph and select graph Utility and Subject Allocation.

See how the estimated analysis is below the true utility when its one and above it when its zero. This is because when the utility function has a plateau that is approached from below or above the averaged estimate of the utility can only be below / above the value of the plateau.
We also examine useful graphs that assist in selecting the thresholds and the desired improvement from Control. On the QOI tab, we had five Posterior Probabilities and Decision Quantities computed for clinically significant differences ranging from 0.5 to 0.9. We evaluate all of these CSDs in one run of simulations to understand how different thresholds (success and futility) and CSDs will perform in the different virtual subject response scenarios.
To do this, we highlight a scenario, go to View Graph, and examine the graph: Explore: Final Success Criteria. This plot displays the proportion of simulations satisfying the final success criteria for each threshold ranging from 0.5 to 0.9 for each of the CSDs in the selected scenario. Examining the Success criteria plot, we determine which cut-offs in the null case, i.e. Flat scenario, will limit false successes to 0.025. A threshold of approximately 0.75 will work for a CSD of 0.6 for example. We balance this with examining the weakest of the other scenarios, i.e. Linear scenario. For each CSD the threshold that controls the type-1 error at a given level in the Null scenario gives the same power in an alternate scenario as the other QOIs using different CSDs and thresholds.

title: Multiple Endpoint (Pain + Drug Tolerability)
text:
5.1 Evaluation Criteria
We note that in the results for the adaptive design with no early stopping, the type-1 error had been reduced relative to the fixed design and was well below the target 0.025. Looking at the Explore Success Criteria for the “Flat” scenario from the results of the adaptive trial with no early stopping, there are fewer curves than the fixed design because we remove the QOIs with the CSDs that we had discarded, leaving us just with the results for the probability of success relative to Control with a CSD of 0.6: Pr((θd – θcontrol) < -0.6)



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


This shows there would have been 0.025% of the simulations successful if the final success criteria had been about 0.63. To be comparable with the fixed design and build in a degree of safety to allow for the variability of the simulations we select a threshold of 0.65 that would have yielded just 0.021% of the simulations successful.
To select the thresholds for early stopping we use Explore: Futility Contours and Explore: Success Contours graphs. To use these graphs it is worth having output weeks files for every simulation (as we did with the adaptive design without early stopping). These graphs take a significant amount of data analysis to draw, and re-draw every time a graph option is changed. Patience is required to use them as this time is nothing compared to repeatedly re-running simulations with different stopping criteria.
To determine the early success criteria we again look at the lowest threshold we can use that would have given a success rate of around 0.02% in the “Flat” scenario.
On the Explore: Success Contours graph for the “Flat” scenario, we select

the VAS Pain Scale endpoint
The Utility Pr(Umax) taget dose
The Pr((θd – θcontrol) < -0.6) probability
The 8th interim to start allowing early stopping for futility. There is a trade-off to made here, the earlier the trial can stop the greater the potential savings, but also the more variable response we expect to see and hence the more conservative the threshold is likely to be. Our first interim is early (60 subjects enrolled and hence with an average accrual rate of 5 per week and a 6 week endpoint, ~30 subjects complete) to give the adaptive allocation plenty of time to adapt. Allowing stopping this early however would require a very high threshold for stopping for success to avoid inflating the type-1 error rate. At the 8th interim – 14 weeks later – we would expect to have roughly 130 subjects enrolled of which ~100 would be complete.
We also set the threshold limit to 0.6 – So we can see contours around the 0.65 limit for final success that we would use if not allowing early stopping.

The graph plots the contours of equal success rate (combining both early success and late success) using equal early and final thresholds. Each contour tracks left and upwards from the points along the diagonal where the same threshold is used for the final success criteria and the early stopping for success criteria. The contour tracks the threshold combinations as the final threshold is reduced and the early threshold increased, until the early threshold reaches 1 and there is no early stopping.
Here we have contours of 0.019 and 0.028. The 0.019 contour starts just below the (0.64, 1) point and runs to the (0.9, 0.9) point. Any combination of final success threshold and early success threshold along that contour should give us approximately the same type-1 error rate of ~0.019.



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


If we imagine this contour transposed to the same graph but for the “linear scenario” we can see that it starts close to the 0.965 contour at (0.63, 1) and ends on the 0.938 contour at (0.9, 0.9). This is a trade-off that we typically see: that the more aggressive we want to be about stopping early for success (lower early stopping threshold) whilst adjusting the final success threshold to control the type-1 error rate, the more power we have to give up. Here though the overall power is high and the drop is less than 3 percentage points.
Here we will be conservative and choose (0.64, 0.98) which seems to offer some chance to stop early with barely any loss in power. We could compare to the other alternate scenarios too, but this scenario has the lowest power and so is likely to be the most sensitive to losing power if we have too low a threshold for early stopping for success.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


Similarly, we can select an early stopping for futility threshold based on the failure rate in the “success” scenario with the lowest success rate. In this example that is the “Linear” scenario. As we are computing the type-2 error rate as any simulation that is not a success, the final threshold is effectively the same we are using to judge success, namely 0.64. We set up the graph to plot contours (this time of futility rate) for the VAS Pain Scale endpoint, evaluated at the Pr(Umax) target dose, computing the Pr((θd – θcontrol) < -0.6) probability from the 8th interim onwards, with a maximum threshold of 0.7.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


We can see that with no early stopping for futility (early threshold of 0) if the final success/futility threshold is 0.6, we are close to the 3rd contour 0.04, hence we can expect the type-2 error in this scenario to be about 0.04. If we move vertically up from (0.64, 0) we reach the 5th contour (0.047) at (0.64, 0.035). Thus for a possible single percentage point drop in power we can use 0.035 as the early stopping for futility threshold.

title: Multiple Endpoint (Pain + Drug Tolerability)
text:
5.2 Success/Futility Criteria

5.2.1 Interim 1
The details for the early stopping for futility and success criteria are set on the interim 8 tab, we are going to delay the application of early stopping by requiring “minimum information”, but this is “belt and braces” just to demonstrate the feature. We leave the “interim 1” unchanged. (we could instead have added the stopping conditions to interim 1, and relied on the “minimum information requirements” to prevent stopping effectively until interim 8 tab. Although we are not allowing early stopping at interims 1 through 7, the response adaptive update of the randomization probabilities will still be occurring.
Notice that we have used more relaxed criteria for the final evaluation (0.64) as well as allowing early stopping. This is because the introduction of adaptive allocation has reduced our type-1 error. For those seeing simulation results for a trail using response adaptive randomization (RAR) for the first time this may be surprising, there is a widely held assumption that “early looks at data” result in inflation of type-1 error. But if the looks are used for RAR then usually the reverse is true. In the “Null” setting the preferential allocation of subjects to arms with good response results in those arms experiencing a “random high” having a greater chance to regress to the mean, and thus type-1 errors are reduced.
and require that for stopping for futility 150 subjects have been enrolled and stopping early for success that there are at least 30 subjects on the dose most likely to have the greatest utility – Pr(Umax). For futility we require 150 subjects to ensure that a reasonable minimum information has been gathered to justify stopping for futility, but this limit could be tuned further. For success we require 30 subjects on the Pr(Umax) dose as an often voiced criticism of stopping for success in a dose finding trial is that there is a need to have a certain minimum number of subjects exposed in order to gather safety data. Here we guarantee more data (30 subjects worth) on the dose that will be selected for phase 3 than the fixed design would have delivered (25 subjects).
The trial will stop early for success if at an interim analysis:

the dose most likely to have the maximum utility, Pr(Umax), has a posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Control plus the clinically significant difference of 0.6, is greater than 0.98 and there at least 30 subjects enrolled on the Pr(Umax) dose.

The trial will stop early for futility if at an interim analysis:

the dose most likely to have the maximum utility has a posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Control plus the clinically significant difference of 0.6, is less than 0.035 and there at least 150 subjects enrolled overall.

Otherwise the trial will continue.
We will create a new file for the changes, so choose File-> Save As, and enter Core-ME-Chronic-Pain-Ex2-Adaptive-2.facts for the new file name, click Save. This new file will automatically load into FACTS.
On the Design->Success/Futility Criteria, add and “Interim 8 tab” and enable stopping for both futility and success and set the criteria as follows:
