section: Steps for calling FACTS from R
text:
Steps for calling FACTS from R
To call FACTS from R, you will need to do the following sequence of steps:

Create a (non-adaptive) FACTS project for your Engine type with the general study info: Number of Arms, number and timing of Visits (if using), Dose response (& longitudinal if using) model specification and MCMC setup.
Configure VSR and Execution profiles to allow a simple simulation run.
Run 1 simulation to produce:

A ‘param’ file which will be passed as an input to the R function.
A ‘patients’ file. This may be useful to illustrate data file format for the input data. See FACTS Execution Guides for details.
An ‘mcmc’ file. This will show you what to expect in the output MCMC file.

If using FACTS to analyze a data set, then

put the data set into the required format
write an R script to call FACTS with the data set
process the MCMC output

If using FACTS within a simulation framework, then:

Write an R script that generates the data you wish to simulate and pass to FACTS to analyze
Write a loop that

generates the data for a simulation
calls FACTS with generated data
process the MCMC output
accumulate the statistics for the overall operating characteristics to be computed

Output the resulting OCs

title: FACTS from R
text:
runFACTS() Usage Notes

Run FACTS MCMC Model from R
runFACTS(
 engine, 
 data.file = “patients.dat”, 
 param.file = “nuk1_e.param, 
 mcmc.file.num = 0, 
 rng.seed = 1, 
 exec.path = getwd()
)
Return Value: runFACTS returns a TRUE/FALSE to indicate a successful/failed execution. In case of errors, R error messages may be printed and in case of a FACTS execution error, a file called ‘error.txt’ will be output, containing the error description.
Arguments:

engine: Name of the FACTS engine to use. Can be one of the following:

For Core Engines: “contin”, “dichot”, “ME”, “TTE”
For Enrichment Design Engines: “ed_contin”, “ed_dichot”, “ed_tte”

data.file: Name of the input data file. Default is “patients.dat”. This file format should exactly match the file format of the ‘patients’ file corresponding to the ones produced by FACTS for the design you setup in FACTS to specify the analysis model. (See the FACTS Execution Guide under the FACTS Help menu for details.)
param.file: Name of the FACTS ‘.param’ file that specifies the model setup. Default is ‘nuk1_e.param’.
mcmc.file.num: The MCMC output is written to a file named ‘mcmcNNNNN.csv. This argument set the NNNNN. Therefore, mcmc.file.num = 1 will create an MCMC output file called mcmc00001.csv. Default value is 0.
rng.seed: Integer-valued random number generator seed. Will use the value from the ‘.param’ file if unspecified.
exec.path The path to the directory where the FACTS executable program is available. Default is the current working directory.



Set Up Files and Folders
It is important to pass files and parameters correctly, as there is not much in the way of helpful error messaging. Setting up the required folder and files is not hard but should be done carefully. The following example shows how.

title: FACTS from R
text:
The “core.dichot.example.facts”
In this example we wish to use FACTS to fit a simple NDLM dose response model across 6 arms (control & 5 doses) with a dichotomous endpoint.
We have entered the following parameters:

Study:

Study Info:

Non-adaptive
Recruit subjects continuously
Max subjects: 300
Response is a positive outcome
Time to final endpoint: 4 weeks

Treatment Arms:

Control and 5 doses with strengths 1, 2, … 5


Virtual Subject Response

Explicitly defined

Dose Response

responses: 0.1, 0.1, 0.125, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25



Execution

Accrual

1 region with mean accrual of 5 subjects per week

Dropout

No dropouts


Quantities of Interest

Posterior probability: Pr(P_d > P_Control)
Probability of being target: Pr(Max)
Decision Quantity: Pr(P_d > P_Contorl); d=Greatest Pr(Max)

Design

Dose Response

Simple NDLM

Initial Dose ~N(0,22)
Tau IG(1,1) “central value”, “weight”


Requentist analysis: none
Allocation: 1:1:1:1:1:1
Success/Futility Criteria

Success: Pr(P_d > P_Control); d= Greatest Pr(Max) > 0.9



Not all these parameters will effect our analysis, but we have to enter sufficient parameters to be able to run a simulation and get a bin1_e.param file. This can be found in the scenario simulation results folder. We only need to run 1 simulation on order to have one written out. This file is copied to our “Example” directory. If we want to change something in the analysis – the model or the prior for example, we can modify this facts file, re-run one simulation, and copy the new bin1_e.param file.

title: FACTS from R
text:
dichot-demo.R
We start by setting the current working directory to the “Example” folder, and setting up some file locations and sourcing the factR.R file.
## Set up Folders and Paths

# This is the directory where the parameter file and patient data must be located
# It will be where the MCMCM files are written
setwd("Z:/FACTS test/FACTS 6 Training/FACTS R interface/Example")

# This must be the location of the factR.R file
FactR.src = "../factR.R"

# This must be the location of the executable files
Exec.dir = "../WindowsExecutables"

# Load runFACTS
source(FactR.src)
We can then copy an example patients file from the simulation results and check that we can run facts.
# Test to check its working
# Copy an example patients file from the simulations results to this folder before running.
system.time(
  runFACTS(
    engine='dichot', 
    data.file = 'patients00001.csv', 
    param.file = 'bin1_e.param', 
    mcmc.file.num = 1, 
    rng.seed = 1, 
    exec.path = Exec.dir
  )
)

genBinaryData()
We now define a simple function to generate the data for a single run of FACTS.
# generates a data frame that can be used to drive a FACTS analysis
# dichotomous endpoint
# no visits
# n.per.arm: int, the number of subjects to be simulated for each arm
# rates: int[], the response rate to be simulated for each arm
# the length if rates defines the number of arms
# returns a dataframe with n.per.arm * length(rates) simulated subjects

genBinaryData <- function(nPerArm, rates) {
  
  patientID <- 1:(nPerArm * length(rates)) # Generate a list of patients
  region <- rep(1, nPerArm * length(rates)) # all patients come from region 1
  date <- 1:(nPerArm * length(rates)) # Generate a list of enrolment dates - here simply one per day
  doseAlloc <- rep(1:length(rates), each = nPerArm) # Allocate patients equally to each dose
  lastVisit <- rep(1, nPerArm * length(rates)) # all patients have last visit data
  dropout <- rep(0, nPerArm * length(rates)) # no patients have dropped out
  baseline <- rep(-9999, nPerArm * length(rates)) # not simulating baseline
  visit1 <- rep(0, nPerArm * length(rates)) # create the outcome vector

  for (d in 1:length(rates)){ # get responses for each dose
  ix <- which(doseAlloc == d) # get indices of patients on dose d
  # assign them a final response based on the rate to simulate for dose d
  if (length(ix) > 0) {
  visit1[ix] <- 
    sample(
     c(0,1), 
     size = length(ix), 
      replace = TRUE, 
      prob = c(1-rates[d], rates[d])
    )
  }
  
}

dat <- data.frame(
  SubjectID = patientID, 
  Region = region, 
  Date = date, 
  Dose = doseAlloc, 
  LastVisit = lastVisit, 
  Dropout = dropout, 
  Baseline = baseline, 
  Visit1 = visit1, 
  row.names = NULL
)

return(dat)
}


runSims
########### Toy Example Trial Sim ##########
### Constants
DATAFILE = "patients.csv"
MCMCFILE = "mcmc00000.csv"
# function to simulate an example data set with dichotomous endpoint
# nSims - the number of sims to run
# nBurnin - the number of MCMC smaples to discard
# (the number of MCMC samples is specified in the parameter file)
# details - a boolean. If TRUE the function returns a data frame with
# the results of each individual simulation,
# otherwise just the win proportion and probabilities of being control

runSims <- function(
    nSims = 10, 
    nBurnin = 1000, 
    rates = c(0.1, 0.1, 0.125, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25),
    details = FALSE
) {

winPpn = 0
pr.gt.ctl.sum <- rep(0, length(rates) - 1)
if (details) {
perSim <- data.frame(Sim = 1)
}

for(sim in 1:nSims) {
dat = genBinaryData(nPerArm = 50, rates = rates)
write.csv(dat,DATAFILE, row.names = FALSE)
if (details) {
perSim[sim, "Sim"] <- sim
# record true rates and observed rates
for (d in 1:length(rates)) {
perSim[sim, paste("sim.rate.", d, sep="")] <- rates[d]
}

for (d in 1:length(rates)) {
perSim[sim, paste("obs.rate.", d, sep="")] <- mean(dat[dat[,"Dose"]==d, "Visit1"])
}
}

cat("run FACTS: ", sim, "\n")

ret <- 
  runFACTS(
    engine = 'dichot', 
    data.file = DATAFILE, 
    param.file = 'bin1_e.param', 
    mcmc.file.num = 0, 
    rng.seed = sim, 
    exec.path = Exec.dir
  )

dat = read.csv(MCMCFILE, skip = 1)

# discard burnin rows and just estimates of rate - the "Pi" columns
dat = dat[(nBurnin + 1):nrow(dat), grep("Pi", names(dat))]

if (details) {
# record est rate
for (d in 1:length(rates)) {
perSim[sim, paste("est.rate.", d, sep="")] <- mean(dat[,paste("Pi.", d, sep="")])
}
}

# success if the first dose is not in the top 2 .. i.e. the resposnse on any 2 doses is > control

success <- apply(dat, 1, FUN = function(x) {ifelse(length(x) - which(order(x)==1) >= 2, 1, 0)})

if (details) {
perSim[sim, "Pr.Success"] <- mean(success)
perSim[sim, "Success.flag"] <- ifelse(mean(success) > 0.9, 1,0)
}

winPpn = winPpn + ifelse(mean(success) > 0.9, 1,0)

# example: calc pr(theta_d > theta_ctl)
gt.ctl.flag <- apply(dat, 1, FUN = function(x){x[2:length(x)] > x[1]})
pr.gt.ctl <- apply(gt.ctl.flag,1,sum)
pr.gt.ctl <- pr.gt.ctl / length(gt.ctl.flag[1,])
pr.gt.ctl.sum <- pr.gt.ctl.sum + pr.gt.ctl

if (details) {
for (d in 1:length(pr.gt.ctl)) {
perSim[sim, paste("Pr.pi.", d+1, ">pi_ctl", sep="")] <- pr.gt.ctl[d]
    }
  }
}

cat("win proportion: ", winPpn/nSims, "\n")

if (details) {
return (list(winPpn/nSims, pr.gt.ctl.sum/nSims, perSim))
} else {
return (list(winPpn/nSims, pr.gt.ctl.sum/nSims))
}
}


Running the Example
Having sourced the above functions and variables holding paths and fllenames we can run the simulations with the default scenario:
runSims(details=FALSE)

> run FACTS: 1
> run FACTS: 2
> run FACTS: 3
> run FACTS: 4
> run FACTS: 5
> run FACTS: 6
> run FACTS: 7
> run FACTS: 8
> run FACTS: 9
> run FACTS: 10
> win proportion: 0.3

> [[1]]
> [1] 0.3

> [[2]]
> Pi.2 Pi.3 Pi.4 Pi.5 Pi.6
> 0.30572 0.45824 0.51936 0.77944 0.92916
If “details” is set to TRUE then the list of results has a dataframe at the end that contains a row per simulation and details of that simulations results.
Hopefully this is sufficient to get you started.

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
This document describes how use the Rule-Based Dose Escalation (DE) Simulator within FACTS (the Fixed and Adaptive Clinical Trial Simulator from now on referred to as Dose Escalation Fixed and Adaptive Clinical Trial Simulator Software). It is intended for all end users of the system.



This document covers the Dose Escalation Fixed and Adaptive Clinical Trial Simulator Software by describing the user interface. It covers the 3+3, mTPI, mTPI-2, i3+3 and BOIN designs. It does not cover the CRM design engine which has its own User Guide.
The screenshots provided are specific to a particular installation and may not reflect the exact layout of the information seen by any particular user. They were taken from FACTS, 5 or later if changed, installed on Windows 7 and Windows 10. Different versions of Windows or the use of different Windows themes will introduce some differences in appearance. The contents of each tab, however, will be consistent with the software.



Please cite FACTS wherever applicable using this citation.



An overview of the acronyms and abbreviations used in this document can be found here.

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
The Rules Based Methods
The methods implemented are:

BOIN (Yuan et al. 2016)
mTPI (Ji et al. 2010)
mTPI-2 (Guo et al. 2017)
i3+3 (Liu et al. 2020)
3+3 (Liu et al. 2013)

See the papers for details, but a summary of the methods is given here.
All these methods start allocating at a given dose (currently in FACTS this is always the lowest dose), and allocate in cohorts of a fixed size (3+3 can only use cohorts of 3, the other methods allow a different cohort size to be specified). After each cohort they consider all the data on the dose just tested (but unlike the CRM not other doses) and decide whether to Escalate (“E), Stay (”S”) or De-Escalate (“D”).
In all these methods (except 3+3) the decisions are based on a specified target toxicity rate \(p_T\) and target interval around that rate (\(p_T \in [p_L, p_U]\), note that \(p_T\) need not be at the center of this interval). How they make that decision is the principal difference between the methods, and these are described in method specific sub-sections below.
All (except 3+3) share in the following:

If at the highest dose the decision is to Escalate, this is converted to Stay instead, if at the lowest dose the decision is to De-escalate, this is converted to Stay instead.
Using a Beta-binomial distribution based on the observed data (with a Beta(1, 1) prior) if the posterior probability that the toxicity rate exceeds the target rate with some probability (0.95 by default) then mark the dose as unacceptable and de-escalate (shown as “DU” in the decision tables). Stopping the trial if this is at the lowest dose. In BOIN a dose is only marked unacceptable once at least 3 subjects have been treated on it; with fewer subjects the decision is De-escalate.
If the decision is to Escalate but the next higher dose is marked unacceptable (the data on that dose give a “DU” decision), the decision is converted to Stay instead.
At the end of the trial, MTD selection is after isotonic regression performed as follows:

Calculate the toxicity rate estimate at each dose (BOIN uses the observed rates, all others use the posterior mean toxicity, assuming a Beta(0.001, 0.001) prior and an independent Beta-Binomial model). Doses with no subjects are skipped. For mTPI, mTPI-2 and i3+3, the first dose where the posterior probability (under this prior) that the toxicity rate exceeds the target is greater than the threshold (0.95 by default), and all doses above it, are excluded.
Impose monotonicity using isotonic regression (pool adjacent violators): where monotonicity is violated, the estimates of toxicity at the respective doses are replaced with their average. Each dose has equal weight in this average, whatever the number of subjects on it.
We then select the dose with isotonically transformed toxicity rate estimate closest to the target toxicity rate.
If there is a tie, if the toxicity rate estimate is above the target toxicity rate then the lower dose is selected, if the toxicity rate estimate is below the target toxicity rate then the higher dose is selected.

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
mTPI
The E, S, D decision rule uses the Beta-Binomial distribution of the toxicity rate on a dose with a prior of Beta(1, 1). The Unit Probability Mass (UPM) is then calculated for three intervals: the interval below the target toxicity band, the interval corresponding to the target toxicity band and the interval above the target toxicity band. The UPM is the probability mass of the area divided by the length of the interval. The decision is then based on the interval with the highest UPM, E if its below the target toxicity band, S if it is the target toxicity band and D if its above the target toxicity band.
Below Figure 1 is taken from Guo et al. (2017). It shows the UPM in the target interval and above the target interval. It also illustrates what was perceived as a problem with the mTPI method, that gave rise to the development separately of mTPI-2, i3+3 and BOIN. With a target toxicity rate of 0.3 and target band of [0.25, 0.35], with 6 observations on a dose of which 3 had experienced a Dose Limiting Toxicity (DLT), the decision by the mTPI method is to Stay. It was generally considered that this was not safe decision.






Figure 1: UPM in mTPI

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
mTPI-2
The E, S, D decision rule of mTPI-2 modifies that of mTPI by dividing the probability range into strips of equal width. The strips (with the possible exception of the first and the last whihc may need to be smaller) are the same width as the target toxicity band) and divide up the range above and below that band. The Unit Probability Mass (UPM) is then calculated for each of these strips and the strip with the highest UPM found. The decision is then based on the strip with the highest UPM, E if its below the target toxicity band, S if it is the target toxicity band and D if its above the target toxixcity band.
Below Figure 2 is taken from Guo et al. (2017). It shows the UPM for various strips with a target toxicity rate of 0.3 and target band of [0.25, 0.35], with 6 observations on a dose of which 3 had experienced a Dose Limiting Toxicity (DLT), the decision by the mTPI-2 method is to De-escalate.






Figure 2: UPM in mTPI

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
i3+3
i3+3 bases its E, S, D decisions simply on the observed toxicity rate. If \(x\) is the number of observed toxicities at dose \(d\), and \(n\) the total number of observations, then

If \(\frac{x}{n}< p_L\), then escalated to the next dose (E).
Else if \(p_L < \frac{x}{n} < p_U\), then stay at this dose (S)
Else if \(p_U < \frac{x}{n}\), then

If \(\frac{x-1}{n} < p_L\), then stay at this dose (S).
Else, de-escalate (D).

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
BOIN
Based on the target Toxicity Band [\(p_L\), \(p_U\)], BOIN uses a formula to calculate the “optimal” boundaries \(\lambda_l\), \(\lambda_u\) to compare the observed toxicity rates to, which minimize incorrect (E, S, D) decisions: \[
\lambda_l = \frac{log \left(\frac{1-p_l}{{1-p_T}} \right)}{log\left(\frac{p_T(1-p)}{p_l(1-p_T)}\right)}
\]
\[
\lambda_u = \frac{log \left(\frac{1-p_T}{{1-p_u}} \right)}{log\left(\frac{p_u(1-p_T)}{p_T(1-p_u)}\right)}
\]
If \(x\) is the number of observed toxicities at dose \(d\), and \(n\) the total number of observations, then

If \(\frac{x}{n} < \lambda_l\) then escalate to the next dose (E).
Else if \(\lambda_l < \frac{x}{n} < \lambda_u\) then stay at this dose (S).
Else if \(\lambda_u < \frac{x}{n}\) then de-escalate (D).

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
3+3
3+3 does not use a target toxicity rate. It always uses cohorts of 3 and decides what to do next from the number of toxicities (DLTs) in the cohort just treated:

The first cohort is allocated to the dose set by Initial dose index.
After a cohort at a new dose:

0 toxicities: escalate to the next dose.
1 toxicity: treat a second, confirmation, cohort of 3 at the same dose.
2 or 3 toxicities: stop, the MTD is the dose below.

After a confirmation cohort:

0 toxicities: escalate to the next dose.
1 or more toxicities: stop, the MTD is the dose below.

If the rules say escalate from the highest dose, the trial stops and the MTD is the highest dose.
If the maximum number of subjects has been reached and the cohort did not stop the trial for toxicity, the trial stops and the MTD is the current dose (no confirmation cohort is treated after 1 toxicity).
If the MTD would be the dose below the lowest dose, the trial stops with the MTD “below the first dose”, and no expansion cohort is treated.

If Include final validation cohort is selected, then when the rules above say stop with the MTD at the dose below, a validation cohort of 3 is first treated at that dose, provided the current dose is not the lowest dose, the maximum number of subjects has not been reached, and the dose below has fewer than 6 subjects. Otherwise the trial stops as above. After a validation cohort, counting all the subjects on that dose:

Fewer than 2 toxicities: the trial stops and this dose is the MTD. If the dose still has fewer than 6 subjects (possible when it is below the initial dose) and the maximum number of subjects has not been reached, another validation cohort is treated at it first and these rules are applied again.
2 or more toxicities: a validation cohort is treated at the next dose down (and these rules are applied again), provided this is not the lowest dose, the maximum number of subjects has not been reached, and the dose below has fewer than 6 subjects. Otherwise the trial stops and the MTD is the dose below.

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
Introduction
To open the application, select FACTS Dose Escalation from your Start menu. At different points in the FACTS GUI, the user is required to make decisions about how to model or simulate various aspects of a clinical trial. To simplify data entry, FACTS shows the user only the information that is relevant to the current decisions.
FACTS has a tabbed design to allow entry of different categories of information about the design.
The File menu allows the user to create a new design, open an existing design, save a design, or copy a design to a new name (Save as). The saved design includes all parameters entered as well as simulation results, if they have been produced.
The Settings menu provides the ability to configure how simulation jobs should be submitted to the Grid. Selecting whether to execute simulations locally or on the Grid is done from the Simulation tab.
The Help menu allows the user to learn more about the FACTS software and verify the application’s version number.
Finally, note that in all tabs of the application, red exclamation points






Figure 4



indicate errors in data entry from the user that must be corrected. Moving the cursor over the exclamation point causes a pop-up help text indicating what the error is, helping the user remedy the error.

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
Treatment Arms
The Study > Treatment Arms tab (Figure 5) provides an interface for specifying the various dose levels available for use in the trial.
The user may add doses either explicitly or by auto-generation, as depicted below. The user may also edit the Dose Names within the table by double clicking on any existing dose name, however the index cannot be edited.






Figure 5: Treatment Arms

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
Explicitly Defined
The Virtual Subject Response > Explicitly Defined > Toxicity sub-tab provides an interface for specifying one or more Toxicity profiles.
Toxicity profiles may be added, deleted, and renamed using the table and corresponding buttons on the left hand side of the screen in Figure 6. Toxicity values are entered directly into the Probability of Toxicity column of the table, and the graphical representation of these toxicity values updates accordingly. The graph may be modified by plotting the log of the dose strength as the x-axis, and by plotting the logit or the probability of toxicity as the y-axis.
This graph – as with all graphs in the application – may be easily copied using the ‘Copy Graph’ option in the context menu accessed by right-clicking on the graph. The user is given the option to copy the graph to their clipboard (for easy pasting into other applications, such as Microsoft Word or PowerPoint), or to save the graph as an image file.






Figure 6: Toxicity Virtual Subject Response (bCRM)

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
Options tab
The first option to choose in the Design > Options tab is the underlying algorithm to be used for the escalation, de-escalation and overdose rules. The choices are:

BOIN (Yuan et al. 2016)
mTPI (Ji et al. 2010)
mTPI-2 (Guo et al. 2017)
i3+3 (Liu et al. 2020)
3+3 (Liu et al. 2013)







Figure 7



Options that are common to all algorithms are:

Max Number of Cohorts: This in conjunction with the cohort size gives the maximum sample size of the trial. After the selected number of cohorts have been included, no further cohorts will be included and the MTD will be selected according to the respective algorithm.
Cohort Size: The number of trial participants included in each cohort. In 3+3, this defaults to “3” and cannot be changed. The maximum sample size of the trial is simply: Max Trial Size (cohorts) * Cohort Size.
Cohort Expansion: The user can specify that after the dose escalation phase of the trial has completed, the simulation is to include an ‘expansion cohort’ (allocated at the final estimate of the MTD) and how large that expansion cohort will be. For 3+3 the expansion dose is the last dose used, or the dose below it if that dose had more than one toxicity. For the other methods it is the MTD selected at the end of the trial (see The Rules Based Methods). If the MTD is below the lowest dose, there is no expansion cohort.

The further options depend on the chosen design algorithm chosen. Please select the algorithm of interest to learn more. If you are interested in mTPI, mTPI-2, BOIN or i3+3, please select “Non 3+3” in the first stage.

Non 3+33+3


Given all the options specified, the matrix of dosing decisions is displayed on the right hand side. This shows the dosing decision given the number of subject treated at the current dose and the number of toxicities observed:

E Escalate
S Stay
D De-escalate
DU De-escalate and do not revisit







Figure 8: mTPI Design tab shwoing the decision matrix on the right hand side



As an example, if the value of row 2, column 6 is “E”, the algorithm would want us to escalate to the next dose if we had observed 2 toxicities in 6 trial participants.
Additional options include:

Maximum probability that dose exceeds target toxicity: This is an option to prevent re-escalating to a dose (the “DU” or Do not Use category in the decision matrix) if the posterior probability (based on a Beta-Binomial model per dose) that the toxicity rate is above the target toxicity is greater than the selected value (0.95 is the default). The posterior uses a Beta(1, 1) prior and the data on that dose only. If the decision at the dose below a DU dose is Escalate, the design stays at the dose below instead. If the lowest dose is DU, the trial stops. In BOIN a dose can only be DU once at least 3 subjects have been treated on it.
Stop if next dose already has X subjects: This is an option that allows an early stopping rule to be specified that if the dose to be allocated next already has the maximum number of subjects on it then it is declared the MTD. Setting this value shrinks the size of the decision matrix.
Target Toxicity boundaries: The user specifies target toxicity rate, as well as the lower and upper acceptable bounds on the toxicity rate, effectively creating four distinct buckets for doses:

Underdosing: Doses with a toxicity rate falling into the [0,lower bound] bucket
Target: Doses with a toxicity rate falling into the (lower bound,target] bucket
Excess Toxicity: Doses with a toxicity rate falling into the (Target,upper bound] bucket
Unacceptable Toxicity: Doses with a toxicity rate falling into the (Upper bound,1] bucket

These bounds are then used in the different algorithms to create the decision table.







CautionBOIN





BOIN has extra options compared to mTPI, mTPI-2 and i3+3:

Use default BOIN bounds: Whether or not the lower and upper toxicity bound should be calculated automatically using the BOIN defaults (lower bound = 0.6*target, upper bound = 1.4*target), or whether they are chosen by the user.
Stay when seeing 1/3 toxicities: Whether or not to overwrite the algorithm’s decision to stay at the current dose level when seeing 1 DLT in 3 trial participants. This is useful to mimic the behavior of 3+3 which is often expected by clinicians.
De-escalate when seeing 2/6 toxicities: Whether or not to overwrite the algorithm’s decision to de-escalate from the current dose level when seeing 2 DLTs in 6 trial participants. This is useful to mimic the behavior of 3+3 which is often expected by clinicians.







Initial dose index: The user may specify the dose level that the first cohort will be allocated to. Might be useful in cases where we believe there is a (small) chance the initial cohort will experience DLTs. In a real world situation, observing too many DLTs on the first dose level likely terminates the study, whereas if we had started at dose level 2, we have a fall back dose level to de-escalate to.
Include final validation cohort: Whether, when the trial would stop with the MTD at the dose below the current dose, to first treat a validation cohort of 3 at that dose to confirm it (see 3+3).

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
To run simulations
Click in the check box in each of the rows corresponding the to the scenarios to be run. FACTS displays a row for each possible combination of the ‘profiles’ that have been specified: - baseline response, dose response, longitudinal response, accrual rate and dropout rate. Or simply click on “Select All”.
Then click on the “Simulate” button.
During simulation, the user may not modify any parameters on any other tab of the application. This safeguard ensures that the simulation results reflect the parameters specified in the user interface.
When simulations are started, FACTS saves all the study parameters, and when the simulations are complete all the simulation results are saved in results files in a “_results” folder in the same directory as the “.facts” file. Within the “_results” folder there will be a sub-folder that holds the results for each scenario.

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
How many simulations to run?

After first entering a design it is worth running just a small number of simulations such as 10 to check that the scenarios and design have been entered correctly. If all 10 simulations of a ‘null’ scenario are successful, or all 10 simulations of what was intended to be an effective drug scenario are futile, it is likely there has been a mistake or misunderstanding in the specification of the scenarios or the final evaluation or early stopping criteria.
Once the design and scenarios look broadly correct, it is usually worth quickly collecting rough estimates of the operating characteristics using around 100 simulations for each scenario. 100 simulations is enough to spot designs having very poor operating characteristics such as very high type-1 error, very poor power, a strong tendency to stop early for the wrong reason, or poor probability of selecting the correct target. 100 simulations is also usually sufficient to spot problems with the data analysis such as poor model fits and significant bias in the posterior estimates.
Typically 1,000 simulations of each scenario of interest is required to get estimates of the operating characteristics precise enough to compare designs and tune the parameters. (Very roughly rates of 5% (such as type-1 error) can be estimated to about +/-1.5% and rates of around 80% (such as power) estimated +/- 2.5%)
Finally around 10,000 simulations of the scenarios of interest is required to give confidence in operating characteristics of a design and possibly to select between the final shortlisted designs (Approximately rates of 5% can be estimated to about +/-0.5% and rates of around 80% estimated +/- 1%).

There may be many operating characteristics need to be compared over a number of scenarios, such as expected sample size, type-1 error, power, probability of selecting a good dose as the target and quality of estimation of the dose-response.
However frequently these will be compared over a range of scenarios, it may not be necessary to run very large number of simulations for each scenario if a design shows a consistent advantage on the key operating characteristics over the majority of the scenarios.

Simulation results
In the main screen the summary results that are usually of principal interest are displayed, the results summarised by scenario.

Show more columns: Allows the user to open additional windows on the simulation results, the windows available are:

All: A window containing all the summary results columns
Highlights: (all) a separate window with the results shown on the main tab
Allocation, Observed: (all) summary results of the number of subjects allocated, the number allocated to each dose, the number of toxicities observed and the number of toxicities observed per dose
Simulation Results: a window displaying the individual simulation results for each simulation of the currently selected scenario

Explore Results: opens the FACTS built in options for visualizing the results for both the currently selected scenario and across all scenarios. See Section 11 below for a description of the graphs.
Aggregate: opens a control that allows the user create aggregated results files from all the scenarios. The user can select which scenarios to include, and whether the results should be pivoted by dose. The resulting files are stored in the simulation results folder.
Open in R: If aggregated files have been created then clicking this button on the simulations tab will open control that allows the user to select which aggregations to load into data frames as R is opened. Otherwise it will offer to open R using the files in the currently selected scenario.
Right Click Menu: right clicking the mouse on a row of results in the simulation tab brings up a ‘local’ menu of options:

Open results folder: Opens a file browser in the results folder of the scenario, allowing swift access to any of the results files.
Simulation results: Opens a window displaying the individual simulation results for each simulation of the currently selected scenario
Open in R: opens a control that will launch R, first loading the selected files in the results folder as data frames.
View Graphs: launches the graph viewer to view the results of the currently selected scenario.




MCMC Settings






Figure 10



The first two values specify two standard MCMC parameters –

The length of burn-in is the number of the initial iterations whose results are discarded, to allow the sampled values to settle down.
The number of samples is the number of subsequent iterations whose results are recorded in order to give posterior estimates of the values of interest (in this case α and β).

If the Number of MCMC samples to output value is set to N, where N > 0, then all the sampled values at each interim in the first N simulations are output, allowing the user to check convergence.
The MCMC output thinning parameter can be used to reduce the amount of data output to the MCMC file. It does not reduce the amount of MCMC samples used within the model fitting.
To obtain the MCMC sampled values for a particular simulation, keep the same Random number seed and use Start at simulation to specify the simulation in question and run just 1 simulation.

FACTS Grid Simulation Settings
If you have access to a computational grid, you may choose to have your simulations run on the grid instead of running them locally. This frees your computer from the computationally intensive task of simulating so you can continue other work or even shutdown your PC or laptop. In order to run simulations on the grid, it must first be configured, this is normally done via a configuration file supplied with the FACTS installation by the IT group responsible for the FACTS installation.

text:
Aggregation
Aggregation combines the csv output from multiple scenarios into fewer csv files. The Aggregate… button displays a dialog which allows the user to select what to aggregate.






Figure 13



The default location for the aggregated files is the results directory for the study, but this can be changed.
Aggregation may be performed with or without pivoting on group, or both.

Unpivoted files will have one row for each row in the original files.
In pivoted files each original row will be split into one row per dose, plus two extra rows for ‘below lowest’ and ‘above highest’.

Where there is a group of columns for each dose, they will be turned into a single column with each value on a new row.
If there is no value for the below lowest or above highest rows, they will be left blank.
Values in columns that are independent of group will be repeated on each row.


The default is to aggregate all scenarios, but any combination may be selected.
Pressing “Aggregate” generates the aggregated files.
Each type of csv file is aggregated into a separate csv file whose name begins agg_ or agg_pivot_, so agg_summary.csv will contain the rows from each of the summary.csv files, unpivoted. cohortsNNN.csv files are aggregated into a single agg_[pivot_]cohorts.csv file. Doses.csv is identical for all scenarios and so is not aggregated.
Each aggregated file begins with the following extra columns, followed by the columns from the original csv file:

text:
Allocation Box and Whisker plot






Figure 15: Allocation Box and Whisker plot



This graph displays a box and whisker plot of the number of subjects allocated to each dose over the simulations. These plots show:

The mean allocation over all simulations at each dose plotted as a solid line.
The median value is plotted as a dashed line.
The 25-75th quantile range is plotted as the “box” portion of each point.
The “whiskers” extend to the largest and smallest values within 1 ½ times the interquartile range from either end of the box.
Points outside the whisker range are considered outliers, and are plotted as small blue dots. Note that it may be difficult to see all of these symbols if they are plotted at the same value.

text:
Simulation Allocation History






Figure 17



This graph shows the allocation and toxicity history for an individual simulation. Each dot represents a subject, the dot is colored red if toxicity was observed, and grey otherwise. The subjects’ outcomes are displayed left to right in the order in which they were dosed, and at a height corresponding to the dose they were given.
The graph also indicates the selected MTD based on all the data (and given the algorithm that was chosen). In case an expansion cohort was included, a separate symbol marks the dose that the algorithm would assign patients to had the trial not stopped at that particular sample size (this is in some way a marker to investigate whether the expansion cohort has changed our beliefs about the true MTD).
The graph includes a drop down selector box allowing the user to select which simulated trial is displayed. A history can only be displayed for trials for which a ‘cohorts’ file has been written out.

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
Cohort Responses






Figure 18



This graph shows the dose allocation and resulting toxicities along with the fitted dose-toxicity rate (based on an isotonic regression) for a single simulated trial after the results have been gathered for a specific cohort of a specific trial. Please note that isotonic regression ensures the monotonicity of the dose-toxicity relationship, but might result in the fitted toxicity rate being different (higher or lower) than the observed toxicity rate. The fitted curve is the isotonic regression of the observed toxicity rates, with each dose weighted by its number of subjects. (This differs from the final MTD selection, where each dose has equal weight and, except in BOIN, the posterior mean toxicity rates are used.)
The graph includes a drop down selector box allowing the user to select which simulated trial is displayed, and a further drop down selector box allowing the user to select at which cohort to display the state of the trial.
These details can only be displayed for trials for which a ‘cohorts’ file has been written out.

title: 3+3 / mTPI / mTPI-2 / i3+3 / BOIN
text:
MTD Change on Expansion






Figure 19: MTD change on expansion graph



This graph plots the dose selected as MTD before the results of the expansion cohort are available, against the dose selected as MTD after the expansion cohort results are available. Each simulation result is plotted as a ‘dot’, and the graph is divided up into a grid and dots located in the correct cell in the grid and then arranged within the cell depending on how many results fall into the cell. This allows the relative number of results in each cell to be appraised quickly by eye.
This graph allows the trial designer to see the degree of risk that the determination of the MTD will change as a result of the expansion cohort and whether the risk is predominantly that the determination will increase or decrease.
There are similar graphs showing the change in the estimate of the MED and OSD after the expansion cohort.

Aggregation
The results files can be aggregated using the “Aggregate…” button on the Simulations tab.
The Aggregate… button displays a dialog which allows the user to select what to aggregate:

The default location for the aggregated files is the results directory for the study, but this can be changed.
Aggregation may be performed with or without pivoting on group, or both.

Unpivoted files will have one row for each row in the original files.
In pivoted files each original row will be split into one row per dose, plus two extra rows for ‘below lowest’ and ‘above highest’.

Where there is a group of columns for each dose, they will be turned into a single column with each value on a new row.
If there is no value for the below lowest or above highest rows, they will be left blank.
Values in columns that are independent of group will be repeated on each row.


The default is to aggregate all scenarios, but any combination may be selected.
Pressing “Aggregate” generates the aggregated files.
Each type of csv file is aggregated into a separate csv file whose name begins agg_ or agg_pivot_, so agg_summary.csv will contain the rows from each of the summary.csv files, unpivoted. Files for the two samples are aggregated into separate files. cohortsNNN.csv files are aggregated into a single agg_[pivot_]cohorts.csv file. title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Single Arm Phase 3 with OPC)
text:
3.1 Early Futility
Interim monitoring for early futility will occur at each interim analysis. The trial will stop early for futility at an interim analysis if there is less than a 10% probability that the response rate with the device is superior to the OPC of 66% plus a minimum delta. Formally if:
Pr(π > 0.66+δ) < 0.10, with δ=0.05
crumbs: Dichotomous Endpoint (Single Arm Phase 3 with OPC)

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Single Arm Phase 3 with OPC)
text:
3.2 Early Predicted Success
Interim monitoring for early success will occur at each interim analysis. Early predicted success will be declared if there is a high probability that the response rate with the device is superior to the OPC of 66%. Formally if:
Pr(π > 0.66) > 0.99.
If predicted success is declared, we stop accrual and wait until all patients have the opportunity to complete their 12-month primary endpoint. At this time a decisive analysis is performed to evaluate treatment efficacy.
If the trial is not stopped early for either futility or predicted success, the decisive analysis when all 242 patients have the opportunity to complete follow-up for the 12-month primary endpoint.
crumbs: Dichotomous Endpoint (Single Arm Phase 3 with OPC)

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Single Arm Phase 3 with OPC)
text:
3.3 Entering into FACTS
First, on the Study-Study Info tab, select “Adaptive” in the Design Options.
Next, on the Design-Allocation tab, set Randomization Ratios of 0 for Control and 1 for Trt.
On the Design-Interims tab, we specify that interims will be conducted when 50, 100, 150, or 200 patients have the opportunity to complete their 52 week analysis. We ensure that the box for “Continue follow-up if study stopped for success” is checked. This implies that early success stopping with be “predicted success” once all enrolled patients have 52 weeks of observations, and not claims of success outright at the interim analysis.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


On the Quantities of Interest tab, we add the posterior probability that the response is greater than (0.66+δ) to both the Posterior probabilities and the Decision Quantities sections. In this case, we select δ=0.05, so that we track Pr(P_d>0.71). This will be used for interim futility rules.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


On the Design-Success/Futility Criterion tab, we click on the Interim 1 tab, then enable both the futility and success criteria. Then we add a futility rule that says to stop the trial for futility if Pr(P_d>0.71)<0.10. Then we add a success rule that says we stop for predicted success if Pr(P_d>0.66)>0.99.

We can then simulate the trial on the Simulation tab.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Single Arm Phase 3 with OPC)
text:
4.1 Longitudinal Model
Patients will be assessed at 3, 6, and 12 months following treatment. We use a longitudinal model of the primary endpoint to allow these earlier observations to predict the final 12-month status. The primary endpoint for an individual patient, i, at time t is labeled as Yit. At each interim analysis, some patients will have completed follow-up and we will have observed their 12-months endpoint Yi12. These patients may also have earlier measures of the primary endpoint, such as at 3 and 6 months. There will be patients with earlier observations of the primary endpoint who have not yet reached 12 months of follow-up. We utilize the information from patients with incomplete follow-up to the extent that these earlier observations are correlated with the final 12-month value. A Bayesian model is built to learn how the early endpoints are correlated with the final 12-month endpoint and patients with complete follow-up information this model.
A linear regression model is created for the correlation between the baseline and 12-month, 3-month and 12-month, and 6-month and 12-month values. We suppress the subject index i and refer to the baseline, 3, 6, and 12 month values as Y0, Y3, Y6, and Y12. There are three instances of the model. We model the log PBLAC score and each model instance is identical and has the following structure
\[\left[\log(Y_{12}) \mid \log(Y_0) \sim N\left(\alpha_0 + \beta_0 \log(Y_0), \lambda_0^2\right)\right]\]
\[\begin{aligned} \left[\alpha_6\right] &\sim N\left(1, 2^2\right) \\ \left[\beta_6\right] &\sim N\left(0.5, 1.5^2\right) \\ \left[\lambda_6^2\right] &\sim IG\left(0.6/2,\ 0.6^2/2\right) \end{aligned}\]
Identical models are assumed for the distribution of Y12 given Y2 and Y16 
The joint posterior distribution of α0, α3, α6, β0, β3, β6, λ0, λ3, and λ6, is updated based on all patients with observed values of Y12. This model is then used (using Bayesian imputation within Markov chain Monte Carlo) to inform the primary analysis.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Single Arm Phase 3 with OPC)
text:
4.2 Entering into FACTS
On the Study-Study Info tab, we click on the box to enable longitudinal modeling, and also the box to Enable Special Longitudinal Options. We denote that the binary endpoint is equal to 1 if the continuous response Y is less than log(75)=4.317488. On the right side of the same page, we add visits corresponding to 1, 12, 26, and 52 weeks.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


On the Design-Longitudinal tab, we select “Linear Regression” from the pull-down menu. We select “Model control separately”, and we change the priors to reflect appropriate values for the chosen model.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


Because we have enabled special longitudinal modeling, we need to re-define the response profiles on the continuous scale. On the Virtual Subject Response-Explictly Defined tab, we create 4 new profiles.
We specify the scenarios for achieving a response at 12 months in terms of the mean and standard deviation of the PBLAC score at 12 months. Because we model the log of the PBLAC score in the longitudinal modeling, we also specify the scenarios for achieving a response at 12 months on the log scale. We consider 2 different standard deviations (SDs) for the log of the PBLAC score and calibrate the mean to achieve a specific proportion of patients who would be considered responders. We consider SDs for PBLAC on the log scale of 1 and 0.5. For example, for a standard deviation of 1.0, we need to find the mean of a normal distribution with sd=1 such that the probability of being less than log(75) is equal to 0.66. This value can be obtained through algebra or computational trial and error. It turns out that a mean of 3.0949 will satisfy this condition

4.1 Study

4.3 Execution

4.3.1 Accrual
Add an accrual scenario by clicking the Add button on the far left. Add a region to this profile by clicking the Add button above the table. Set the following parameters:

Region 1 peak accrual rate 3.75 subjects per week, starting at week 0, select ramping up to full accrual in week 12.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (HIV)
text:
4.4 Quantities of Interest
The Quantities of Interest (QOIs) are the criteria on which decisions, interim or final analyses, will be made. Numerous QOIs are available and you may select multiple quantities for evaluation. A basic set of QOIs is provided by default. Additional QOIs may be added by clicking the Add row in the table. A QOI can be removed by clicking the X on the right side of the cell. Each QOI may be edited by clicking on it, which opens a pop-up box.
The trial will be judged a success at the end of the trial (after 400 subjects are completed) if the dose most likely to be the maximum effective dose has a high probability of success in a future trial, i.e. a phase 3 trial. A default QOI already exists to monitor the predictive probability of a future trial. We edit the existing Pr(Succ. Future Trial) quantity by clicking on it and a pop-up box will open. In this box:

Select a Phase of “Future Trial”
Select Test Type of “Superiority”
Specify 250 Subjects Per Arm
Specify a One-sided Alpha of 0.025
Specify a Superiority Margin of 0

The probability of success in the future trial will be calculated for each dose, assuming that dose is the one carried forward into the future trial. Thus, this is a vector quantity.

We also would like to see the probability each dose is the maximum effective dose. In the Probability of being Target box we click Add… and select Max for the target type. Note that this quantity may appear as one of the default QOIs. It is another vector quantity that is calculated for each dose.

Note, the Alternative Name box contains the name seen in the output files for the quantities.
To make decisions in the trial, we must specify which dose will be evaluated, thus reducing the vector quantity above to a scalar quantity. This information is captured in the Decision Quantities (Scalars) window at the bottom right. We click Add… and a popup window opens. We select:

QOI(Vector Quantity) of Pr(Succ.Future Trial): N=250; Sup. α=0.025; δ=0
Evaluation Dose: Greatest Pr(Max)


We deleted all the other default QOIs to reduce the amount of output, however they can be left entered in which case they will be computed, and the values output, but they will have no impact on the simulation of the trial.
For the Standard Evaluation Variables at the bottom:

We will not be using the Clinically Significant Difference (CSD), so leave it at its default of 0.1
Specify the Default QOIs compare to: Control
Specify the Trial Type as: Superiority

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (HIV)
text:
4.5 Design

4.5.1 On Setting Priors
On setting priors – as a rule it is recommended that the user specifies weakly informative priors rather than non-informative ones. There are a number of reasons for this:

In a few circumstances non-informative priors can end up being informative.
What values make a prior non-informative vary depending on the range of the value being estimated, a measure with a SD of 1000 requires quite a different value for a prior to be non-informative than one with an SD of 1.
Measures that are log-odds or log hazard ratios can have parameters that are then exponentiated and used as parameters to other distributions as a maximum these values should have range of (-10,10) and (-5,5). Greater than this and numeric overflows can occur.
Using a “non-informative” prior can sometimes be used as an excuse for not thinking about the prior. Not thinking about a prior is never a good idea.
There are some priors, particularly for the variance parameters of hierarchical models where (as we use inverse Gamma distributions for the priors, weakly informative priors are preferred to uninformative ones [Gelman 2006, “Prior distributions for variance parameters in hierarchical models” Bayesian Analysis Vol 1 Number 3]
When simulating clinical trial designs there is a balance to be struck between the MCMC sample length used in the within-trial analyses and the number of simulations run. Weakly informative priors can help the MCMC to converge and allow us to use shorter sample lengths.

For many priors the weakly informative is easily judged where the priors directly correspond to values that we are simulating. Others are not so easily judged, for these we used “non-informative” priors ran some simulations and looked at the means and SDs of the posterior estimates of the parameters over all the scenarios and then based a weakly informative prior on these. You will see these priors below being described as having an “initial un-informative” prior and then a weakly informative one. Care must be taken with this approach to not over specify a prior based on the selection of scenarios, and it must be borne in mind that the scenarios may not capture the full potential variability in what the “truth value in nature” might actually be.


4.5.2 Dose Response
Select the ‘Independent Dose Model’ option; this option does not do dose response modeling.
Use a prior mean for the log-odds for each dose of 0.4 with a standard deviation of 0.5.

Initial dose: μ0 mean = 0.4, Std Dev of mean = 0.5 (μ0 ~ N (log(0.6/0.4), 0.52), and log(0.6/0.4) = 0.4055, the log odds of the control rate)
The prior was selected to be centered around the log-odds of the control rate.




4.5.3 Frequentist Analysis
The required alpha and the contrast coefficients can be set for the frequentist analysis trend test.
We leave them unchanged.


4.5.4 Allocation
Because we selected Non-Adaptive on the Study Info screen, only fixed allocation is available, specify a ratio of 1 on control and on each study dose.


4.5.5 Success/Futility Criteria
We will define a trial to be successful if the probability of success in the future trial is >0.80. A trial will be defined as futile if the probability of success in the future trial is <0.50. A trial that finishes with a probability of success in phase 3 of between 0.5 and 0.80 is deemed inconclusive.
Set the following parameters for Futility Criteria:

Select the QOI to be the probability of success in a future trial that we defined on the Quantities of Interest tab.
Select a Condition of <
Enter a threshold of 0.50


Set the following parameters for Success Criteria:

Select the QOI to be the probability of success in a future trial that we defined on the Quantities of Interest tab.
Select a Condition of >
Enter a threshold of 0.80


Here we only have one criterion for futility and one for success. You may enter multiple criteria and combine them using AND (all criteria must be met to trigger the rule) or OR (at least one of the criteria must be met to trigger the rule).

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (HIV)
text:
4.6 Simulation
For an initial check, set the number of simulations to run to 10, Select All, then press Simulate.
If the results look reasonable, increase the number of simulations to run to 100, Select All, then press Simulate.
What constitutes ‘reasonable’?

Only a small proportion (<2.5%) of early or late success outcomes for the ‘Flat’ response scenario, these are equivalent to type-1 errors.
A high proportion (~80%) of early or late success outcomes for the ‘Linear’ or ‘Peak at 3’ response scenarios, these give our estimate of the designs ‘power’.
A good proportion of trials for the ‘Linear’ or ‘Peak at 3’ scenarios that select the correct dose as having the maximum response. What constitutes a ‘good proportion’ cannot be specified at a fixed level. What can be reasonably achieved is very dependent on the number of doses, number of subjects, nature of the endpoint and the details of the dose response scenario. In this example ~80% is achievable, but it is not uncommon for it to be difficult to be better than 50%.

To achieve more precise estimates of the operating characteristics, you should run 1,000 or 10,000 simulations of each scenario. We only ran 100 simulations here for example purposes.
By default, FACTS simulations run locally on your computer. If you have access to a grid and your FACTS installation has been correctly configured you may use the grid’s parallel computing capabilities to improve computation speed. Select “on Grid”. Select All and then press Simulate again.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (HIV)
text:
4.7 Results
Check the number of simulations per scenario (note the order of the scenarios) and the mean # of subjects per scenario.
Check following results:

Type I error: For the ‘Flat’ response scenario, only 3.8% of the trials were late successes. These are equivalent to type-1 errors and we want them less than 2.5%.
Power: For the ‘Linear’ or ‘Peak at 3’ response scenarios, 66% and 50% respectively, of trials were late successes. These give our estimates of the designs ‘power’ and are less than the desired 80%. We will hope to improve the power in the adaptive designs simulated later in this tutorial




A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


Note that the sum of the proportions of success and futility outcomes may be less than 1 for a scenario; the remainder is the probability of an inconclusive study –not crossing either the success or futility boundary. It is important to treat ‘inconclusive’ consistently. As in the ‘Flat’ case, we are only happy with the type 1 error if inconclusive studies are unlikely to be treated as successful, we can’t include the inconclusive studies with the successful ones in the other scenarios when we are estimating the power of the design.
Check the ability to correctly determine the target. We click the Show Other Columns button, then click “Probabilities”, and look at the probabilities of a dose being the maximum effective dose.



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


Note that Dose 4 is correctly identified in 75% of the simulations of the Linear scenario and Dose 3 is correctly identified in 88% of the simulations of the ‘Peak at 3’ scenario. So this aspect of the design looks promising.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (HIV)
text:
5.1 Dose Response Model
The incorporation of side-effects in the endpoint means that the response may not be monotonic across doses, so a normal dynamic linear model (NDLM) is used.
Control (placebo) is included in the model.
We assume the dose strengths give a linear range of doses in terms of the expected change in dose effect, so they are given dose levels of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (on the Study Treatment Arms tab).
The probability of a response for a subject on dose d is Pd. We will model on the log-odds response:
\[\theta_d = \log\left(\frac{P_d}{1 - P_d}\right) \text{ for } d = 0,1,\ldots,4\]
The prior for the control is:
\[\theta_0 \sim N\left(\log\left(\frac{0.6}{0.4}\right), 0.5^2\right)\]
The prior for each subsequent dose is centered at the mean of the previous dose:
\[\theta_d \sim N\left(\theta_{d-1}, \tau^2\right) \text{ for } d = 1,\ldots,4\]
The smoothing parameter has prior:
\[\tau^2 \sim IG(0.5, 0.32)\]
(using the usual Bayesian α, β parameterisation)

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (HIV)
text:
5.2 Design
To add the dose-response model, we make changes to the Design -- Dose Response tab.

5.2.1 Dose Response
Set the following parameters:

Select the Simple NDLM, a Normal Dynamic Linear Model
For the prior distributions for the 2 parameters for this model

Initial dose: μ0 mean = 0.4, Std Dev of mean = 0.5 (μ0 ~ N (log(0.6/0.4), 0.52), and log(0.6/0.4) = 0.4055, the log odd of the control rate). This prior is the same as was used in the fixed design with an independent model.
Tau smoothing parameter: τμ = 0.8 τn = 1, (0.8 is used because given the 3 response scenarios, when using a very weak prior for tau, the mean of the posterior distribution for tau ranges between 0.5 and 0.9)

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (HIV)
text:
5.3 Longitudinal Modeling
To add the longitudinal model, on the Study -> Study Info tab, make the following changes:

Check the “Adaptive” option
Check the “Use Longitudinal Modeling” option.
Auto generate 3 visits, starting at 4 with a spacing of 4

The Visit Name may be edited by double-clicking on it.


5.3.1 Simulating Subjects Longitudinal Data
Because we are using longitudinal modelling, on the Virtual Subject Response tab we now have a Longitudinal tab in which to specify how subjects’ responses at the intermediate visits are to be simulated. To avoid this specification being too onerous – requiring transition probabilities to be specified for every dose in each response scenario - FACTS provides a mechanism where you specify one set of transition probabilities and these are then adjusted for each dose in each scenario to give the required final rate.
Assume the 3 month rate to be simulated is Π.
We model the transition matrix for each time step t by the probability of “entering”, PE, (becoming a response if previously a fail) and the probability of “retaining”, PR, (remaining a response if previously a response).
\[\begin{array}{cc} & \begin{array}{cc} 0 \qquad\quad & \quad 1 \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 1 \end{array} & \begin{bmatrix} 1 - P_t^E & P_t^E \\ 1 - P_t^R & P_t^R \end{bmatrix} \end{array}\]
To fit Π use an offset on the log-odds scale, φ:
\[P_t^X = \frac{\exp\left(\log\left(\frac{P}{1-P}\right) + \varphi\right)}{1 + \exp\left(\log\left(\frac{P}{1-P}\right) + \varphi\right)}\]
Assume the following default transition probabilities:
\[P_1^E = 0.6,\ P_2^E = 0.4,\ P_3^E = 0.2\]
\[P_2^R = 0.8,\ P_3^R = 0.9\]
For each value of Π the program fits the appropriate value of φ.

5.3.2 Fitting a Longitudinal Model
In order to make use of the longitudinal data, the longitudinal modeling needs to be specified within the Design – Longitudinal tab. This specifies how the visit data will be analyzed in order to impute final results for subjects who have not completed their final visit. For each visit, we model the probability of being a responder at the final visit conditional on the outcome at the current visit.
Set the following parameters:

Select the Beta Binomial model



Select to model control separately. This means that control subjects with an unobserved final visit will be imputed using only the data from other control subjects to inform the transition probabilities between early visits and the final visit. For subjects on the active doses, the transition probabilities will be informed by pooling data across the active doses.
For Model Priors, select: same priors across all model instances and visits. Separate priors can be specified for each model instance (e.g. the control model and the active doses model) and visit, but for simplicity we use one set of priors for all time points and doses:

P(response at 3 month observation | response at visit) ~ Beta(4,1). A Beta distribution for the probability of final response given being a responder at the visit equivalent to having 4 observations of final responders and 1 observation of a non-responder (i.e a mean of 80%). Thus we are specifying a weakly informative prior in line with our expectation that someone who is a responder will remain a responder.
P(response at 3 month observation | no response at visit) ~ Beta(2,2). A Beta distribution for the probability of final response given being a responder at the visit equivalent to having 2 observations of final responders and 2 observation of a non-responder (i.e. a mean of 50%). Here we are specifying a weakly informative prior in line with an expectation of a roughly 50% response rate.
These are weakly informative priors that will be overwhelmed by the observed data during the trial – which has a maximum sample size of 400 and with early stopping we will require to have enrolled at least 100 subjects. Also note that as we give every arm the same prior we will not be biasing the results in favor of one arm rather than another.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (HIV)
text:
5.4 Allocation
On the Design – Allocation tab we will specify the details for the adaptive randomization. The goal is to preferentially allocate subjects to the most promising arm(s).
In the adaptive design we are going to increase the proportion allocated to control. As we are comparing each dose to control, a rule of thumb if that the greatest power is when the allocation ratio is sqrt(D) : 1 : 1 : 1 … where D is the number of treatment arms being compared to control. Although this gives greater statistical power, such an allocation can be unpopular with clinical teams as it means there will be less data on the dose selected at the end of the trial compared to using a 1:1:1 … ratio. An advantage of response adaptive allocation is that it tends to boost the allocation to the dose that is eventually selected at the end of the trial making this greater allocation to control more acceptable.
Initially we will use a fixed allocation of 2:1:1:1:1, then once adaptation starts (after 80 subjects enrolled), randomly allocate in a block size of 6 where 2 in every block are allocated to the control arm, and the remainder of the block is allocated adaptively.
We will conduct an interim every month adjusting the allocation of subjects to the study drug doses to be in proportion to the probability that the dose is the maximally effective arm. If the randomization probability for any dose falls below 0.05 then we temporarily drop the dose and re-normalize the probabilities for the remaining doses.
Set the following parameters:

Select Adaptive Allocation
Set the allocation ratio to be used before the first interim to be 2 for control and 1 for each study dose
For the control arm check the “Fix Alloc” option and specify that after the first interim it should be allocated 2 times in each randomization block.
Set the Post first interim block size to 6
Select Add… under Adaptive Allocation Target

Select QOI: Pr(Max)
Select Weight For: Information

We chose to weight for information because it is less aggressive on the adjusting of the randomization probabilities compared to weighting for probability. Either may be used.

Set Relative Weight to 1

Set the “Allocation probability set to zero for values lower than” at 0.05
Set Raise allocation to power: 1

If you choose a power less than 1 the adaptive randomization will be less aggressive. Different options could be examined.

5.6 Success/Futility Criteria
Under Design-Success/Futility Criteria we specify the criteria for early stopping for success and futility as well as the final evaluation criteria.

5.6.1 Interim 1 Criteria
On this tab we specify the interim analyses criteria for early stopping of accrual. In this example we keep the same criteria across all interims. If we wanted to have different criteria for different interims we would select Create new interim criteria at interim and specify the interim where criteria changes.
Stop early for futility if there are at least 100 subjects randomized and the dose most likely to be the maximum effective dose has a probability of success in phase 3 of < 15%. We also require that at least 50 subjects have been enrolled on the selected maximum effective dose.

5.6.2 Final Evaluation
The final analysis is used to judge whether or not the trial is successful. If an early accrual stopping for futility rule is met, then this criterion is evaluated at that time. If an early accrual stopping for success rule is met, then this criterion is evaluated after all subjects have been followed through the 3-month endpoint. If no early stopping rule is met, then the criteria are evaluated after all subjects have been followed through the 3-month endpoint. The final evaluation criteria stay the same as in the fixed design.
The trial will be judged a success if:

the dose most likely to be the maximum effective dose has a probability of success in phase 3 of > 80%.

The trial will be judged futile if:

the dose most likely to be the maximum effective dose has a probability of success in phase 3 of < 50%.

5.7 Simulation
Similar to the fixed design, we set the number of simulations to run to 10 as an initial check, Select All, then press Simulate.
If the results look reasonable, increase the number of simulations to run to 100, Select All, then press Simulate. The criteria for “reasonable” are the same as stated above in 4.6. When the design is calibrated you should run a higher number, 1,000 or 10,000 simulations.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (HIV)
text:
5.8 Results
Check the number of simulations per scenario (note the order of the scenarios) and the mean # of subjects per scenario.
Check the type-1 error and power, as well as the success to futility flip-flops. The success to futility flip-flops need to be checked because we continue follow-up if enrollment is stopped early for success.

Note that the power of the study in the Linear scenario is approximately 84%, (0.57+0.27), and the power in the Peak scenario is approximately 62% (0.30+0.32). The type I error is determined by looking at the Flat scenario, and is 2%. It is important to note that small proportions are not well estimated at only 100 simulations, so, as we noted above, once calibrated the design should be run with 1,000 or 10,000 simulations. The Success to Futility Flip flop is 0, but should be checked again when a higher number of simulations are performed.
Check the ability to correctly determine the target:



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


Note that Dose 4 is correctly identified in 79% of the simulations of the Linear scenario and Dose 3 is correctly identified in 83% of the simulations of the ‘Peak at 3’ scenario. So this aspect of the design looks promising.
We can also look at the average number of subjects randomized to these doses in these scenarios:



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


So on average around 74 subjects are allocated to Dose 4 in the Linear scenario and around 79 to Dose 3 in the Peak scenario. Recall that in the fixed design, allocation was 80 per arm, so the adaptive design allocates almost as many subjects to the better performing arms, even with the increased allocation to control. At the same time the average study size has fallen from 400 in the fixed design to between 329 and 366 depending on the scenario.
So whilst maintaining a the desired level of type-1 error (<2.5%), and almost as many subject data on the selected dose, the adaptive design delivers a good chance (30%-57% depending on the scenario) of stopping enrollment early for success, saving on average 10-20% of the sample size, whilst increasing the power by about 15-16 percentage points. A higher number of simulations should be run to confirm these conclusions.
The dose response model fit should also be checked using the View Graph button. Select Per Scenario Graphs. We can select Response and Subject Allocation to see the fit over all the simulations. In the Peak at 3 scenario, we observe that the dose-response model tends to smooth out the peak to some degree. This graph also illustrates that Dose 3 is allocated the highest number of subjects, approximately 79, other than the control dose which had allocation fixed. Alternatively, we can Per Sim: … graphs to view the model fit and various quantities for each simulated trial.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


When comparing the adaptive design to the fixed design you should see the type-1 error remains controlled (proportion of success results under the ‘Flat’ scenario < 0.025), the power of this design is higher and the correct selection of the max dose is similar to the fixed design but tends to be a little better.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Phase 3 Goldilocks)
text:
TipExample files



Download the FACTS files used in this tutorial and open them in FACTS with File > Open.

Core Dichotomous Goldilocks Ex1.facts (Design 1: fixed design)
Core Dichotomous Goldilocks Ex2.facts (Design 2: adaptive design)
Core Dichotomous Goldilocks Ex3.facts (Design 3: adaptive design with longitudinal modeling)





1 Introduction
In this example, we investigate whether a novel medical device is superior to standard of care. The primary endpoint is dichotomous, and defined as freedom from negative outcome within 12 months. After complete follow-up, the final analysis based on a pre-determined p-value controlling the overall type I error below 0.025 will be performed.
This is a confirmatory Phase 3 trial where an adaptive design will be used to select the trial’s final sample size based on the accruing data. Prior to full accrual, several pre-specified interim sample size looks are conducted. At each interim, predictive probabilities are used to determine whether to stop accrual at the current sample size for either expected success or futility or to continue accrual further. This has been referred to in the literature as a “Goldilocks” trial. The design’s goal is to select a sample size not too big, not too small, but just right.
To improve interim decision-making, interim predictive probabilities will incorporate partial data from subjects who have not yet reached their 12-month endpoint through a longitudinal model.
The design is presented in an iterative fashion. Three designs are described:

Fixed Design
Adaptive Design
Adaptive Design with Longitudinal Modeling

Additional FACTS features are incorporated with each successive design. The third design (Adaptive Design with Longitudinal Modeling) represents the complete example.


2 Design 1: Fixed Design
We start with a fixed design.

Select the type of probability that is needed. Here, a p-value on the bottom left portion of the QOI tab is needed. Select ‘Add…’ to create the p-value. Missing data will be ignored and no adjustment for multiple testing will be incorporated. FACTS will now compute this p-value for every treatment included within the Study tab (in this example, there is only one treatment arm).
For a Success/Futility decision to be taken, as well as the quantity to be tested, it is necessary to first specify the treatment arm whose value is to be used in conjunction with the above probability measure. Select the decision quantity associated with the particular treatment that will be used at the final analysis. On the bottom right select ‘Add…’. In the first drop-down menu, having selected the required p-value in the previous step, ‘p-value, Ignore, Unadjusted’ will now be available. The evaluation dose is ‘Trt’, previously defined on the Study Tab.

Pr(failure-free | dose d) = pd
The prior is specified in terms of the log-odds:
θd = logit(pd)
