The design requires 840 subjects. The type I error rate is less than 2.5% and high power is maintained at the high effect sizes.


3 Design 2: Adaptive Design
In this design, we build upon the fixed design described above and add adaptive features. In particular, we incorporate adaptive sample size looks by allowing the trial to stop early for either expected success or futility.
Interim looks are made at the data when 300, 400, 500, 600, and 700 subjects have been accrued. Interim decisions are based on the following two predictive probabilities:

PPn: the predictive probability of superiority for a trial with the currently enrolled sample size of n.
PPcap: the predictive probability of success if the full sample size of 840 were enrolled.

The following adaptive decisions will be made:

At 300, 400, 500, 600, and 700 subjects, if trial success is highly likely with the current sample size accrual will be stopped. The current sample size will be followed through 12 months when a single final analysis is conducted.

More specifically if PPn > 0.90 then accrual will be stopped.




At 500, 600, and 700 subjects, if trial success by the maximum sample size of 840 is small the trial will be stopped for futility.

More specifically if PPCap < 0.01 then the trial will be stopped for futility.





A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


Study/Study Info: We indicate the design is now adaptive.



A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated



Quantities of Interest: The following two steps are needed to define the predictive probability calculations used for interim decision-making.

Create the probabilities that will be used. Select ‘Add…’ on the middle left portion of the QOI tab to create these predictive probabilities. Both are based on predicting the outcome of the current trial, ignore missing data, and make no pre-defined adjustment for multiple testing. One is based on the probability of success with the full trial maximum sample size (840 subjects) while the second is based on the probability of success with the currently enrolled sample size. In each case, success is based on a final p-value for a test of superiority at the 0.0163 level. This p-value cut-off was selected to control the type I error of the adaptive design below 0.025 under the trial’s design assumptions as well as planned sensitivities to those assumptions.





For the interim Success/Futility decisions to be taken, as well as the quantities to be tested, it is necessary to first specify the treatment arm whose value is to be used for each predictive probability calculation. On the bottom right select ‘Add…’. Select each of the predictive probability calculations now defined. For both, the evaluation dose is ‘Trt’, previously defined on the Study Tab.




A screenshot of a social media post Description automatically generated


Design/Interims: Interims are triggered based on the number of subjects enrolled and will occur when 300, 400, 500, 600, and 700 subjects enter the study.



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


Design/Success/Futility Criteria: Interims 1-2 (when 300 and 400 subjects are enrolled) may stop for expected success only while the remaining interims 3-5 (when 500, 600, and 700 subjects are enrolled) may stop for either expected success or futility. Hence, two interim tabs will be defined. The first tab (‘Interim 1’) applies to Interims 1 and 2. The second tab (‘Interim 3’) applies to all subsequent interims, i.e., Interims 3, 4, and 5.
At Interims 1 and 2, the study will stop accrual for expected success if there is a high predictive probability (>90%) of reaching trial success with the current sample size once follow-up is complete.



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


At Interims 3, 4, and 5, the study will stop accrual for expected success if there is a high predictive probability (>90%) of reaching trial success with the current sample size once follow-up is complete. The study will stop for futility if there is a low predictive probability (<1%) of reaching trial success with the maximum sample size of 840 subjects once follow-up is complete.



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


At the final analysis, the study will be declared a success if the final p-value for a test of superiority is less than 0.0163.

4 Design 3: Adaptive Design with Longitudinal Modeling
We can use interim data to predict the outcome of subjects with an unobserved final endpoint. In this example, preliminary data is collected at 1-month (Week 4) and 6-months (Week 26) post-baseline. At the time of each interim analysis, there will be patients who have completed Week 4 and Week 26 failure free and patients that have failed before their Week 52 follow-up. These data are incorporated to the predictive probability calculation through a longitudinal model. Bayesian Multiple imputation is used for calculating the predictive probability.
Study/Study Info: The initial study tab is updated to indicate multiple visits within the visit schedule; at Weeks 4, 26, and 52.
Design/Longitudinal:
For patients with interim data, model the likelihood that a patient that is failure-free at Week 4 and Week 26 will be failure free at Week 52.



A screenshot of a cell phone Description automatically generated


Let the probability of a patient that is failure free by week j being failure free at Week 52 (j = 1 is Week 4 and j=2 is Week 26) for treatment group t (t = 1 is treatment and t = 2 is control) be Ptj. The prior distribution for each of these probabilities is a beta(\(\mathbf{\alpha}_{\mathbf{j}}\mathbf{,}\mathbf{\beta}_{\mathbf{j}}\)) distribution. We use the following prior distributions:

If a patient has a failure by any interim visit (Week 4 or Week 26, or between) then that subject is known to be a failure. No modeling is required for these subjects and the Beta-binomial priors associated with early failures are defined to reflect this assumption.

title: Continuous Endpoint (RAR Design - Chronic Cough)
text:
2.1 Study Info:

Time to primary endpoint is specified as 2 weeks. The primary endpoint of the trial is cough ratio at 2 weeks compared to baseline and lower response corresponds to a subject improving and coughing less frequently. The total number of subjects enrolled is 200 and they will be enrolled sequentially.

title: Continuous Endpoint (RAR Design - Chronic Cough)
text:
2.2 Treatment Arms:

We include a control arm as well as 12 doses of the therapy (25mg – 300mg in increments of 25mg).

title: Continuous Endpoint (RAR Design - Chronic Cough)
text:
2.3 Simulation Scenarios:
We consider three simulations scenarios (pictured below) for the dose-response curves: 1) Low targets where the ED25 = 18mg and ED70= 78mg, 2) Mid targets where the ED25 = 75mg and ED70= 170mg, and 3) High targets where the ED25 = 170mg and ED70= 221mg. Values of the dose-response for the 12 doses of the therapy are specified under virtual subject response for each scenario. We assume a sd = .3 for each dose.

title: Continuous Endpoint (RAR Design - Chronic Cough)
text:
2.4 Accrual:

We assume that 4.6 subjects are accrued per week

title: Continuous Endpoint (RAR Design - Chronic Cough)
text:
2.5 Quantities of Interest:
Target doses: We are interested in finding two target doses: ED25 and ED70. The doses are specified relative to the control so that the doses represent 25% and 70% of the effect of the maximum dose relative to the control dose.



Decision Quantities: These quantities will be used in the trial to define success. In particular, we want to define success if we have found both target doses with some certainty. The evaluation doses are the doses with the greatest probability of being the ED25 or ED70 and if the probability of each of these evaluation doses being the ED25 or ED70 exceeds some threshold we will declare success.

title: Continuous Endpoint (RAR Design - Chronic Cough)
text:
2.6 Dose Response Model:
We assume a sigmoidal dose-response model.

title: Continuous Endpoint (RAR Design - Chronic Cough)
text:
2.7 Allocation:
We will use Adaptive Allocation.
After 10 subjects are enrolled on the control, 150mg and 300mg, we start interims. Post the burn-in of 30 subjects enrolled we allocate a fixed 1 out of every 10 subjects to control. The remaining 9 subjects are allocated equally based on the probability that each is the ED25 and the probability that each is the ED70

title: Continuous Endpoint (RAR Design - Chronic Cough)
text:
2.8 Interims:
Interims occur every 4 weeks after the initial 30 subjects are enrolled.

title: Continuous Endpoint (RAR Design - Chronic Cough)
text:
2.9 Success / Futility Criteria:
There is no early stopping for success or futility in this trial. We declare success once all 200 subjects are enrolled and have their final data if we are certain we have found our target doses. In particular we declare success if we meet the following two requirements

Pr(Dose maxED25 = ED25) > .5 for the dose that is most likely the ED25
Pr(Dose maxED70 = ED70) > .5 for the dose that is most likely the ED70

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (with Predictor)
text:
2.1 Study Info
To simulate this trial, we set up a FACTS file for a time-to-event endpoint (OS) with a time-to event predictor (EFS). We indicate that both EFS and OS events are failures. We set the sample size at 350 patients and we will allow a follow-up period of 156 weeks (3 years) after accrual is complete.

2.2 Treatment Arms
This trial will have two arms, an experimental therapy and a SOC control arm.
Click Add, to add a new Dose, then click twice on the new “Dose 1” to change the default name to “Treatment”.

2.3.1 Predictor

2.3.2 Control Hazard Rate
We then define the time from an EFS event to an OS event, referred to as “Survival Post Progression” SPP. We assume that median SPP on the control arm will be 9 months.



2.3.3 Dose Response
We assume there will be no “Survival Post Progression” SPP difference between treatment and control. Therefore, we define a single hazard ratio scenario for SPP – the null hazard ratio of 1. We assume that no EFS events will be deaths.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (with Predictor)
text:
2.4 Execution

2.4.1 Accrual
Accrual rates into this trial were provided as peak accrual rates per quarter. We define the peak accrual rate in each quarter and assume a linear ramp up within each quarter to the peak accrual rate.



2.4.2 Dropout Rate
We assume no drop-outs.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (with Predictor)
text:
2.5 Quantities of Interest
Next, we define the quantities of interest (QOIs) for this trial. Stopping for futility will be based on having a low probability that the experimental therapy is a clinically meaningful improvement over control in terms of EFS. We define the clinically significant hazard ratio as 0.8, and so enter this as the delta of -0.2. Success will depend on having a high probability that the experimental therapy has superior EFS. We define these two quantities of interest in terms of the posterior probability of the new therapy versus control on the predictor variable, EFS (zd). Success will also depend on having a high probability of superiority in terms of OS in a future phase III trial. For our prediction of success in a future phase III trial of OS, we assume a trial with 850 events. A trial of this size would be required in order to have 90% power to detect a HR of 0.80 for OS based on a one-sided test at the 0.025 level. We add the predictive probability of phase III success as a quantity of interest.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (with Predictor)
text:
2.6 Design

2.6.1 Predictor Model

2.6.1.1 Hazard Model



2.6.1.2 Dose Response
We set the gamma prior distribution for the hazard rate for EFS on the control arm. We give it the same mean as we used in our virtual patient scenarios and a weight of 1. For the dose response model of the predictor, we use the independent dose response and set the prior as mean 0 with SD 10 for both control and treatment.



2.6.1.3 Relationship to Endpoint
The longitudinal model of OS based on EFS is OS = EFS + SPP. On this tab we set the gamma priors for SPP for treatment and control for the purpose of this longitudinal modelling. We give treatment and control the same prior, with mean equal to the SPP hazard rate we assumed for our virtual patient scenarios. Each prior has weight of 1.




2.6.2 Hazard Model
We now set the gamma prior for the SPP hazard rate. We give this the same prior mean as we defined for our virtual subject response and give it weight 1. We define the dose response model exactly as we did for EFS under the predictor model tab.



2.6.3 Allocation
This trial will equally randomize all patients between treatment and control.



2.6.4 Interims
With 350 patients enrolled within 21 months and an additional follow-up period of 36 months, we expect to observe approximately 175 EFS events and approximately 130 OS events within the maximum duration of the trial. Interim analyses are planned based on the number of observed OS events when approximately 25%, 50%, and 75% of total information on OS has been observed. This corresponds to interims after 32, 65, and 98 OS events have been observed respectively at each interim analysis.



2.6.5 Success / Futility Criteria

2.6.5.1 Interim 1



2.6.5.2 Interim 2



2.6.5.3 Interim 3



2.6.5.4 Final Evaluation

We base early stopping for futility on the minimally clinically significant hazard ratio (HR) of 0.80. If there is a low probability that the experimental therapy provides at least this benefit for EFS the trial may stop early for futility
We base early stopping for success on both the observed benefit for EFS and the likelihood that this benefit would translate to success in a phase III trial with OS as the primary endpoint. If, at an interim analysis we observe both superiority in terms of EFS and a high probability of success for in a future phase III trial, the trial may stop early for success
If the trial is not stopped early it will enroll to the maximum sample size of 350 patients and all enrolled patients will continue to be followed for an additional 36 months. At the final analysis, we evaluate only whether the new experimental therapy will be considered of interest for further study. Success at the end of the trial will be declared if either there is a high probability of superiority in terms of EFS or a high probability of success in a future phase III trial.
The critical values required for early stopping at each interim look as well as for declaring success should the trial continue to completion are shown in the table below. We require more extreme critical values for stopping early in the trial, with fewer observed events than later in the trial when more data has accumulated.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (with Predictor)
text:
3.1 Results

In the null scenario, there is a 72.2% probability of stopping early for futility. There is a 3.6% of early success and a 1.9% probability of declaring success at the final analysis. Therefore, the total probability of success under the null for this phase II trial is 5.5%.
We assess the operating characteristics of the trial here based on 1000 simulations. Most trials enroll to the maximum sample size of 350 patients. In the null scenario, where trials tend to stop early for futility, and in more optimistic EFS HR scenarios where trials tend to stop early for success, the total trial duration is shorter.


3.1.1 Plots
This plot shows the cumulative probability of early futility stopping at each interim analysis under the null scenario. There is >40% probability of stopping at the first interim analysis and an additional 20% probability of stopping at the second interim analysis.
When the EFS HR is 0.70, this trial has a 61.5% probability of early success and a 17.4% probability of success at the final analysis. Therefore, the total probability of success in this scenario is 78.9%.

The following two plots show the distribution of the two QOI for success for the scenario where the HR on EFS is 0.7. We see the probability of superiority on EFS tends to be higher that the predictive probability of success in a future phase III.


The following four plots show interim analyses from a single simulated trial that stopped early for success. We show the interim analysis at 32 events and then at 65 events. The left plot shows the probability of success in a future phase III trial and the right plot shows the probability of superiority for EFS. In this example, we observe a large benefit. At the first interim analysis, the two QOIs are not quite high enough to stop early for success, but they are at the second interim analysis.

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
This tutorial introduces three new dose-response models available beginning in FACTS 6.4. These models are the Simple Linear Model, the Hierarchical Model, and the Linear Hierarchical Model. First we illustrate the Linear and Linear Hierarchical models with dichotomous data. Then we create a design based on the Hierarchical model for time-to-event data.
Screenshots are from the 6.4 release of FACTS. The screenshots provided are approximate and may not reflect the exact layout of the information in later versions of FACTS. The contents of each tab, however, will be consistent with the software.
The designs presented are examples and may not be optimally calibrated.

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
3.1 Study
Start FACTS 6.4 or later, double click on: Core Design – Dichotomous.

Using the menu option “File > Save As”, save this design as “LinearExample” in a convenient location (e.g. in a folder called FACTS\Tutorials--example in your ‘My Documents’ folder).

3.1.1 Study Info
On the Study -> Study Info tab, select the following options:

Under Design Options, select Adaptive, not Fixed
Uncheck Use longitudinal modeling
Under Study information, Recruit subjects Continuously
Set the Maximum number of subjects to be 600
Check “Response indicates negative outcome”
Under Schedule of Post-Baseline Visits, Time to Final Endpoint should be 1 week




3.1.2 Study > Treatment Arms

Include a control treatment arm
Enter “0.5” in the Dose level box and then click Add. Repeat to add dose levels of 0.75, 1, 2.5, and 5.


You do not need to enter anything on the Study -> Variants tab.

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
3.3 Execution

3.3.1 Accrual
Add an accrual scenario by clicking the Add button on the far left, then add 1 region by clicking the Add button above the table. Set the peak accrual rate to 12 subjects per week, to give an overall recruitment period of approximately 50 weeks.
The names of the accrual profile and the region may be renamed by double-clicking on them.



3.3.2 Dropout Rate
Select “No Dropouts”.
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
3.4 Quantities of Interest
FACTS has considerable flexibility in allowing the user to define Quantities of Interest (QOIs) to drive adaptations in the trial and decisions at the end of the trial. A basic set of QOIs is provided by default. Additional QOIs may be added by clicking the Add row in the table. A QOI can be removed by clicking the X on the right side of the cell. Each QOI may be edited by clicking on it, which opens a pop-up box.
Recall that a 10% benefit relative to control is considered to be a large enough benefit. We will define a QOI based on the probability of a better than a 5% benefit, so that a null arm will eventually have small probability of a 5% benefit and a good arm with at least a 10% benefit will eventually have a large such probability. The trial will be judged a success if at the end of the trial:

The arm with the largest dose has a posterior probability of at least 90% that it is 5% better than control.

Otherwise the trial will be judged to be futile.
Set the following parameters:

At the bottom of the page, set the Clinically significant difference (CSD) to be 0.05. Default QOIs compare to control, and the Trial type is Superiority.
For Posterior Probabilities:

Verify that Pr(P_d – P_(Control) <-0.05) is already added. It should have been automatically filled in because we already specified the CSHRD.

We are not interested in any Predictive Probabilities, p-values, or Probabilities of being Target. The Pr(Max) probability in FACTS calculates the probability that each dose is the best dose. This probability in particular is not useful with the Linear model, because no dose between two other doses can possibly be the best dose.
For Decision Quantities (Scalars):

QOI: Pr(P_d – P_(Control) <-0.05)
Evaluation Dose: Dose 5
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
3.5 Design

3.5.1 Dose Response
The linear model assumes that the probability of outcome \(P_{d}\) for arm number \(d\), which has dose level \(\nu_{d}\), is
\[P_{d} = \frac{e^{\theta_{d}}}{1 + e^{\theta_{d}}}\]
Here the \(\theta_{d}\) are the dose parameters and they satisfy the linear model:
\[\theta_{d} = \alpha + \beta\nu_{d}\]
FACTS gives the option of not including the control arm in the linear model. But here we include it (we leave “Model Control Separately” unchecked), so the parameter \(\alpha\) is the logit of the outcome rate corresponding to dose level zero, i.e. the control outcome rate is equal to
\[P_{0} = \frac{e^{\alpha}}{1 + e^{\alpha}}\]
First select “Simple Linear” from the Model list. In FACTS we must specify prior distributions for the unknown parameters. We set the prior mean for \(\alpha\) to be -0.405, the logit of the expected control probability 0.4, and other prior parameters as in the screenshot. In the graph, select Graph Type: Dose-Response Samples to view samples from the prior distribution for the Dose-Response model. In Dichotomous and Time-to-event models in particular, it can be easy to inadvertently choose prior distributions that are so non-informative that most prior samples look absurd.



3.5.2 Frequentist Analysis
We will not use the Frequentist Analysis tab.


3.5.3 Allocation
To institute response-adaptive randomization, check the “Adaptive Allocation” box. Set the “Pre First Interim Allocation Ratios” to be 5 for control and 2 for each of the experimental arms. Check “Fix Alloc.” for the control arm, and enter 5 for the Post First Interim Alloc. per Block. Below the table, enter 15 in the Post first interim block size.
In the “Adaptive Allocation Targets” dialog, click “Add”. Select Pr(P_d - P_(Control) < – 0.05) in the QOI pull-down. Check (Weight For) Probability, and give it relative weight 1.



3.5.4 Interims
We will update randomization probabilities at each of three interims. Check “Opportunity to Complete at Specified Visit”. This means that an interim analysis scheduled for 150 patients will happen 1 week after the 150th patient is randomized and treated, and the randomization probability update will usually not take effect until more than 150 patients have been randomized. If we selected “Subjects Enrolled” instead, the interim would necessarily occur before 150 patients have complete data, but randomization probabilities would be updated in time for the 151st patient. Either choice can be good.
In our simulated study, there are no dropouts and no unexpected delays in data availability, so it is equivalent to define information based on complete data or on opportunity to complete. In practice, basing interim timing on opportunity to complete can make interims more predictable and meetings to discuss the results easier to schedule.
Check (Specify Interims By) Information. Click the Add button three times and enter 150, 300, and 450 in the Subjects (opportunity) column.



3.5.5 Success/Futility Criteria
The trial will be judged a success if at the end of the trial:

the arm with the largest dose has a posterior probability of at least 90% that it is 5% better than control.

Otherwise the trial will be judged to be futile.
Go to the “Final Evaluation” tab. (Since this design does not allow early stopping, we will not select anything on the “Interim 1” tab, nor will we create tabs for the other interims.) Set the following parameters:

Futility criteria: Add QOI

QOI: Pr(P_d – P_(Control) < - 0.05), d = Dose 5
Condition: <
Threshold: 0.9

Success criteria: Add QOI

QOI: Pr(P_d – P_(Control) < - 0.05), d = Dose 5
Condition: >
Threshold: 0.9


We have left no room between futility and success, so the trial can not be declared inconclusive.
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
3.6 Simulation
In order to get an initial check on the design set up, set the number of simulations to run to 10, then press Simulate. This allows us to make a quick assessment of whether the design is behaving as expected: that the Null scenario ends up mainly futile and the Strong Logistic scenario mainly successful.
If the results look reasonable, increase the number of simulations to run to 1000, re-check all the scenario combinations and then press Simulate again. This is a design that is very fast to simulate, even running 10,000 simulations for each scenario takes less than an hour on a laptop. If you have access to a computer grid, and your FACTS installation has been correctly configured to use it, you may use the grid’s parallel computing capabilities to improve computation speed. To do so, select “on Grid.”
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
3.7 Results
Looking at the operating characteristics for each scenario:

The design as very high probability of success for the Very Strong Logistic scenario, and high probability of success in the Strong Logistic scenario. The Weak Logistic and Threshold scenarios are more borderline with success probabilities between 0.4 and 0.5. Type I error (probability of success in the Null scenario) is quite low, at 0.9% in this set of simulations. More than 1000 simulations should be run if it is desired to have a more accurate estimate of this small probability.
Next we investigate the sample size properties of the design. Click on “Show Other Columns” in the Results Options area, and then select Allocation. An additional window opens, and after adjusting the widths of the columns, we can inspect average sample sizes.

The average sample sizes for Dose 1 are just above 20. Since the design randomizes 20 patients to each experimental arm out of the first 150, the design is aggressive at reducing allocation to this arm using response adaptive randomization. The user should consider whether these sample sizes are adequate for their purposes, and perhaps consider less aggressive randomization or a later first interim.
In all scenarios, the design randomizes a large number of patients to the largest dose. This happens even in the null scenario, in part due to the linear model. Even though the data from all five experimental arms should be suggesting that no arm is 5% better than control, the linear model infers that if any arm is, it must be the largest dose, tilting the randomization probabilities accordingly. In the plateau scenario, in which the two largest doses are in fact equally effective, the design prefers to allocate to the largest dose.
We can also look at the graphs supplied by FACTS to help understand the design. Close the Allocation table window and return to the main FACTS window. Click in the Threshold scenario row to highlight it, and click on “View Graph” in the Results Options area. Then choose “Show Per Scenario Graphs”. In the new window, select “Response and Subject Allocation”.

This graph compares the true dose-response relationship in black to the mean fitted response. This scenario is not a linear model, so the model cannot fix it exactly, and this leads to downward bias in favor of Dose 5 (and the small doses) and an upward (i.e. in the direction of less efficacy) bias for Dose 4. This does not necessarily make the linear model a poor choice; it may still make reasonable allocation decisions, and the threshold scenario may be thought to be highly unlikely.
We can also look at FACTS graphs associated with individual simulated trials. Still in the graphs window, select “Per Interim: Response and Subj. Alloc” to display summaries of data and model fits for each interim analysis and each simulated trial. In this example, we show the data after 150 patients have opportunity to complete (160 subjects enrolled in this simulation). The linear model fit is quite reasonable.
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
4.1 Design
We will create this example from the Linear example already created in this tutorial. With the linear example open in FACTS, go to the File menu, select Save As, and save to a different .facts file, such as HierarchicalLinearExample.facts.
Now go to the Design tab and the Dose Reponse sub-tab. Select “Simple Hierarchical Linear” from the Model list. The prior parameters for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) from the linear example are still available, and now we need to select a prior distribution for \(\tau^{2}\). We choose parameters 0.1 and 2. We encourage users to experiment with different prior parameters and inspect the operating characteristics and graphs.
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
4.2 Quantities of Interest
To take advantage of the more flexible model, we will define and use and additional quantity of interest: the probability that each experimental arm is the best one. On the Quantities of Interest tab, click “Add…” in the Decision Quantities dialog.

Under QOI, select Pr(P_d – P_(Control) < -0.05)
Under Evaluation Dose, select Greatest Pr(Max)
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
4.3 Allocation
We will change the response-adaptive randomization to be based on the probability that each dose is the best. In the Design -> Allocation tab, click the X next to the old adaptive allocation target to delete it. Then click Add…

Select Pr(Max) as the QOI
Select Weight For: Information. This choice encourages the design to gather more data on arms with relatively smaller sample sizes when they have similar efficacy estimates.
Set the Relative Weight to be 1
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
4.4 Success/Futility Criteria
In the linear model, we based trial success and futility on the inference about the largest dose. Since we are now making inference about the best arm, we will change the trial success definition accordingly.
On the Design -> Success/Futility Criteria tab, select the “Final Evaluation” tab.
Delete the existing futility and success criteria by clicking the X’s. Then for a Futility Criterion, click Add…

For QOI, select Pr(P_d – P_(Control) < -0.05); d=Greatest Pr(Max)
Select Condition to be <
Select Threshold to be 0.9

Then for a Success Criterion, click Add…

For QOI, select Pr(P_d – P_(Control) < -0.05); d=Greatest Pr(Max)
Select Condition to be >
Select Threshold to be 0.9

The trial will now be identified as a success if the dose most likely to be the best dose has at least a 90% probability of being 5% better than control.
We will leave the other design choices as in the linear example.
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
4.5 Results
The operating characteristics for each scenario are, at first glance, similar to the results for the linear model. The design here has been set an additional task: that of identifying the best dose. When we used the linear model, we just told the design that Dose 5 was the best dose, and we didn’t simulate any scenarios where any other dose was better. 
Looking at the sample size numbers (click on Show Other Columns under Results Options, then select Allocation) shows that the allocation patterns are quite different from the Linear model. In the Very Strong Logistic scenario, the design identifies Dose 5 as the top candidate very early and seldom goes back to the other arms. In the null scenario, however, the design is much more skeptical of the largest dose, and assigns many more patients to other arms as compared to the linear model design. Dose 5 is still favored relative to Dose 4 by the approximate linear structure of the model in the Plateau and Threshold scenarios where those two arms are actually equivalent.

We will look at two graphs to illustrate how the model reacts to data. Select “View Graph”, then “Show Per Scenario Graphs”, and then “Per Interim: Response and Subj. Alloc.” from the list of available graphs. The first interim (160 subjects randomized) for Simulation 1 is shown below. The model fit is not exactly linear, but it is guided by the linear structure while recognizing the good performance of Doses 1 and 2.

It is useful to look through several sets of these graphs to develop intuition for and comfort with how the design performs. For example, here is the graph from the final analysis of a different simulated trial. Here, the data suggest that the model should allow substantial deviations from linearity, and the model is capable of doing so.
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
5.1 Study

5.1.1 Study Info
On the Study -> Study Info tab:

Choose “Adaptive” under Design Options
Enter 400 as the Maximum number of subjects
Enter 400 as the Maximum number of events
Enter 52 (weeks) as the Follow-up after full enrollment.
Events should indicate Failure.




5.1.2 Visits
The Visits tab should already have “Restrict Event Times to Visits” unchecked. We will assume that events can be observed at any time.


5.1.3 Treatment Arms
On the Study -> Treatment Arms tab, under “Dose”, click “+ Add” four times to add four experimental arms. FACTS will set the dose levels to be 1, 2, 3, and 4, and these are not relevant to the hierarchical model.

These are defined on the Virtual Subject Response -> Dose Response tab. New profiles are added with the “Add” button, they can be renamed by clicking in the Profiles table, and the hazard ratios are entered in the Endpoint Values tables. The boldface arms in the table have effects of better than 25% and “Should Succeed.”
We have a null scenario, and two “Linear” scenarios where the arms with larger labels have greater efficacy. We have a scenario where all experimental arms are effective; the hierarchical model should do well at inferring that all experimental arms are similar and that they are different from control. We have a scenario where three arms are identical to control but one has a large effect; this scenario could be challenging for the hierarchical model. Finally we have an “Overdose” scenario which might be challenging for many parametric dose-response models, in which “Doses” 2 and 3 have good effects, but “Dose” 4 is too much drug and leads to side effects and worse outcomes than control. The hierarchical model doesn’t care about the order of the doses, so it has no concept of overdose, but it does need to learn that there are widely varying treatment effects on both sides of control.

text:
5.4 Quantities of Interest
We will use two decision quantities in the trial. First, at the bottom of the Quantities of Interest tab, set the Clinically significant hazard ratio delta to be 0.25. Then add a decision quantities by clicking Add… under Decision Quantities (Scalars).

For the first QOI, choose Pr(HR_d – 1 < -0.25), and select Evaluation Dose to be Greatest Pr(Max)
For the second QOI, choose Pr(Max) and select Evaluation Dose to be Max probability over all doses. We will not use this QOI to make decisions during the trial, but we want the output to tell us the probability of selecting each arm as the most likely best arm.
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
5.5 Design

5.5.1 Hazard Model
On the Design -> Hazard Model tab, set the prior mean hazard rate for control to be 0.04. We will use an exponential model with a single piece.



5.5.2 Hazard Model
Choose the Simple Hierarchical model from the drop-down Model menu on the Dose Response tab. We are going to use a statistical model that estimates a hazard rate \(\lambda_{s}\) for the control arm, and also estimates log hazard ratio parameters \(\theta_{d}\) for the experimental arms relative to control. The \(\theta_{d}\)’s are drawn from a normal hierarchical model:
\[\theta_{d}\sim N(\mu,\tau^{2})\]
with prior distributions for \(\mu\) (normal) and \(\tau^{2}\) (Inverse Gamma). We will use the default values of the prior parameters. Using \(\mu = 0\) means that the treatment effects are centered around zero (i.e. the experimental arms are expected to be about the same as the control arm). It is also possible to choose a different value for the prior mean for \(\mu\) if, for example, one expects all the experimental arms to be 25% better than control, but this is likely to be an unusual situation.
In most FACTS models, the user has the option of choosing whether or not the control is included in the dose-response model or modeled separately. For technical reasons, this option is not available for time-to-event data with a hierarchical model. By estimating the parameter \(\mu\), the FACTS hierarchical model, in effect, always uses the data to determine whether the control should be modeled separately or not: if \(\mu\) is close to zero, then the control is, in effect, in the model.

We won’t use the Frequentist Analysis tab.


5.5.3 Allocation
We will use response-adaptive randomization to encourage collecting more data on experimental arms, while fixing the control allocation at 1/3.
On the Allocation tab, select “Adaptive Allocation.” Click “Fix Alloc.” for the control arm, then set the Pre First Interim Allocation Ratios to be 2 for control and 1 for each of the four experimental arms. Then set the Post first interim block size to be 6 and the control allocation post first interim to be 2.
Then define an adaptive allocation target by clicking Add…,

set the QOI to be Pr(HR_d – 1 < -0.25)
select Information weighting
set the relative weight to be 1.




5.5.4 Interims
We will define four interims, after 200, 250, 300, and 350 patients enrolled.



5.5.5 Success/Futility Criteria
We will define a futility stopping rule that applies at each interim analysis. On the Design -> Success/Futility Criteria tab, and on the “Interim 1” sub-tab, check the “Futility Criteria” box Then Add a criterion that stops the study for futility if the experimental arm most likely to be the best arm has less than a 25% probability of having better than a 25% effect relative to control.

We will not stop the study for expected success. However, if we wanted to change the futility stopping criteria at each interim, we could Create new interim criteria and enter new values on the resulting tab.
For the Final Evaluation, we will define the study to be a success if the most likely best arm has at least a 90% probability of being at least 25% better than control. We will define the study to be futile at the final analysis if the most likely best arm has less than a 50% probability of being 25% better than control. The study is inconclusive if the probability is between 50% and 90%.
crumbs: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)

title: Simple Dose Response Models (Dichotomous and Time-to-Event)
text:
5.6 Simulation
After simulating all twelve scenario (6 efficacy x 2 control hazard rates) we can inspect operating characteristics:

The Linear, All Doses, One Dose, and Overdose scenarios all have high probabilities of Late Success. In all these efficacy scenarios, the design loses some power when the event rate is cut in half (“Rare”), but the drop is not catastrophic. Type I error as measured by “Late Success” in the Null scenario is very small; there is room to experiment with different success rules if desired. Futility probabilities are 64% and 52% in the null scenarios; it may be desired to experiment with the futility rule to increase the probability of futility. The Weak Linear scenario is borderline, and the most common outcome is inconclusive, which is appropriate because the best arm has exactly the effect (25%) that we are hoping to exceed.
We now click on Show Other Columns from Results Options, and select Probabilities. This gives us information about dose selection, as shown below. In the All Doses scenario (and also in the Null scenario), all experimental arms are roughly equally likely to be identified as the best arm. When the experimental arms differ, the design is likely to make a correct identification, with the task being most difficult in the Weak Linear scenario. When events are Rare, the power to choose the best arm is reduced, but the design appears to still be adequate in the Rare event rate scenarios.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint
text:
3.1 Trial
Start FACTS 7.0 or later, double click on: Platform Trial Design – Dichotomous.



Graphical user interface, text, application Description automatically generated


Using the menu option “File > Save As”, save this design as “PlatformTutorial2” in a convenient location.

3.1.1 Trial \(\rightarrow\) Trial Info
On the Trial \(\rightarrow\) Trial Info tab, select the following options:

Under Design Options, select Enable adaptive features
Uncheck Use longitudinal modeling
Under Trial information, check Max enrollment time (wks) and enter 104
Set the Max number of participants per treatment to be 50
Set the Max concurrent treatments to be 3
Check “Response indicates positive outcome”
Under Schedule of Post-Baseline Visits, Time to Final Endpoint should be 1 week




Graphical user interface, application Description automatically generated




3.1.2 Trial \(\rightarrow\) Trial Arms

3.1.2.1 Trial \(\rightarrow \ \) Trial Arms \(\rightarrow\) Definition

Include a control treatment arm. (As of FACTS 7.0, including a control arm is required.)
Click “Add arm” six times so that Treatment 1 through Treatment 6 are added.




Graphical user interface, application Description automatically generated




3.1.2.2 Trial \(\rightarrow \ \) Trial Arms \(\rightarrow\) Arrivals
First we will define a deterministic schedule for when treatments become available. Then we will define arrival schedules to allow for the possibility that treatments take longer than intended to join the trial.
Click “Add” and rename the Profile to “Fixed Arrival”. Then set the Latest Possible Arrival times for the six treatments to be 0, 0, 26, 26, 39, and 52 weeks. Set the Earliest Possible Arrival times to be the same as the Latest times, and set all the “Withdrawn if Not Used Within” values to be 52.



Graphical user interface Description automatically generated


Then Click +Add again, rename the new Profile to be “Uncertain Arrival”, and use the same values in the table, except for adding 13 weeks to the Latest Possible Arrival times for Treatments 3 through 6.



Table Description automatically generated


Finally, to capture the risks of a more unpredictable drug development process where each treatment’s arrival time is more uncertain than the last, click on Add again, rename the profile to “V Uncertain Arrival”, and set the Latest arrival times to be 39, 52, 78, and 91, with the other table entries the same as for previous arrival schedules.



Table Description automatically generated

title: Dichotomous Endpoint
text:
3.2 Virtual Response

3.2.1 Virtual Response \(\rightarrow\) Treatment Classification
In the Platform Trial engine, a specific treatment may be defined to have a random treatment effect which is sometimes highly efficacious and sometimes not. We want FACTS to keep track of outcomes for arms based on their simulated treatment effects, and the “Classification of Simulated Treatments” dialogue facilitates this.

Enter 0.1 in the “We would want a treatment to be a success if treatment effect >” box
Enter 0 in the “We would want a treatment to be a failure if treatment effect \(\leq\)” box
Check the “Rates” box to the right of “Specify treatment classification thresholds in:”.




Graphical user interface, application, Word Description automatically generated




3.2.2 Virtual Response \(\rightarrow\) Response Specification
We will define seven treatment effect scenarios. In the first five of these, control has a 30% probability of a good outcome.

a Null scenario, where all six treatments are equivalent to control
a Small Effects scenario where all six treatments have the same 5% benefit over control
a Fixed Improving scenario where all experimental treatments are better than control by amounts 5%, 5%, 10%, 10%, 15%, and 20%
Good 4, where Treatment 4 has a 20% benefit and all the others have 5% benefits
Good 6, which is like Good 4 except that it is Treatment 6 that has a 20% benefit
Random Control, which is similar to the Fixed Improving scenario except that the control arm success rate is random. The treatment effects are defined in terms of fixed benefits on the log-odds scale, which would be equivalent to 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% benefits if the control had a 30% success rate.
Uncertain, where the control has a random distribution as in Random Control, and all six treatments have random treatment effects that are zero with probability 2/3, and otherwise range from 0% to 20%.

To add the null scenario, select the Virtual Response, Explicitly Defined tab and click the “+ Add” button. Rename the Profile from “Resp 1” to “Null” by clicking and then typing “Null” in the Profiles dialog. Then select “Fixed Response Rate” for all the treatments using the menus in the Response Rate Fixed/Sampled column, and enter 0.3 in all the cells in the Value column.

Now we define the Random Control scenario. Click +Add again and name the scenario accordingly. Select Sampled for the Control arm and Fixed Effect (Log-Odds) for all of the Treatments. Enter 0.23, 0.23, 0.44, 0.44, 0.65, and 0.85 for the Values for the treatment effects; these values correspond to response rates of 0.35, 0.35, 0.40, 0.40, 0.45, and 0.50 when the control rate is 0.30, e.g. \(0.23 = \log{\left\{ 0.35/(1 - 0.35) \right\} -}\log\left\{ 0.30/(1 - 0.30) \right\}\). Enter 0.1 for the Mean, 0.05 for the SD, and 0 and 0.2 for the minimum and maximum. This time, we have chosen the SD to give a distribution peaked at 0.1 and with less probability near 0 and 0.2. title: Dichotomous Endpoint
text:
3.3 Accrual
Add an accrual scenario by clicking the Add button on the far left. Set the peak accrual rate to 4 participants per week. We have scheduled the trial to last for 104 weeks, so an average of 416 participants can be accrued, enough for 50 participants for each experimental treatment and over 100 for control.
The names of the accrual profile and the region may be renamed by double-clicking on them.



Graphical user interface Description automatically generated with medium confidence

title: Dichotomous Endpoint
text:
3.4 Quantities of Interest
FACTS has considerable flexibility in allowing the user to define Quantities of Interest (QOIs) to drive adaptations in the trial and decisions at the end of the trial. A basic set of QOIs is provided by default. Additional QOIs may be added by clicking the Add row in the table. A QOI can be removed by clicking the X on the right side of the cell. Each QOI may be edited by clicking on it, which opens a pop-up box.
In this trial we intend to stop a treatment for futility if it would have insufficiently large probability of a successful result in a future Phase III trial with 250 participants on each of control and the experimental treatment. This is one of the default QOIs; if we wanted to tweak the details of the notional future Phase III trial we could click on the definition of the QOI in the Predictive Probability section.
We also intend for the design to label a treatment to be a success if it has a high posterior probability of being superior to control. This is also a default QOI, so again no changes are required here.



Graphical user interface Description automatically generated

title: Dichotomous Endpoint
text:
3.5 Design

3.5.1 Control Response
We will use a prior distribution for the control response centered around the expected rate of 0.3 and that is fairly noninformative. The logit of 0.3 is -0.85, so we use that for the mean of the log odds, and use 0.85 as the Prior SD.



Chart, line chart Description automatically generated




3.5.2 Treatment Response
We will use the default prior distribution for the treatment response rates; it is highly non-informative with a prior mean of 0 for the treatment effect on the logit scale and a prior SD of 2. To see samples from this distribution, select “Treatment-Response Samples” from the menu under Graph Type.



Graphical user interface, application Description automatically generated




3.5.3 Allocation
We are going to use fixed allocation, with the randomization probability for control and every experimental treatment arm in the trial always being equal. FACTS allows other options, such as fixing the control allocation regardless of the number of treatments in the trial.



Graphical user interface, application Description automatically generated




3.5.4 Trial Updates
FACTS allows considerable flexibility in the choice of how to schedule trial updates. They can be conducted on a fixed calendar schedule; it is often appropriate that the data analysts and reviewers have a predictable schedule for reviewing data. In this internal pharma trial, we will conduct an analysis whenever any experimental treatment reaches a milestone that requires a decision. In particular, we will give each treatment an opportunity to stop for futility when it randomizes its 20th, 30th, and 40th participants.
Select “Participants Enrolled” to define the measure of Participant Information: i.e. we will conduct a treatment’s first analysis when it reaches 20 participants enrolled, regardless of how many of them have complete data. Information can also be defined based on participants with Complete Data. (Opportunity to Complete is another option that can apply, and be different from Complete Data, when there are dropouts.) Select “Updates occur whenever a treatment milestone is met”. Uncheck both boxes under “Participant Follow-Up Options”: if a treatment stops for futility, it cannot be a success after further follow-up, while the success box does not apply in this trial because we are not allowing early stopping for success.
Now under Treatment Milestones, click the +Add button three times to add three milestones, and enter 20, 30, and 40 in the Participants Enrolled column.



Graphical user interface, application Description automatically generated




3.5.5 Success/Futility Criteria
We will define one futility rule that is used at each of the three milestones, and one success rule that is used at the Final Evaluation for each treatment. To define a set of criteria for the milestones, from the “All Treatments” tab under “Design” and “Success/Futility Criteria”, enter “1” for “Create new criteria at milestone” and hit the Create button. This allows us to create a set of criteria that begins applying at the first milestone (20 enrolled participants) and continues applying for subsequent milestones (unless we create new criteria that begin applying at a later milestone). Under the newly created Milestone 1 tab, check the Futility Criteria box, and click on Add… to bring up the Add Stopping Criterion dialogue box. Select the Pr(Succ. Future Trial) QOI, select < and enter 0.25 for the threshold, so that a treatment will stop for futility if its predictive probability of success in a future Phase III trial is less than 0.25.



Graphical user interface, application, Word Description automatically generated


A treatment will be judged a success if it reaches 50 participants and if the data at the end of its follow-up yields a 97.5% posterior probability of having a higher response rate than control. To define this success rule, first click on the Final Evaluation tab while still under “All Treatments”. On the “Success Criteria” side of the tab, click on “Add…” under QOI. Select the \(Pr(P_{d} > P_{Control})\) option from the QOI drop-down menu, select “>”, and enter 0.975 as shown in the figure below. We will not enter any futility criteria. The trial will be declared inconclusive if it reaches its final sample size and falls short of a 97.5% probability of superiority to control. We reserve futility for treatments that stop before reaching 50 participants.



Graphical user interface, application, Word Description automatically generated

title: Dichotomous Endpoint
text:
3.6 Simulation
We are now ready to begin simulating the trial. Normally we recommend running a small number of simulations per scenario first to get fast feedback. Set the number of simulations to 10, click “Select All” then press Simulate. This allows us to make a quick assessment of whether the design is behaving as expected.



Graphical user interface, application, table Description automatically generated


All scenarios have Mean Treatments Enrolled of 6, so we are not stopping the trial before the sixth treatment even begins. However, some scenarios have Mean Treatments Analyzed smaller than 6, so the trial sometimes stops at 104 weeks before reaching final analysis for all treatments.
Use the scroll bar at the bottom to scroll to the right until reaching “Mean Successes”. We see that in the Null scenarios, the numbers of successes are smaller than for the other scenarios, which matches our expectations.



Graphical user interface, application, table Description automatically generated


If the results look reasonable, increase the number of simulations to run to 1000, re-check all the scenario combinations with Select All and then press Simulate again. Platform trials can be slow to simulate; this run of 1000 simulations will still serve as a rough guide to whether we have done anything badly wrong. If you have access to a computer grid, and your FACTS installation has been correctly configured to use it, you may use the grid’s parallel computing capabilities to improve computation speed. To do so, select “on Grid.”

title: Dichotomous Endpoint
text:
3.7 Results
We will now investigate the operating characteristics.
In the Platform Trial Design engine, treatments are categorized into three types: Good, Mediocre, and Unacceptable. Recall that we defined a Good treatment to be one with a treatment effect of larger than 0.1, an Unacceptable treatment to be one with zero or negative treatment effect, and a Mediocre treatment to be one with a treatment effect larger than zero but no larger than 0.1.

3.7.1 Type I Error (Unacceptable Treatment Successes)
Registration is not a goal of this trial, so we don’t necessarily need to control Type I error carefully at the 0.025 level. It is still unsatisfactory if treatments with no treatment effect are too likely to be successful, especially since we are investigating six treatments and would prefer not to proceed to Phase III with any unacceptable treatment. The fraction of unacceptable treatments that succeed is an analogue of Type I error in a simpler trial, although note that if many unacceptable treatments are harmful, the probability of success will generally be smaller than if they are all equivalent to control.
We will primarily investigate Type I error using the Null efficacy scenario, in which all the treatments have the same response rate as control, 0.3. In the Simulations output table, click in the row for the Acc 1_Drop 1_Null_Fixed scenario, and then click on View Graph, selecting the Show Per Scenario Graphs option. The Outcome by Treatment graphs will appear.



Graphical user interface, application, Excel Description automatically generated


The Late Success probabilities are all small, visibly less than 0.05, and the most likely outcome is Early Futility. Treatment 6 has a small probability of being Incomplete. To get the precise simulation results, go back to the table and scroll to the right until you reach the “Ppn Successes | Treatment Unacceptable” column. For the three Null scenarios with the different arrival schedules, this column has values of 0.0268, 0.024, 0.0225. These values are not surprising: since we did not allow early success and since we defined success to be a posterior probability of at least 0.975 of a benefit, we expect the success probability to be close to 0.025 for null treatments. The Uncertain scenarios at the bottom of the table also have Unacceptable treatments, and their success probabilities are similar. The other scenarios do not feature any Unacceptable treatments.



Graphical user interface, table Description automatically generated


We can also consult the “Mean Unacceptable Treatment Successes” column for results summed over all unacceptable treatments. These values range from 0.13 to 0.16 in the null scenarios and are less than 0.10 in the Uncertain scenarios. All treatments are Unacceptable in the null scenarios, compared to only two-thirds of treatments in the Uncertain scenarios.



Graphical user interface, table Description automatically generated


We consider the Type I error probabilities and average number of treatments that succeed in the null scenarios to be satisfactory, so we don’t decide on any design changes at this point. We make a note that we might want to consider making the final success rule less stringent to increase power if we are comfortable with slightly higher Type I error probabilities in this Phase II trial.


3.7.2 Futility for Unacceptable Treatments
It is also desirable if Unacceptable treatments stop for futility before reaching the maximum sample size. Referring back to the graphic showing “Ppn Successes | Treatment Unacceptable”, the column to its right is “Ppn Futilities | Treatment Unacceptable” and we see that 64% to 67% of Unacceptable treatments stopped early for futility. This seems satisfactory as well.


3.7.3 Power (Good Treatment Successes)
An analogue of power in a simpler trial is the proportion of Good treatments that achieve trial success. Scroll to the “Ppn Successes | Treatment Good” column. We have run a variety of scenarios with Good treatments and we get a wide array of success probabilities. The “Good 4” scenarios are relatively simple: Treatment 4 is a Good treatment with a 20% benefit, and all other treatments are Mediocre with 5% benefits. So the Good treatment operating characteristics are about Treatment 4 in this scenario. (FACTS also provides treatment-specific success, futility, and inconclusive probabilities, and sometimes it is more convenient to consult them). We see that the proportion of successes ranges from 0.6884 to 0.7295 in the Good 4 scenarios. We would like these probabilities to be higher.



Graphical user interface, table Description automatically generated


The “Good 6” scenarios are not very different from the “Good 4” scenarios: if a Good treatment does not appear until the sixth treatment, it still appears that the design can give that treatment a fair shot compared to if it entered earlier. There is a suggestion that power may drop by 3% from Treatment 4 to Treatment 6 if the arrivals are Very Uncertain, but this could be an artifact of only 1000 simulations. Note, however, that the denominator in this column is the number of times that the treatment reached its final analysis, so if results are incomplete too often, we will not see that here.
We also see that the futility probabilities in the Good 4 scenarios range from 5.6% to 6.5%. These futility probabilities are probably too high for Good treatments. And the futility probabilities for Good treatments are higher for other scenarios, which we will discuss further later.
We discuss these numbers with the team, and they decide to consider increasing the maximum sample size from 50 to 60, while simultaneously rescheduling the futility milestones to 30, 40, and 50 participants. It is very common that the culprit when futility numbers are too high for good treatments is that most of the problem is due to the earlier futility look (here, the 20 participant look). To confirm that this is the case here, click on the Good 4 row in the Table, click “View Graph \(\rightarrow\) Show Per Scenario Graphs”, select “Time Course for Futility Stopping”, select “Treatment 4” for the “Arm” menu, and select “Cumulative over sample size”. The 20-participant update is the largest contributor to futility; the reader can confirm that this is dramatic in other efficacy scenarios. 
The team also believes that faster accrual rates can be achieved, so we will increase the accrual rate in the simulations by 20% to compensate for the larger sample sizes. The team is also comfortable with a proportional increase in the number of participants to be randomized to control.


3.7.4 Power in Random Control Scenarios
Referring back to the previous figure, the probability of success for good treatments is much lower, uncomfortably low, in the Random Control scenarios. A reason for this is that our random response rates for control arms allow too much randomness. We defined the response rate for controls to have the Uniform distribution on [0, 0.6]. In particular, we are allowing small response rates that require larger sample sizes to accurately estimate, and that are most likely unrealistic given what we know about the control treatment.
One way to see the problem is using the “Per Sim: Response and Participant Allocation” graphs provided by FACTS. Select the “Acc 1_Drop 1_Random Control_Fixed Arrival” scenario in the simulations table, click on “View Graph \(\rightarrow\) Show Per Scenario Graphs”, and then select “Per Sim: Response and Participant Allocation” from the Graphs menu on the resulting window. To make it easier to see what’s going on, we click the “Set Y axes…” button and tell FACTS to always use the [0,1] range for response rates.

We can then flip through the Simulations, until Simulation 6 provides a great example of a simulated trial that wasn’t what we intended.



Chart Description automatically generated with low confidence


It looks like several of the treatments never got any responses at all, with the “Mean raw response” symbols pegged at zero.
The team is comfortable with a much tighter distribution on control treatment response rates, for example uniform on [0.2, 0.4]. If we observed a response rate outside that range in the trial, the team would be concerned that the population recruited in the trial is too different from the target population for the treatment.


3.7.5 Good Treatments: Comparing Apples to Oranges
The proportion of Good treatments that succeed is also too low in the Uncertain scenario and the Fixed Improving scenario. In the Uncertain scenario, the control response rate is random, but we were more careful about specifying a reasonable distribution, uniform on [0.25,0.35]. The Fixed Improving scenario more clearly illustrates the issue. Recall that in the Good 4 and Good 6 scenarios, the only Good treatment had a 20% benefit relative to control. In the Fixed Improving scenario, Treatment 5 has a 15% benefit and Treatment 6 has a 20% benefit. Therefore, the operating characteristics for this scenario are a mixture of treatments as good as the Good 4 scenario and treatments not quite so good, so power numbers are inevitably less impressive.
The effect is more dramatic in other scenarios. For example in Random Control, two Treatments have a fixed log-odds effect of 0.44, which will translate into an effect (slightly) larger than 10% if the control response rate exceeds 0.3. So these two treatments will be counted as Good treatments roughly half the time, even though they barely qualify.
In the Uncertain scenario, treatments with nonzero effects have benefits uniformly distributed on [0, 0.2], so all treatments have benefits less than in the Good 4 and Good 6 scenarios and we should certainly expect reduced power. Many treatments will barely qualify for being Good treatments. We can confirm that Treatments 3 and 4 are often being scored as Good treatments by consulting the graphs. Select the “Acc 1_Drop 1_Random Control_Fixed Arrival” scenario in the simulations table, click on “View Graph \(\rightarrow\) Show Per Scenario Graphs”, and select “Simulated Treatment Classification”. Not only are Treatments 3 and 4 often Good, Treatments 5 and 6 are often falling into Mediocre territory, as will happen with log-odds effects of 0.65 and 0.85 when the control response rate is too small.
For this scenario, we decide to modify the treatment effect assumption so that benefits can be as large as 0.3. It seems consistent with the idea of an uncertain scenario to allow for the possibility of effects larger than in our standard fixed effect scenario. With this modification, effect sizes for Good treatments will range from 0.1 to 0.3, and should be more comparable to the Good 4 and 6 scenarios.
We consider changing the definition of Good treatments to only include treatments with benefits larger than 15%. This isn’t completely satisfactory, we are still interested in the operating characteristics for treatments with 12% benefits for example. In the end we decide to make a smaller change to the definition, where Good treatments have to exceed 11% benefits. Note that in the Random Control scenario, if the Control arm has its highest response rate of 40%, Treatments 3 and 4 with effect sizes of 0.44 on the logit scale will have response rates of 50.8%, falling just short of the 11% requirement, so these two treatments will not be included in the Good treatment population.
A further issue appears in the Outcome by Treatment graphs for the Fixed Improving scenario. Note that Treatment 6’s success probability is not much larger than Treatment 5’s, and the culprit appears to be that Treatment 6’s outcome is Incomplete close to 30% of the time. We did not see such a large Incomplete rate for Treatment 6 in the Good 6 scenario: in that scenario, Treatment 6 was competing for participants with treatments whose response rate was only slightly larger than control and were likely to stop for futility. In the Fixed Improving scenario, other treatments remain in the trial and as a result, Treatment 6 often fails to randomize its 50th participant by the scheduled end of the trial. In practice, if we reached 104 weeks and at least one Treatment remained short of 50 participants and was outperforming the futility rule, we would want to keep the trial open and collect the full complement of participants on the remaining experimental treatment(s).



Graphical user interface, application Description automatically generated


We decide to respond to this finding with a further increase in the accrual rate for the trial, which we think is realistic. Recall that we decided to increase the accrual rate from 4 to 4.8 participants a week because of the increase in sample size from 50 to 60. We decide to double this increase to 5.6 participants per week.

2.1 Response Model
Let the probability of observing toxicity for a subject given dose j be pj
We will model the probability of toxicity across the range of doses:
\[\log\left( \frac{p_{j}}{{1 - p}_{j}} \right) = \alpha + \beta\widehat{x_{j}}\]
With α and log β given a normal bivariate prior. The actual parameters of this distribution are estimated based on user supplied quantiles for the prior probability of the toxicity rate for each dose.
Each dose j is given a ‘strength’ \(\widehat{x_{j}}\) by taking the log of the doses scaled to a reference dose:
\[\widehat{x_{j}} = log\left( \frac{d_{j}}{d^{*}} \right)\]
The paper defines 8 dose-toxicity scenarios.

title: CRM
text:
4.3 Design

4.3.1 XHats
The “CRM” model always uses some sort of transformation from the actual doses to a set of “effective dose strengths” for use in the logistic model. These are traditionally shown as \(\widehat{x}\) in the formula, hence the term “X-hat”. In the N-CRM the transformation uses two simple choices:

The “reference dose” which all the dose strengths are relative to. At the reference dose strength (which doesn’t have to be one of the available doses) the value of \(\widehat{x}\) is 0, and the estimate of the logit of the toxicity rate at this dose strength will be α in the Bayesian Logistic Regression formula. One convention is to use the median of the dose range as the reference dose, (this minimizes the correlation in the estimate of α and β), others are is to use the start of the dose range or the dose thought, a priori, the most likely to be the MTD. If the reference dose is changed, the prior for α and β must be re-calibrated. Here we set it explicitly to the middle dose 100mg.
The strength transformation can be log of the dose ratio (if the expected dose effect is expect to be roughly log linear) or a linear transformation (if the doses’ have been specified with linear dose strength – e.g. the dose strengths have simply been left at 1, 2, 3, …). Were we set it to the log of the dose ration (as in the paper).

4.3.4 Allocation Rule

4.3.5 Stopping Criteria
Set the parameters as follows:

Uncheck the “Rules for stopping trial early”. In the paper we are comparing with results where no stopping rule was applied. This is probably unrealistic in practice, and it will be interesting to investigate whether a well-chosen stopping rule can yield similar performance in terms of correct identification of the MTD whilst giving lower expected average study sizes.
Minimum toxicities required before stopping: 2. This is not mentioned in the paper, but there is a problem common to all CRM methods – what to do if an early toxicity causes the expected toxicity at all doses to be too high for allocation to continue by the normal rules? Currently in the other CRMs the allocation stops. If the simulation specifies a low but non-zero probability of toxicity (0.01 say) at the first (or second) dose, a single toxicity in a cohort of 3 will show up in some simulations (~3% if the probability is 0.01), causing a number of outlier simulations with small sample size and no selected MTD (or first dose as MTD). If this occurred on a trial in practice there is likely to be an ad hoc assessment of whether to allocate a further cohort at the lowest dose, and the precise rules governing this case might be quite hard to formulate; this parameter allows a simple approximation of this decision making – by specifying that should all doses be inadmissible allocation to the lowest dose should continue until a the specified number of toxicities (over all doses) has been observed.

4.5 Alternative Stopping Rule
After running simulations two things were noted: whilst the 3+3 did a poor job of MTD selection, so did the N-CRM with over dose control enabled at <25%, and N-CRM’s sample size was larger on many scenarios (because no stopping rules had been specified). Thus a second N-CRM design was created with an overdose control threshold of 33% and the following stopping rule:
Using File > SaveAs to create a new copy of the design, on the Study > Study info tab, change the “Limit max excess/unacceptable toxicity” threshold from 0.25 to 0.33.
On the Design > Stopping Criteria tab:

Enable Rules for stopping trial early
Select Combined Rules
Set the Probability of dose being MTD greater than: 0.4
Set the Minimum cohorts accrued: 3

This specifies that the trial should not stop until at least 4 cohorts have been treated and one dose has a probability of being the MTD of at least 0.5.
Return to the simulation tab and run 1,000 simulations of this modified design. You should find that in all scenarios the proportion of times selection of the correct MTD has increased, but with an increase in the average number of subjects used.

title: CRM
text:
5.1 Observations

5.1.1 FACTS LRcat25 Results
It was instructive that the LRcat25 and FACTS LRcat25 results differed, as this led to an interesting analysis of how our implementation of the ‘overdose control’ differed from that used by the authors of the paper. Helped by correspondence with the authors we have identified two differences in implementation that fully account for the differences in the results:

In the method as implemented in the paper the full number of cohorts is always allocated. In the implementation in FACTS if overdose control is enabled, when there are no admissible doses, even if no stopping conditions have been specified the trial will stop. This seems to be the most likely behavior of a clinical team in practice if faced with this situation. However we have allowed this behavior to be overridden through the “minimum toxicities required before stopping”, as the rule can lead to stopping with very little data and in practice teams might decide further allocation to the lowest dose was permissible. If this value is set to the maximum number of subjects then the behavior of the method implemented by the authors is recovered.
In the method as implemented in the paper the final selection of MTD is done without regard to overdose control, whereas the current implementation in FACTS still takes overdose control into account in the final selection. We will await feedback from users to see if this was the correct decision or whether it needs to made optional.



5.1.2 FACTS LRcat33 Results
The overdose threshold of <25% in FACTS LRcat25 has possibly made the selection of the final MTD too cautious. The ability to correctly identify the correct MTD in this design is starting to resemble that of 3+3.
In order to see if an N-CRM could be used to do a better job of selecting the MTD than 3+3, whilst stopping early to achieve samples sizes similar to 3+3, and control of overdosing that is as cautious as 3+3, the LRcat33 design was created. As well as increasing the overdose threshold to <33%, an early stopping rule was introduced that allowed the trial to stop once one admissible dose had probability of being in the target band of > 0.4 and a minimum of 3 cohorts has been tested (though this can be overridden by the overdose control).
With the exception of scenario F1 and to a lesser extend S6, LRcat33 is still consistently better at identifying the correct MTD, and has similar expected sample sizes (larger in S2, F2, equal in S4, F4 and smaller in S, F6). LRcat33 has a smaller range of average expected sample sizes than FATCS LRcaat25 or Neuenschwander’s LRcat 25. LRcat33 has slightly higher expected toxicity than 3+3, but that is due to 3+3’s tendency to under dose.

title: CRM
text:
6.3 The Subject.csv file
The file is a simple ascii file with the different data items separated by commas. Any line starting with ‘#’’ is ignored, here we use that to include a header row. The data may also include spaces to aid readability (but not, currently, tabs). Each line defines the dose given to a single subject and that subject’s response.
For historic reasons the CRM subject.csv file format includes patient identification data. The FACTS design engine does not use this data, and the fields may be left blank – but the commas separating the columns still need to be included. As this design engine only analyses the toxicity outcomes the only two columns we need to enter are “Dose” and “Tox”. “Dose” needs to contain the dose level (not the dose index)) of the dose given to the subject, in this design the dose levels were specified as 12.5, 25, 50, 100, 150, 200 and 250 so this column should contain one of these values. “Tox” needs to contain either a ‘1’ (to indicate toxicity observed) or a ‘0’ (for no toxicity). A value also in the final “Efficacy” column is also required although it will be ignored by the N-CRM method, it should be left as ‘0’.
The first cohort will have been allocated the lowest dose ‘12.5’ and we will report that no subjects experienced toxicity (‘0’). The subjects.csv file looks like this:
#Patient ID, Patient Initials, Year, Month, Day, Time, Cohort, Dose, Toxicity, Efficacy
1,,,,,,1,12.5,0,0
2,,,,,,1,12.5,0,0
3,,,,,,1,12.5,0,0

title: CRM (Toxicity 2-Sample)
text:
2.1 Response Model
If the probability of observing toxicity for a subject given dose j pj
We will model the probability of toxicity across the range of doses:
\[\log\left(\frac{p'_{ij}}{1 - p'_{ij}}\right) = \log(b_k) + \alpha + \beta_i \widehat{x}_{j}^{i},\ b_1 = 1,\ b_2 = b\]
Where b1 is used for sample 1 and b2 for sample 2. With α set to –3 and β distributed:
\[\beta \sim U[0,3)\]
Each dose j is given a ‘strength’ \(\widehat{x_{j}}\) by fitting the user supplied prior expectations of the average toxicity for each dose p0j across the two samples, to the above model with β set to 1. i.e. solving:
\[\log\left(\frac{p^{0}_{j}}{1 - p^{0}_{j}}\right) = \alpha + \widehat{x_{j}}\]
for \(\widehat{x_{j}}\).
The range for b is exp(+/-3 max(\(\widehat{x_{j}}\))). This allows the second sample to be shifted so that its lowest dose has the same probability as the highest dose of sample one, or vice versa.

title: CRM (Toxicity 2-Sample)
text:
2.3 Expected performance
In [Quigley] the reported % of times the correct dose was identified as the MTD was:

Scenario A: Sample 1 Dose 3 31%, Sample 2 Dose 3 31%

As a way of ranking the designs over all the scenarios, for each design we sum the squares of the difference for its score from the best score for that sample in that scenario. This favors designs that score consistently well and penalizes those that have an Achilles’ heel or blind spot. [One might consider that samples where the responses are the same are under represented or that scenario A should have a > 1 weighting]. This method of scoring ranks the use of the logistic the highest with either the uniform or exponential prior.
The FACTS tanh with uniform prior does extremely well with all but scenario H. It get the best results for the second sample in 5 of the scenarios. But never selecting the top dose for sample 2 in scenario H lets it down.
