title: CRM 2 Samples and Open Enrollment
text:
2.1 Toxicity response model
The model is the standard N-CRM model for adults:
\(\theta_{d} = log\left( \frac{\pi_{d}}{1 - \pi_{d}} \right)\), \(\theta_{d} = \alpha + \beta d\)
And for the pediatric population the model uses the same slope but has a potential offset to the intercept
\[\theta_{ped\_ d} = \alpha + \alpha_{ped} + \beta d\]
The following priors were used:
\(\alpha\sim N\left( - 3,1^{2} \right)\), \(\alpha_{ped}\sim N\left( 0,1^{2} \right)\), \(\beta\sim N\left( 0.5,\ \ {0.2}^{2} \right)\)
Plus prior pseudo data of half an observation on the lowest dose with no DLT, and half an observation on the highest dose with half a DTL (the paper is not explicit on which population these pseudo patients are added to but we can assume that it is the adult population).
Note:

that the prior on Beta is specified on Beta not Ln(Beta), we will need to adjust this when we enter the prior in FACTS
that a bivariate-Normal prior was not used, so we will simply set the correlation parameter to 0

title: CRM 2 Samples and Open Enrollment
text:
2.2 Enrollment
The maximum sample size is 60, comprising 35 adult and 25 pediatric patients.
The assumed accrual rate is 3 per month for adults, and 1 per month for children.
Open enrollment will be used, with enrollment suspended in the respective groups if there are 3 adult or 3 pediatric patients with unknown DLT information.
Enrollment into the pediatric population starts once 6 adults have been enrolled, and the initial dose allocation is to the dose one below the highest safe dose for adults where there is data from at least 2 adults. (Strictly the first 6 adults were recruited in 3 cohorts of 2, but we couldn’t replicate this specifically in FACTS).

title: CRM 2 Samples and Open Enrollment
text:
2.3 Allocation
For doses 1 – 3, data from 2 patients was required for a dose before it was considered ‘cleared’, for doses 4 -7, data from 3 patients was required for a dose to be considered ‘cleared’. When escalating, no dose could be skipped. Escalation for the adult patient group depended on just the adult patients.
The pediatric population followed the same rules as the adults, but could escalate if just adults had been tested on a dose, as long as adults had also been tested on the dose above as well and both doses were considered safe for adults. (FACTS does not currently support different escalation rules for the two groups so this could only be approximated).

title: CRM 2 Samples and Open Enrollment
text:
2.4 Stopping
Stopping was triggered for adults if 8 patients were treated on the MTD and 20 patients on the MTD or a dose either side of it, and for the pediatric group if 5 patients had been treated on the MTD and 10 patients on the MTD or a dose either side of it. It was also required that if three additional hypothetical patients were treated on the MTD and experienced no DLTs that that should not change the MTD.

title: CRM 2 Samples and Open Enrollment
text:
2.6 Designs for comparison
Two possible alternative designs that it would be straightforward to evaluate in FACTS would be to replace the open enrollment with cohort enrollment and to replace the MTD target with a toxicity band target. These are left as exercises to the user and not presented in this tutorial.

title: CRM 2 Samples and Open Enrollment
text:
3.1 Study

3.1.1 Study Info
To simulate the paper we are going to simulate using “Open Enrollment” – dosing subjects as they arrive, but imposing a limit on how many subjects we can have treated but not complete (3) and “2 Groups” for adult and pediatric patients. We will recruit up to 35 Adult, and 25 Pediatric patients. Adult patients are expected to accrue at 3 per month (=0.75 per week) and pediatric patients at 1 per month (=0.25 per week). The treatment cycle is 21 days. We will start recruiting pediatric patients after 6 adult patients have been recruited.
Note that since this trial was run two features have been added to FACTS that might improve the design but are not used at this stage

Two maximums for the number of “subjects we can have treated but not complete” can now be specified – one if the current dose has not been ‘cleared’ and another if it has been cleared. The specification of what counts as a ‘cleared’ dose is done on the Design > Allocation tab. To be cleared a dose must have had the specified number of patients tested at that dose. This is a fixed number through the trial, though a smaller number can be used initially by specifying an initial run-in that will be followed until the first toxicity is observed. By having two maximums, we can allocate more cautiously to doses while clearing doses and escalating until we can allocate to the target dose, then we can continue to allocate more aggressively to this dose once it as cleared.
Backfilling: this allows us to allocate patients that arrive while the number of subjects treated but not complete are at the maximum, by allocating them to a lower dose (rather than losing the opportunity to use them in the trial).

Set the following parameters:

Endpoints: Don’t include efficacy.
Recruitment: use Open Enrollment
Groups: use Two group populations
Open Enrollment

Maximum size (subjects) for group 1: 35
Time unit: week
Mean recruitment rate (0.75)
Time unit final result: 3 weeks
Maximum subjects without final results if dose is uncleared: 3
Maximum subjects without final results if dose is cleared: 3

Two Group recruitment

Start group 2 after subject reaches: 6

Open Enrollment for Group 2

Maximum subjects in Group 2: 25
Group is a property of the subject
Mean subject recruitment rate, Group 2: 0.25
Group 2 Queue options:

Maximum subjects without final results if dose is uncleared: 3
Maximum subjects without final results if dose is cleared: 3






3.1.2 Toxicity
To replicate the operating characteristics of the design in the paper, we will target a single dose (MTD) rather than a toxicity band. And we will define toxicity bands so we can specify a overdose control such that a dose will be deemed unsafe if the expected probability that the toxicity rate is > 30% is above 50%.
We set the following parameters:

We are not using Ordinal toxicity.
The type of target is “Target a single dose”

The target probability of toxicity at MTD is 0.3.
Find the dose Nearest the target. (Note we will tend not to select doses with toxicity rates estimated to be above the target because of the overdose control limit).

Specify target bands of

0-0.15 (Under-dosing),
0.15-0.3 (Target)
0.3-0.6 (Excess)
0.6-1.0 (Unacceptable

Specify that we want to limit excess + unacceptable toxicity to < 0.5, the change in this limit per cohort is 0 – so the limit remains the same throughout the trial.




3.1.3 Treatment Arms
Create 7 doses, 1 to 7 with no control, we leave the dose strengths as nominal 1, 2, ,3, … 7.



3.1.4 Variants
We don’t specify any variants. If we did this would allow us to easily create designs that were identical except in maximum sample size – allowing us to easily explore the effect of different sample sizes.

text:
3.2 Virtual Subject Response

3.2.1 Explicitly Defined – Toxicity
Create the 12 scenarios that combine 4 adult toxicity rates (AllSafe, Steep, Shallow & UnSafe) with 3 pediatric scenarios (A, B, C) and enter the probability of toxicity for each dose for each scenario corresponding to the table above (see section 2.5)

There are no parametric or externally defined curves in this example.

title: CRM 2 Samples and Open Enrollment
text:
3.3 Design

3.3.1 XHats
Here we define the dose strength values to use for each dose in the BLRM model. In this instance we are simply going to use the values (1, 2, 3, … 7) for each dose respectively. So we set the reference dose to 0 and define the X^ conversion as linear: dose strength – reference dose.



3.3.2 Toxicity Response
The only model available is the BLRM, which is the model used in the paper. In the paper a common estimate of the gradient is used for both groups and an offset [αped in the paper, ‘a’ in FACTS] on the intercept. The priors in the paper are:
\(\alpha\sim N\left( - 3,1^{2} \right)\), \(\alpha_{ped}\sim N\left( 0,1^{2} \right)\), \(\beta\sim N\left( 0.5,\ \ {0.2}^{2} \right)\)
In FACTS the prior on β is on ln(β), so we convert the above prior to \(Ln(\beta)\sim N\left( - 0.7,\ \ {0.5}^{2} \right)\). [The prior in the paper on \(\beta\) ranges from 0.1 to 0.9 (+/- 2 standard deviations) the Ln of these values is: -2.3, -1.2, -0.69, -0.36, -0.11 (in steps of 1 SD), we have chosen a prior on \(Ln(\beta)\) that has the corresponding values: -1,7, -1,2, -0.7, -0.2, 0.3. As we shall see this results in some small but not significant differences from the paper.
Set the parameters as follows:

Priors

Alpha: N(-3,1)
Ln(Beta): N(-0.7, 0.5)
Rho: 0

Asymptotes

Minimum: 0
Maximum: 1

Group 2 priors

A: N(0, 1) (no restriction)
Common slope


Figure 3‑1 Toxicity Response showing the effect of the prior on the model for group 1
Figure 3‑2 Toxicity response showing the effect of the prior on the model for group 2


3.3.3 Prior Pseudo-subjects
As per the paper, we add 0.5 prior pseudo-subjects to the model for group 1 (adults) at the lowest and highest doses. With no DLTs at the lowest dose and 0.5 DLT at the highest dose. This makes our prior very slightly more informative, in a way that it is hoped is meaningful to the clinical team.
Note we can explore the effect of adding pseudo subjects to the prior by simply creating a version of the design without them and then comparing the simulation results.



3.3.4 Allocation Rule
Here in FACTS we have to depart from the paper somewhat – we can’t completely replicate the described rules. We will use both overdose control and escalation rules, require 2 subjects per dose before escalating, and only allow one dose strength to be increased at a time. This will apply separately to both groups. Group 1 starts at the lowest dose, Group 2 at one dose below the Group 1 MTD.
Set the parameters as follows:

Specify that allocation will be limited by using the ‘overdose control’ specified on the study tab and additional rules specified on this tab.
Allocation:

The dose allocation rules will use dose levels (not dose strengths)
There must be a minimum of 2 subjects on a dose before incrementing
The increment is the same across the whole dose range
The maximum increment is 1 dose level
The increment is relative to the most recently cleared dose

Set the starting dose level: Dose 1
The Initial dose for the second population (pediatrics): one dose below the MTD of the first population





3.3.5 Stopping Criteria
As with the allocation rules, what we can specify in FACTS is not as complex as defined in the paper. We will use a required minimum number of subjects on MTD of 8, and that if 3 further subjects were to complete on the MTD with no DLTs that the selection of MTD would not change.
Set the parameters as follows:

Check the “Rules for stopping trial early
Required number of subjects on MTD: 8
Stop if adding another DLT free cohort does not alter the MTD. Size of cohort: 3
Minimum subjects accrued: 8
Combine all the above rules with AND. They all have to be met for the trial to stop.
Minimum toxicities required before stopping: 2. This solves the problem of what to do if an early toxicity causes the expected toxicity at all doses to be too high for allocation to continue by the normal rules. This parameter allows the user to specify that, should all doses be inadmissible, allocation to the lowest dose should continue until at least the specified number of toxicities has been observed.

title: CRM 2 Samples and Open Enrollment
text:
3.4 Simulation
Set the number of simulations to 1000, and the packet size to 100. Select all the scenarios and run the simulations (In FACTS terms this takes a relatively long time to run, because with Open Enrolment there is an analysis every subject. It took ~90 minutes on a dual core 2.2 GHz Intel i7).



Graphical user interface, application, table Description automatically generated


We can use the “Across Scenario Graphs” plots of selected MTD for group 1 and group 2 to get a quick overall impression of the ability of the trial to “pick the right dose”.



Chart Description automatically generated





Chart Description automatically generated


These results look very good.

In all the scenarios where there is one or more doses in the target range these are the most likely doses to be picked.
In the scenarios where no doses are safe the lowest dose is picked with probability > 95%
In the scenario where all doses have rates below the target band, the highest dose is picked with probability > 95%
In the Steep scenarios where there is a ~30% change of more of picking a dose for Group 1 with a toxicity rate above the target range, that dose is Dose 3 simulated with a toxicity rate of 0.35. So this is a “near miss”.
In the Steep-C scenario where there is a ~30% chance of picking a dose for group 2 with a toxicity below the target range, that dose is Dose 2 with a simulated toxicity rate of 0.132, only just below the range, so this is a “near miss”.
In the Steep-B scenario where there is a ~40% chance of picking a dose for group 2 with a toxicity below the target range, that dose is Dose 1 with a simulated toxicity rate of 0.08, well below the target range so this is a “significant miss”, however the simulated toxicity rate on Dose 2 (the “correct target” in this scenario) is 0.292, very close to the top of the target band, so it is almost certain that in the nearly 40% of scenarios where Dose 1 has been selected it will be because the observed data on Dose 2 has made it look too toxic.

text:

Individual simulations can be used to check that the behavior of the design would be acceptable to the clinical team, and to check the explanations given above for the results in those scenarios where the chances of selecting a non-optimal dose were quite high.
Note that in Steep-A, Steep-B and Steep-C the virtual subject response being simulated for group 1 is the same, so the same allocation histories can be seen in occurring across the 3 scenarios.
On the face of it these example dose escalation histories seem to back up our analysis of the results of these scenarios, and there are no obvious glaring poor decision being made. In practice a more detailed review would be carried out to confirm this.

This is to be consistent with the graph in the paper where the MTD is not selected if all doses are ‘unsafe’.

title: CRM 2 Samples and Open Enrollment
text:
4.4 Observations
It looks as though the prior in FACTS has a slightly lower expectation of toxicity at the higher doses. This difference is only observable early on and disappears as the amount of data increases and dominates the prior.
We can see the difference in the allocation rule between the paper and FACTS that arises from the change in the number of subjects required on a dose from 2 to 3, after dose 3. FACTS does not have the facility to implement such a rule so we required just 2 per dose for all doses. The difference can be seen in the “AllSafe” scenario where the paper shows mean allocations of ~6 (adult) and ~3 (pediatric) at doses 4, 5 & 6 whilst FACT shows mean allocations of ~4 and ~2 respectively.
The higher mean allocation in FACTS to Dose 7 in this scenario is simply because there are more subjects left to allocate at the top dose before the max sample size is reached.
While the allocation distributions are not identical, the allocation of subjects in FACTS is very similar to the paper and looks to be entirely appropriate to the scenarios being simulated.
The MTD selection distribution in FACTS is very similar to that of the paper, except in the extreme scenarios where FACTS has a slightly higher selection of MTD at the top dose in the “Allsafe” scenario, and slightly higher selection of the lowest dose as MTD (as opposed to no selection of MTD) in the “UnSafe” scenario.

title: CRM (Toxicity)
text:
2.1 Response Model
If the probability of observing toxicity for a subject given dose j is pj
We will model the probability of toxicity across the range of doses:
\[\log\left(\frac{p_j}{1 - p_j}\right) = \alpha + \beta\widehat{x_{j}}\]
With α set to –3 and β given the prior distribution:
\[\beta \sim U[0,3)\]
Each dose j is given a ‘strength’ \(\widehat{x_{j}}\) by fitting the user supplied prior expectations of toxicity for each dose p0j to the above model with β set to 1. i.e. solving:
\[\log\left(\frac{p^{0}_{j}}{1 - p^{0}_{j}}\right) = \alpha + \widehat{x_{j}}\]
for \(\widehat{x_{j}}\).

title: CRM (Toxicity)
text:
4.4 Design
Use the default “maximum probability that dose exceeds target probability of 0.95. This sets the”DU” dose decisions. It applies an overdose control. The lower the threshold more tox observed / total observed combinations will become “DU”, the higher the threshold, the fewer will become “DU”. A dose that meets the DU criterion will no longer be allocated to by mTPI, it will not permit re-escalation to the dose (whereas doses from which it simple de-escalated “D” can be returned to).
Specify a stopping rule of a maximum of “9” subjects on a dose: if the next dose to be allocated to already has 9 subjects allocated to it (3 cohorts) then the trial will stop and declare that dose the MTD.
The table then shows the mTPI decision rules for up to 9 subjects.
For example with the current parameters settings if 6 results have been observed on the last dose tested:

If there have been 0 toxicities (“E”), escalate to the next dose.
If there have been 1 or 2 toxicities (“S”) re-dose at this dose.
If there had been 3 toxicities (“D”) then de-escalate to the previous dose.
If there have been 4 or more toxicities (“DU”) then de-escalate to the previous dose and do not allow re-escalation to this dose.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Genomic Biomarker)
text:
4.1 Study

4.1.1 Study Info
Under the study info tab we define

Whether comparison will be against a control arm, or an Objective Control (or “Historical”) level of response.
Whether events indicate a subject is improving or deteriorating.
The design options we wish to use:

An adaptive or non-adaptive design
Frequentist Analysis (or only Bayesian)
Whether subjects are all followed up for the same length of time (per-subject follow up) or there is a cap on follow-up beyond the end of full accrual – so subjects accrued earlier are followed up for longer.

How many groups there are in the analysis and whether we wish to cap enrolment into any group.



TTE requires that you specify either the maximum time that each subject is followed up, or how long you will follow up subjects after the final subject has enrolled. Here we limit follow up to 17 weeks after full enrolment.
The trial is intended to run with a maximum of 400 patients. Groups caps are specified to allow every group to have as many subjects as possible. Here we limit most to 80 subjects – in part to help prevent any one group from dominating.




4.1.2 Group Info


As in the other engines, prediction of Phase3 success may also be used for decision making, but we will not be using it here.
The clinically significant target HRs to determine success and futility can again be specified separately. The target HR is expressed as a ‘margin’ – a difference from 1. So here we have a target HR of 0.80 for futility stopping and so specify a target Clinically Significant Hazard Ratio Difference of 0.2 to be used in the futility criteria.



4.1.3 Visits
In this trial event’s the timing of events will be known, we will not be restricted to subject’s interim visits to observe them.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Genomic Biomarker)
text:
4.2 Virtual Subject Response
On these tabs we define profiles of how the subjects might respond during the trials.

4.2.1 Control Hazard Rates
Unlike other endpoints, in Time-to-Event we specify the simulation of the response on the control arm separately. This is because we are going to specify the response on the treatment arms as simply Hazard Ratios.
We assume a constant hazard rate so only have one time segment for the simulation of the control hazard rate.

For each group we specify the same control hazard rate of 0.087 (corresponding to a median survival time of 8 weeks).


4.2.2 Group Response
Here we specify the ‘true’ Hazard Ratios compared to control in each group. You can see on the left we have created 5 different true profiles. These range over null hypotheses (everything the same as the historical rate), to a range with equal probabilities, to a set of mixed profiles where there is a treatment effect in different subgroups.

Strong—X represents the case when the patients with G3 mutation have a have a strong treatment effect (irrespective of their G1 and G2 status). And there is no treatment effect for the others.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Genomic Biomarker)
text:
4.3 Trial Execution

4.3.1 Accrual

Here we specify the accrual rate of 7 patients per week. This is also the tab in which we input the group enrolment start times (here all subgroups start enrolling at week 0) and the relative prevalence of the subgroups. Note that the accrual rate of 7/week is for all subgroups enrolling. If one or more subgroups are stopped early then the accrual rate will drop depending on how rare the remaining subgroups are.


4.3.2 Dropout Rate
We do not simulate dropouts for this example.

title: Time-to-Event Endpoint (Genomic Biomarker)
text:
4.4 Design

4.4.1 Hazard Model

For the analysis model, we can use a piecewise exponential model for the baseline hazard function for each group. We specify a single segment which corresponds to a constant hazard rate (simple exponential model). Here we also specify a hierarchical model to borrow across groups for the estimation of the group-wise hazard rates. The gamma-based hierarchical model for γ’s is as shown in the equation tab. We use a setting here that uses mild borrowing. But we do not discuss much of that here since it isn’t the major objective of this example.


4.4.2 Frequentist Analysis
The frequentist analysis tab allows us to specify the Alpha values to use for the various p-value tests. Here we leave them all at 0.05 two-sided.



4.4.3 Treatment Model

The analysis model for the treatment effects in each group, is again formulated as a piecewise exponential – the baseline hazard is proportionally multiplied by a factor (the hazard ratio, HR, of the treatment relative to control) as shown in the first equation in the equation panel.
Borrowing across groups is done using a hierarchical normal model on the log(HR) for each group. Again, we have set it up here for some mild borrowing.


4.4.4 Allocation
We use 1:1 allocation Control:Treatment in each group in blocks of 6 subjects.



4.4.5 Interims
We will also conduct interim analysis every 6 weeks (after the first 100 patients have accrued) to determine if any subgroup should be discontinued for futility. We indicate here that we will discontinue follow-up for subjects on a subgroup that is stopped for futility, and also discontinue interims after full accrual. (We will not be using early stopping for success here, so the “continue follow-up” option for success is irrelevant in our case.)



4.4.6 Stopping Criteria
In this example, we use early futility stopping as the primary adaptation. We will focus on the individual group stopping behavior here. In the upper half of the tab, we indicate that any group should stop for futility if Pr(1-HR > CSHRD of 0.2) < 0.15.



4.4.7 Final Evaluation Criteria
We also set the criteria for evaluating group success at the end of the trial. We set that as success if Pr(1-HR > 0) > 0.90. whereas end of study futility will be if Pr(1-HR > 0.2) < 0.2. The study will be futile if all groups are futile and the study will be a success if any group is a success.

text:
4.1 Study

4.1.1 Study info
Under the study info tab we define

Whether comparison will be against a control arm, or an Objective Control (or “Historical”) level of response.
Whether a response rate indicates a subject is improving or deteriorating.
The design options we wish to use:

An adaptive or non-adaptive design
Frequentist Analysis (or only Bayesian)
Longitudinal modelling (and hence subject intermediate visits)
Whether longitudinal data should be modelled as following a restricted Markov.

How many groups there are in the analysis and whether we wish to cap enrolment into any group.


In this example we include a control arm for each group and place the appropriate group caps on enrollment. This trial is also adaptive because of the interim analysis at 200 subjects. We will not be using longitudinal modeling or frequentist analysis so we ensure this are not checked.


4.1.2 Group Info
In the Group Info tab the target differences for success and futility are both 0 (we are interested in a straight superiority trial) and we do not utilize phase III criteria.

Under the visits tab, we note the endpoint is observed at 13 weeks.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Dominant Group)
text:
4.3 Trial Execution
Under the execution we specify how to simulate key logistical aspects of the trial – how fast subjects are accrued and their probability of dropping out.

4.3.1 Subject Accrual

We have the potential to accrue 10 patients per week, with 50% from group 1, 20% from each of groups 2-3, and 10% from group 4. However, we are only opening the trial to group 1 for the first year, so groups 2-4 do not start until week 53.
Note when graphing accrual, FACTS accounts for group percentages and caps. Thus, the cap of N=300 produces an expected stopping time around week 60 for group 1, after which we are only enrolling groups 2-4. This reduces the accrual rate in the trial as we can no longer enroll the group 1 subjects. Purely on the basis of expected value, we expect the last weeks of the trial to only enroll group 4, the rarest group in the population and thus the slowest to reach cap.


4.3.2 Dropouts
On the dropout tab, we assume no dropouts.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Dominant Group)
text:
4.4 Design

4.4.1 Control Model

Within each treatment group we place a N(0,1.82) prior on the logit of the control rate. This is roughly equivalent to a uniform distribution on the control rate.


4.4.2 Treatment Model

For the treatment model we use moderate borrowing, placing a weak N(0,1) prior on μ and a moderately strong IGamma(1,0.05) prior on τ2. Note the prior on τ2 needs to be calibrated on the basis of the scale of the data.


4.4.3 Allocation

We allocate subjects equally within block of 4 subjects (this is done separately within each group).


4.4.4 Interims
We conduct one interim analysis at N=200 enrolled, and there will be a final analysis at the study cap specified on the Study Info tab, (N=500 complete).


Recall we have timed the interim analysis (based on the accrual pattern) to occur when N=200 subjects in group 1 are accrued. At that interim we enable early stopping solely on the basis of group 1. The trial (both the group and the trial) is declared futile if the probability treatment is superior to control is less than 90%. We have selected “Study stopping rules combined by: OR” to give “study to stop if any selected groups stop” in order to give group 1 “control” over the study.


4.4.5 Final Evaluation Criteria

If the futility criteria is not met at the interim, the trial continues to full enrollment at N=500, where we have a more nuanced view of success. Here we will measure success within each group (all 4 groups will have patients at that point). Thus there are four separate decisions, one of success or failure within each group. Each group is declared a success if the probability treatment is better than control is greater than 90%, while the group is declared a failure if the probability treatment is better than control is less than 50%. Values between 50% and 90% are listed as inconclusive.
Note that we have not defined “study” success or futility criteria, only group criteria. To specify study success or futility criteria we would have to specify which groups’ success or futility (including “Across Groups”) determine study success or futility, but have left them all unchecked.

title: Dichotomous Endpoint (Dominant Group)
text:
4.5 Simulation

We run 1000 simulations. Note the only two possible sample sizes are 200 or 500, so the expected sample size gives us a glimpse at how often the trial continues to full enrollment.

In the null case, we can see that most trials are declared futile early, with a small number continuing to full enrollment. Of those, none are declared successful. The labels on the remaining groups 2-4 are somewhat uninformative given that in most cases no data is observed in those groups by design.

When all the groups are good (treatment rate 40%) it is still difficult to achieve the fairly high bar at N=200, and thus we have a fair amount of early futility in the trial. However, trials that continue are largely successful, and the borrowing results in reasonably high powers for the minimal sample of N=75 in the other three groups.

When group 1 is good but the other groups are ineffective, the borrowing does not overwhelm the results. Groups 2-4 are still rarely incorrectly declared successful. While the type I error for these groups is slightly increased from the 10% one might expect with the posterior probability cutoff of 90%, this comes with the benefit of greatly increased power.

text:
4.1 Study

4.1.1 Study Info
The Study tab captures basic information about the trial. Set the following parameters:

Select the Adaptive option for Stage 1, but leave the checkbox unchecked for Stage 2
For simplicity, clear the “Use longitudinal model” check box.
Set the time to final endpoint to 4 weeks.
Set the maximum number of subjects to 300 and the maximum number in Stage 1 to 200, but leave the maximum for Stage 2 blank so that Stage 2 can continue until the overall maximum is reached.
Higher response is subject improvement, indicating that higher change from baseline values are good.

The Dose Name may be changed by double-clicking on the relevant cell in the table. While these names are simply labels for the treatment arms, the Effective Dose Strength (vd) is the dose value that will be used in dose-response modeling.

We will not use variants yet, but it also allows us to set a target dose QOI which will be used by various summary columns and graphs. We are interested in the arm with maximum response so:
Set “Selected dose defined by:” to Pr(Max).

4.4 Execution

4.4.1 Accrual
Add an accrual scenario by clicking the Add button on the far left. Add a region to this profile by clicking the Add button above the table, and leave the rate at the default value of 5 per week.


4.4.2 Dropout Rate

title: Continuous Endpoint
text:
4.5 Quantities of Interest
The Quantities of Interest (QOIs) are the criteria on which decisions, interim or final analyses, will be made. Numerous QOIs are available and you may select multiple quantities for evaluation. A basic set of QOIs is provided by default. Additional QOIs may be added by clicking the Add row in the table. A QOI can be removed by clicking the X on the right side of the cell. Each QOI may be edited by clicking on it, which opens a pop-up box.
In this case a trial will be judged a success if at the end of the trial:

the dose most likely to be Maximum has a greater than 80% posterior probability that its mean improvement is better than Control by at least 2 (the clinically significant difference).

We begin by specifying the Posterior Probabilities to be calculated comparing each dose to both the control. Since each of these probabilities are calculated per dose, they are considered vector quantities. We can create the required Posterior Probability QOI either by clicking Add… and entering its properties, or by changing the CSD value at the bottom right, which will set one of the default QOIs to what we require. If using CSD, ensure the Trial type is set to Superiority.
To make decisions in the trial, we must specify which dose will be evaluated, thus reducing the vector quantity above to a scalar quantity.
This information is captured in the Decision Quantities (Scalars) window at the bottom right. Here we require one QOI:

QOI (Vector Quantity): Pr(θ_d- θ_(Control) > 2)

Evaluation Dose: Greatest Pr(Max)



Giving:

Since we are not using them, we could reduce clutter in the results by deleting the other QOIs.

title: Continuous Endpoint
text:
4.6 Stage 1 Design

4.6.1 On Setting Priors
On setting priors – as a rule it is recommended that the user specifies weakly informative priors rather than non-informative ones. There are a number of reasons for this:

In a few circumstances non-informative priors can end up being informative.
What values make a prior non-informative vary depending on the range of the value being estimated, a measure with a SD of 1000 requires quite a different value for a prior to be non-informative than one with an SD of 1.
Measures that are log-odds or log hazard ratios can have parameters that are then exponentiated and used as parameters to other distributions as a maximum these values should have range of (-10,10) and (-5,5). Greater than this and numeric overflows can occur.
Using a “non-informative” prior can sometimes be used as an excuse for not thinking about the prior. Not thinking about a prior is never a good idea.
There are some priors, particularly for the variance parameters of hierarchical models where (as we use inverse Gamma distributions for the priors, weakly informative priors are preferred to uninformative ones [Gelman 2006, “Prior distributions for variance parameters in hierarchical models” Bayesian Analysis Vol 1 Number 3]
When simulating clinical trial designs there is a balance to be struck between the MCMC sample length used in the within-trial analyses and the number of simulations run. Weakly informative priors can help the MCMC to converge and allow us to use shorter sample lengths.

For many priors the weakly informative is easily judged where the priors directly correspond to values that we are simulating. Others are not so easily judged, for these we used “non-informative” priors ran some simulations and looked at the means and SDs of the posterior estimates of the parameters over all the scenarios and then based a weakly informative prior on these. You will see these priors below being described as having an “initial un-informative” prior and then a weakly informative one. Care must be taken with this approach to not over specify a prior based on the selection of scenarios, and it must be borne in mind that the scenarios may not capture the full potential variability in what the “true value in nature” might actually be.


4.6.2 Dose Response
For Stage 1 we will use an NDLM, which is the default.
The prior for the initial dose is by default 0 with a standard deviation of 10. This is broader than the actual range of our VSRs, but we will leave the standard deviation at 10.
The prior on tau expresses how much variability in response we expect per unit of drug. Since our doses are 25 apart, the default mean of 10 is too wide. We will reduce it to 1, leaving the weight as 1 (dose).
(To see the effect of tau, we can change selection on the prior graph to “Dose-Response Samples”, however with a prior weight of 1, the distribution of tau is heavy tailed so the graph tends to be dominated by one or two wild curves. Increasing the weight to 10 gives a more informative graph, but the variability is then dominated by the initial dose. Setting the standard deviation on the initial dose to 1 finally gives a good illustration of what tau=1 looks like,

These curves vary more than our scenarios so there may be a case for further reducing the mean tau.
Of course the changes made to visualize tau need to be undone before proceeding!)
Given our endpoint we can leave the prior mean for sigma at 10 (the expected SD of the response) and the number of observations weight for the prior to 1 (so the prior is weak, equivalent to a single subject’s responses and the impact of the prior on the final posterior will be negligible). Note that the inverse-gamma distribution is parameterized in terms of mean and weight. If you prefer to see the standard alpha and beta parameters, click the Settings menu at the top of the screen. Select Options and a pop-up window appears. Navigate to the tab for Gamma Distribution Parameters, and toggle the radio button to Show Alpha and Beta.
Thus the Stage 1 Dose Response is:



4.6.3 Frequentist Analysis
We are not interested performing any frequentist analysis, so we can uncheck the LOCF checkbox, which will reduce simulation time and the number of files that are output.


4.6.4 Allocation
To try to steer allocation toward successful doses we will use adaptive allocation, weighting allocation according to the probability that the response is 2 greater than control. Thus:

select the “Adaptive Allocation” radio button
click Add… under “Adaptive Allocation Targets”,
select the Pr(theta_d – theta_(Control) > 2) QOI
set the “Relative Weight” to 1. (Since this is the only target, the value is unimportant)
Click Update


The default is to allocate equally up until the first interim and we leave this unchanged.



4.6.5 Interims
Stage 1 can run to a maximum of 200 subjects, so we will try two interims at 100 and 150 enrolled subjects.
We leave the follow-up options at their defaults, so subjects are followed up if the study stops for success, but not if it stops for futility. If the study graduates to Stage 2, stage 1 subjects will be followed up as part of Stage 2. (Note that disabling the follow-up after graduation will prevent Stage 1 subjects from being used in Stage 2)
If the study graduates, we can specify a delay before selecting the arms to use in Stage 2. The choices are:

Wait until all Stage 1 enrollees complete
Wait a fixed time
No delay

If there were a long gap between enrolling a subject and their final response, it might be useful to use this delay to improve our chances of selected the correct dose(s), but in this case the final response comes after 4 weeks, so we will stick with default of No delay.
Finally, since, if we go to Stage 2, we are not interested in analyzing the final results of Stage 1, we can uncheck “Perform Stage 1 complete data analysis,” which removes an unwanted output file.



4.6.6 Success/Futility/Graduation Criteria
In Stage 1 we can set a range of rules for when the stage ends and what happens next.
Initially we have two tabs, Interim 1 and Final Evaluation. The Create box would let us create more tabs, so we could create one for Interim 2, Otherwise the rules on a tab remain in force until the next tab is reached, so in this case interim 2 will use the same rules as interim 1.
On the Interim 1 tab we will set up two rules, for early futility and early graduation:
If early results are so unpromising that the early futility rule is met, the trial will stop for early futility without going to Stage 2.
If the early graduation rule is met, the trial will graduate to Stage 2.
We could also set a rule to stop early for success without going to Stage 2.
To set up the rules:

Check the “Futility Criteria” checkbox
Click on Add,,,
Select the decision QOI (we have only one), set the condition to “<”, the threshold to 0.1.





Press Update
Check the “Graduate to Stage 2 Criteria” checkbox
Click on Add,,,
Select the decision QOI, set the condition to “>”, the threshold to 0.9.
Press Update

We could also set minimum numbers of subjects required before these rules can apply. Since our rules use the Greatest Pr(Max) dose, setting a minimum number of subjects on that dose might be a way to reduce incorrect decisions if that is a problem.

At final evaluation, we get to set rules for futility and success, but not for graduation because that is the default. Any trial which reaches the end of Stage 1 and does not meet either the success or futility criteria will graduate to Stage 2.
We will set a rule for futility similar to that above, but with a higher threshold of 0.2. We will also set a success criterion with a condition of “>” and a threshold of 0.95.

title: Continuous Endpoint
text:
4.7 Transition

4.7.1 Dose Selection
This is where we decide which arm(s) are taken into Stage 2. There are a large number of options, but what we want in this case is the default.
We use Standard Selection Logic, so decisions are made arm by arm rather than treating arms in groups.
The Control checkbox should be checked, so that we can continue to allocate to control in Stage 2.
Because what we want is simple, we can leave the Individual Dose Decisions and Target Dose Decisions empty and just use the All Dose Decisions tab.
We want to have a single treatment arm in Stage 2, so we can leave Keep selected and the minimum and maximum set to 1.
The sort criterion should be Pr(theta_d – theta_(Control) > 2) and the Sort Priority “keep highest” which means that we will keep the arm with the highest value for the QOI and drop the rest.
Since we are taking a fixed number of arms, we do not need to add any QOIs.

(Note that we could achieve the same thing by selecting Drop, specifying to drop a minimum and maximum of 3 arms and selecting “drop lowest”, so we drop all arms except the one we want)
(If 2 arms are doing well, we could allow two to be kept by setting the maximum number of arms to 2 and adding a condition, e.g. Pr(theta_d – theta_(Control) > 2) greater than some threshold. Then if two arms meet the condition, they will both go into Stage 2. If no arm meets the condition, because the minimum is 1 rather than 0, the best arm will still go through.)


4.7.2 Data Inclusion
This tab selects what Stage 1 data is included in the Stage 2 analysis.
The options are:

Not used – which would make the two stages two separate trials
Included in full – here we could use this option and use the NDLM (or another model) in Stage 2, so that subjects on the arms that were not selected still contribute.
Included where the subjects are on arms that are kept in Stage 2 – we will select this option to give us a simple two arm Stage 2 that we can analyze with the independent dose model.
Included in full and pooled with the one Stage 2 treatment arm – this option is only available if we are keeping exactly one arm. Since we expect the different arms to have different responses, this is would dilute our treatment effect.
Restricted to only those subjects that did not complete… - If the two stages are two separate trials, this option allows us to use in Stage 2 those subjects which were recruited for Stage 1, but which did not get chance to contribute to the results of Stage 1.

This tab also lets us select whether arms which were not selected for Stage 2 can be picked as the target dose in Stage 2. We will leave this as “only arms selected for Stage 2”

title: Continuous Endpoint
text:
4.8 Stage 2 Design
This tab contains sub-tabs that define the various aspects of Stage 2.

4.8.1 Stage 2 Response
For Stage 2 we do not want a dose response model; that is, we model each arm independently. Select the ‘Independent Dose Model’ option, this option does not do dose response modeling.
For this case the default priors will do – the same prior for all doses with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 10, which encompasses the range of responses we are simulating.



4.8.2 Frequentist Analysis
Again we will uncheck the boxes since we are not using frequentist results


4.8.3 Allocation
Because Stage 2 is non-adaptive and we always have two arms in Stage 2, the only thing to set is the allocation ratio. We will leave it as 1 to 1 with a block size of 2.


4.8.4 Success/Futility Criteria
Because Stage 2 is non-adaptive, we can only set the final futility and success criteria.
These are similar to those in Stage 1, but with bounds that are closer together, so the futility criterion is Pr(theta_d – theta_(Control) > 2) < 0.5 and the success criterion is Pr(theta_d – theta_(Control) > 2) > 0.8.

title: Continuous Endpoint
text:
4.9 Simulation
Because we have only a small number of interims, no longitudinal modelling or frequentist analysis, simulations are quick to run, so to get an initial check on the design set up, set the number of simulations to run to 100, Select All, the press Simulate.
To achieve more precise estimates of the operating characteristics, you may need to run 1,000 or 10,000 (or more) simulations of a scenario. By default, FACTS simulations run locally on your computer, which can take a significant time for large numbers of simulations. If you have access to a computer grid and your FACTS installation has been correctly configured to use it, you may use the grid’s parallel computing capabilities to improve computation speed. To do so, select “on Grid.”

title: Continuous Endpoint
text:
4.10 Results
Staged designs generate a lot results, but there are several ways to get a quick overview of what happened.

4.10.1 Summary Table Columns
The summary table contains two columns, “Ppn Overall Success” and “Ppn Overall Futility” which combine all the different forms (early/late, Stage 1/2) into single numbers. The table also contains “Ppn Correct Arm” and “Ppn Incorrect Arm” which, for successful simulations, show how often the selected arm was one that should succeed. The selected arm is determined by the QOI that we set on the Variants tab and we set “should succeed” for each dose and scenario on the VSR tabs.

From only 100 simulation we cannot drawn any definitive conclusions but the false positive rate (0.07 for overall success on the Null scenario) is in the right area. The power achieved on the Late scenario is only 0.35, but the maximum response is only 3 for this scenario compare to 4 or 5 for the others, so this may not be something that can be fixed.
The value of 0.07 for “Ppn Incorrect Arm” on the Null scenario reflects the fact that for this scenario all arms are incorrect. For the other scenarios the number of incorrect arms is reassuringly low.


4.10.2 Across Scenario Graphs
The same information can be view graphically. Clicking on the “View Graph” button reveals a small menu:

Show Stage 1 Graphs – results from Stage 1
Show Stage 1 DS Graphs – results from those Stage 1 trials that went to Stage 2.
Show Stage 2 Graphs – results from Stage 2
Show Overall Graphs – results for the two stages together
Show Across Scenario Graphs – graphs comparing the different scenarios.

Select “Show Across Scenario Graphs”


4.10.3 Selected Arms (Stage 1)

We get one small bar chart for each scenario. The colors are:

Green – Selected – the dose was selected for Stage 2 and should succeed.
Yellow – Mis-Selected – the dose was selected for Stage 2 but it was not flagged as one that should succeed.
Blue – Successful – the dose should succeed and was selected (i.e. had the maximum Pr(Max)) in a simulation that succeeded in Stage 1 (and so did not go to Stage 2)
Red – Should not Succeed – as Blue, but the dose was not flagged as one that should succeed. These could be viewed as a form of type I error.
Light Blue – Unsuccessful - the dose was selected (i.e. had the maximum Pr(Max)) in a simulation that stopped for futility without going to Stage 2.

The yellow bars for the Null scenario show that it is often graduating to Stage 2, while the other show where Stage 2 has been run with the wrong arm.


4.10.4 Selected Arms (Stage 2)
This is similar to the previous graph, but for Stage 2. Therefore there are no colors for arm (mis-)selection.

We can see that the Null scenario is seldom succeeding. We can also see that while the Late scenario is usually taking the correct arm into Stage 2, it is beating the success threshold less than half the time.


4.10.5 QOI Box Plots
We can view box plots of the QOIs for Stage 1 or 2:



4.10.6 Allocation
We can compare the allocation between scenarios either for Stage 1 alone or for the entire study. For Stage 1 we get:

Which shows that adaptive allocation has put some extra subjects onto the successful arms, though it would be interesting to rerun with fixed allocation to see whether the adaptive allocation actually improved power or the false positive rate.

title: Continuous Endpoint
section: 5.1 Variants – Would increasing the sample size help?
text:
5.1 Variants – Would increasing the sample size help?
What is the effect on our design of the maximum sample size and the maximum sizes of Stage 1 and 2? This can be explored using the Variants tab.
On the Variants tab, select “Multiple Variants” and set the number to 5. (It may be necessary to tab away from the “Number of variants” spinner to get the table to update.)
Enter the following:

The first variant, 300_200_X corresponds to what we have already tried. The others are different ways to increase the number of subjects. The last pair stipulate that the number of subjects recruited in Stage 2 will always be 300 irrespective of how many were used in Stage 1.
Now that Stage 1 can go up to 300 subjects, we need more interims, so on the Stage 1 Design, Interims tab, add interims at 200 and 250 subjects. In variants that have a maximum of 200 Stage 1 subjects these will have no effect.
On the Simulation tab we now have not 5 scenarios, but 25 as each has been replicated for each variant.
Run 100 simulations of each.

With this many scenarios to view, the across scenario graphs come into their own.

On the lattice plots, scenarios are shown across and variants down. The scenarios and variants that are displayed can be filtered using the “Select Scenarios/Variants…” button.
With multiple variants, the “Ppn Success” graph becomes a useful summary:

As can be seen, increasing the maximum sample size, whichever way it is done, has reduced the false positive rate. Likewise the power for the Late scenario is improved with greater sample size, though it remains poor.
Otherwise there seems little to choose between the different variants. X_200_300 may be the best, but we would need to run more simulations to see what differences are real.

title: Continuous Endpoint
text:
5.2 Optimizing the thresholds
Most of the simulations are using the maximum number of subjects, so it would be interesting to see whether more aggressive rules for futility would reduce the numbers of subjects without having a significant effect on power.
Running more simulations would reveal the true false positive rate and therefore whether there is scope for being more aggressive about stopping early for success.
Running simulations without early stopping in Stage 1 would allow us to use the Explore graphs for Stage 1 to explore the effects of different thresholds without rerunning simulations.

title: Continuous Endpoint
section: 5.3 Other things that might be improved
text:
5.3 Other things that might be improved
Is the Late scenario telling us something useful about how the design behaves given a marginally effective drug, or should we increase the response on the highest dose to 4 to match the other scenarios?
Given that we seem to be picking the correct arms, is there scope for a shorter Stage 1 and longer Stage 2?
If a short Stage 1 results in incorrect arm selection, would taking 2 treatment arms into Stage 2 mitigate the problem, or would delaying dose selection until all Stage 1 subjects have complete help?
Would early stopping in Stage 2 be a good idea?
Thus Staged Core Design offers a great many possibilities for optimizing a design.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
This document describes the use of FACTS in command line mode. The command line mode of FACTS provides simple access to open FACTS project files (*.facts files) and run all available simulations for the project.
Once a FACTS project file has been created, there are certain cases where it is useful to be able to run simulations for the project, or simulations for a set of projects as a batch action, rather than using the GUI to open and run simulations for each project.
The FACTS project files contain a complex set of interrelated parameters and must be edited with care. FACTS expects files created by FACTS and to be consistent, errors will not be handled or reported gracefully.



This document describes the command line options for using FACTS in a command line mode. It does not include guidance on the use of the graphical user interface (GUI) or how to create FACTS project files.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
This document describes the use of FACTS in command line mode. The command line mode of FACTS provides simple access to open FACTS project files (*.facts files) and run all available simulations for the project.
Once a FACTS project file has been created, there are certain cases where it is useful to be able to run simulations for the project, or simulations for a set of projects as a batch action, rather than using the GUI to open and run simulations for each project.
The FACTS project files contain a complex set of interrelated parameters and must be edited with care. FACTS expects files created by FACTS and to be consistent, errors will not be handled or reported gracefully.

title: FACTS Command Line
text: This document describes the command line options for using FACTS in a command line mode. It does not include guidance on the use of the graphical user interface (GUI) or how to create FACTS project files.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.1 –[b | batch ] (Batch Mode)
The batch mode command line flag instructs FACTS to run simulations without displaying the user interface. Without specifying the –b command line argument, the user interface will open and any other command line options will be ignored (or misinterpreted).

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.2 –[h | help] (Help)
The –h command line option displays the command line help options in the terminal. No simulations will be performed when the –h option is specified.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.3 –[v | version] (Version)
The –v command line option displays the FACTS version in the terminal. No simulations will be performed when the –v option is specified.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.4 –[f | file] FILE (Run a specific .facts file)
The –f command line option is used to specify the “.facts” file for which to run simulations. The –f option must be followed by a valid path to an existing “.facts” file or directory containing one or more “.facts” files. Hint: Remember to use quotes around the path if it includes spaces.
If the supplied file name is a directory, then FACTS will simulate each “.facts” file in the directory in turn. As this only starts FACTS once, this can be quite a bit quicker than using a batch file or script that loops and starts FACTS separately for each “.facts” file.
Furthermore, if the supplied file name is a directory then FACTS also automatically recurses through every sub-directory simulating every “.facts” file it finds.

title: FACTS Command Line
section: 4.5 –[n | nSim] N (Run N simulations for each scenario)
text:
4.5 –[n | nSim] N (Run N simulations for each scenario)
The –n command line option is used to specify the number of simulations to run. The –n option must be followed by an integer value greater than 0. For each scenario in the “.facts” file, the application will run N simulations. Default if unspecified is 5.

title: FACTS Command Line
section: 4.6 –[p | packet] N (Set the packet size for simulations)
text:
4.6 –[p | packet] N (Set the packet size for simulations)
The –p command line option is used to specify the packet size for parallelization of simulations. The –p option must be followed by an integer value greater than 0. When using the –g option to run on a grid, or when running on a multicore machine it is often beneficial to parallelize simulations using the packetization process (see grid documentation for more information on packetization). The packet size must be greater than zero, but as in the GUI, there is no restriction that it be less than the number of simulations. If it is greater than the number of simulations, the simulations will not be packetized. Default if unspecified is 1000.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.7 –[g | grid] (Run on grid)
The –g command line option instructs the application to send simulations to the grid (assumes that the grid is correctly configured). When running on the grid, the action is still performed synchronously (ie. FACTS will wait while the simulations run and collect the results before exiting). This option is useful to parallelize long running simulations more than they can be parallelized locally. Default if unspecified is to run locally.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.8 –[a | agg] Mode (Aggregation Mode)
The –a command line option specifies the aggregation action to take for completed simulation results. The available modes for this option are:

None – no aggregation will be performed
NoPivot – Only standard aggregation will be performed
Pivot – Both standard and pivoted aggregation will be performed.

Default if unspecified is None.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.9 –aggPrefix prefix (Prefix for aggregation files)
The –aggPrefix command line option specifies the prefix to use when naming aggregated files, and must be followed by a valid file prefix. This option is only used when –a is set to NoPivot or Pivot. The aggregation files produced by aggregating across all scenarios will be named using the prefix<_pivot>_(filename).csv pattern, where <_pivot> is included for pivoted files only, and (filename) is replaced by the name of the file being aggregated. Defaults to “agg” if unspecified.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.10 –nBurn N (Number of MCMC burn-in iteractions)
The –nBurn command line option specifies the number of burn-in MCMC iterations to use in the simulation, and must be followed by a valid integer value greater than 0. Defaults to 1000 if unspecified.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.11 –nMCMC N (Number of MCMC sample iterations)
The –nMCMC command line option specifies the number of MCMC sampling iterations to use in the simulation, and must be followed by a valid integer value greater than 0. Defaults to 2500 if unspecified.

title: FACTS Command Line
section: 4.12 –nWeeksFiles N (Number of weeks files to output)
text:
4.12 –nWeeksFiles N (Number of weeks files to output)
The –nWeeksFiles command line option specifies the number of weeks files to output from the simulation, and must be followed by a valid integer value at least 0. Defaults to 100 if unspecified.

title: FACTS Command Line
section: 4.13 –nFreqWeeksFiles N (Number of weeks files to output)
text:
4.13 –nFreqWeeksFiles N (Number of weeks files to output)
The –nFreqWeeksFiles command line option specifies the number of frequentist weeks files to output from the simulation, and must be followed by a valid integer value at least 0. Defaults to 100 if unspecified.

title: FACTS Command Line
section: 4.14 –nSubjectFiles N (Number of subjects files to output)
text:
4.14 –nSubjectFiles N (Number of subjects files to output)
The –nSubjectFiles command line option specifies the number of subject files to output from the simulation, and must be followed by a valid integer value at least 0. Defaults to 1 if unspecified.

title: FACTS Command Line
section: 4.15 –nMCMCFiles N (Number of MCMC files to output)
text:
4.15 –nMCMCFiles N (Number of MCMC files to output)
The –nMCMCFiles command line option specifies the number of MCMC sample files to output from the simulation, and must be followed by a valid integer value at least 0. Defaults to 0 if unspecified.
NB: This option potentially produces a very large amount of output data and may fail if sufficient disk space is not available.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.16 –nMCMCThin N (MCMC output thinning value)
The –nMCMCThin command line option specifies the MCMC thinning value to apply to the MCMC output, and must be followed by a valid integer value at least 1. The thinning parameter applies only to the MCMC output, all MCMC samples are used for analysis. Defaults to 1 if unspecified.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.17 –nMCMCImpute N (MCMC length per imputation value)
The –nMCMCImpute command line option specifies the number of MCMC sampling iterations to use in the simulation for each imputation. Defaults to 1 if unspecified.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.18 –seed (Random number seed)
The –seed command line option sets the random number generator seed value. The default value (3500) is the same as that used in the GUI. It can be set to any positive integer.

title: FACTS Command Line
text:
4.19 -offset (Offset from random number seed)
The -offset command line option specifies the rand number to start at, offset from the supplied rand number seed, and must be followed by q valid integer at least 1. Defaults to 1 if unspecified.
In order to ensure reproducibility, the FACTS uses random number seeds is to use the supplied random number seed to first generate a list of random number seed, one per simulation, to be used as the starting random number seed of that simulation. Thus it is possible to re-simulate a specific simulation by re-running FACTS with the same seed, but by specifying the offset of the required simulation. Note the offsets are ‘1’ based, simulation 1 has offset 1.
This allows a simulation with interesting characteristics to be re-run with greater output (such as weeks file, patients file, MCMC file) without having to re-run all the other simulations leading up to it.

title: FACTS Command Line
section: 4.20 -scenarios (Flag indicating which scenarios should be processed)
text:
4.20 -scenarios (Flag indicating which scenarios should be processed)
The –scenarios command line option instructs FACTS command line to run the specified scenarios by name. The names of the scenarios to run should be provided as a comma separated list. If not specified, all scenarios will be processed.

title: FACTS Command Line
section: 4.21 -report (Flag indicating whether a design report should be generated)
text:
4.21 -report (Flag indicating whether a design report should be generated)
The –report command line option instructs FACTS command line to generate a design report once it completes the design’s simulations. The report is generated by FACTS itself as a Microsoft Word document; R, RStudio, R packages and pandoc are not needed. (The -rpath option used by earlier versions of FACTS to locate R for the design report has been removed.)

title: FACTS Command Line
section: 4.22 -useDifferentSeedPerScenario (Flag indicating whether to use a different seed for each simulated scenario)
text:
4.22 -useDifferentSeedPerScenario (Flag indicating whether to use a different seed for each simulated scenario)
The –useDifferentSeedPerScenario command line option provides FACTS command line with an option to set a different random number seed for each of the scenarios that are being simulated. FACTS command line simply takes the base random number seed as set in the -seed flag, uses this for the first simulated scenario and then adds 1111 to the random number seed of any additional scenarios being simulated. For example, if three scenarios are being simulated and the -seed flag is set to 3500, the first scenario will have a random number seed of 3500, the second scenario a random number of 4611 and the third scenario a random number seed of 5722. This deterministic way of setting different random number seeds allows for reproducible simulation results.

title: FACTS Command Line
section: 4.23 -useDifferentSeedPerDesign (Flag indicating whether to use a different seed for each simulated design)
text:
4.23 -useDifferentSeedPerDesign (Flag indicating whether to use a different seed for each simulated design)
The –useDifferentSeedPerDesign command line option provides FACTS command line with an option to set a different base random number seed for each of the designs that are being simulated. This option is only used when a directory containing multiple FACTS designs is passed as an argument to the FACTS command line, rather than a single design. FACTS command line simply takes the base random number seed as set in the -seed flag, uses this for the first simulated design and then adds 1234 to the random number seed of any additional designs being simulated. For example, if three designs are being simulated and the -seed flag is set to 3500, the first design will have a base random number seed of 3500, the second scenario a random number of 4734 and the third design a base random number seed of 5968. This deterministic way of setting different random number seeds allows for reproducible simulation results.

title: FACTS Forward Simulation
text:
This document describes the detailed functionality for running forward simulations using FACTSTM (Fixed and Adaptive Clinical Trial Simulator) via the command line execution of the FACTS engines (we refer to this as Forward Simulation Mode). It describes the functionality for all four of the FACTS Core engines that have forward simulation mode.
The design engines are simple command line programs that require no complex installation. They are supplied in a ‘Zip’ archive from which they should be extracted to an easy to locate directory.
For example:
C:\Program Files\BerryConsultants\FACTS 7.1.0\bin
This places them in a subdirectory (‘Bin’) in the standard FACTS install directory.
The following files are available:

aipf_contin.exe - the Enrichment Design engine for a continuous endpoint (not used here)
aipf_dichot.exe the Enrichment Design engine for a dichotomous endpoint (not used here)
aipf_tte.exe the Enrichment Design engine for a time-to-event endpoint (not used here)
contin.exe the FACTS Core engine for a continuous endpoint
bCRM.exe the Dose Escalation engine (not used here)
dichot.exe the FACTS Core engine for a dichotomous endpoint
multep.exe the FACTS Core engine for a multiple endpoints
tte.exe the FACTS Core engine for a time-to-event endpoint

To run the engines, open a command prompt window. Navigate to the directory where the various input files for the run are located and enter the command, for example:
C:\Program Files (x86)\BerryConsultants\FACTS 7.1.0\Bin\contin.exe p n 100 –-current-week 25 –-interim 2
For this example, three files are required:

a copy of the nuk1_e.param file from a simulation results directory of the FACTS design to be used; and
a patients data file (the formats of the patients data files are given below).
a ‘forward simulation parameter file’ so the simulation knows the ‘current time’ in the trial and which arms (if any) have been dropped and when

The engine will output the requested number of Sim Forward patients files (100 in the example above)..
The Enrichment Design and Dose Escalation engines do not include a forward simulation capability.

title: FACTS Forward Simulation
text:
2.1 Input
The execution mode can be invoked from the command line by running the engine executable program with the appropriate option flags. The user will also have to provide a dataset with data on subjects enrolled in the trial at the time the analysis is required, and a parameter file describing the trial design, a short data file fsim.param describing the state of the trial and some additional inputs via command line options. The required input files and command-line options are as follows.

title: FACTS Forward Simulation
text:
2.2 The trial specification (‘param’) file
The trial specification parameters should be provided in a file named nuk1_e.param (C/ME), bin1_e.param (D) or tte1_e.param (TTE) in the directory in which the executable is run (or some other file name may be specified with the ‘f’ option). This is the file produced by the GUI in the design/simulation phase of the trial.

title: FACTS Forward Simulation
text:
2.3 The Forward Simulation (‘fsim’) parameter file
The forward simulation specification parameters should be provided in a file named contin_fsim.param, dichot_fsim.param, me_fsim.param or tte_fsim.param in the directory in which the executable is run (or some other file name may be specified with the --fsimparam option). The parameters to be provided are:

fsim_start_week : The time (in weeks) when the data were recorded and from when the forward simulation should begin
arm_dropped (Optional) : A comma separated list of 0/1 of length = number of dose arms, that provide an indicator of whether a particular arm has already been dropped at the present time.
arm_drop_week (Optional if arm_dropped is not specified) : The arm drop times in weeks corresponding to the 1’s in arm_dropped (the drop times for arms that have not been dropped should be set to -9999).

Lines beginning with a ‘#’ and are skipped. The parameters arm_dropped/arm_drop_week may be omitted if there is no arm dropping in the study or if no arms have been dropped to date (the engine will issue a warning which may be ignored). A sample file might look like this:
#======================================
fsim_start_week=17.43
# 4arm study where arm #2 has been dropped
arm_dropped=0,1,0,0
arm_drop_week=-9999,12.14,-9999,-9999
#======================================
Note that “fsim_start_week” and “–current-week” will usually have the same or similar values – the former is the time from which further recruitment occurs and the latter the time of the current data. It must be supplied in addition to fsim_start_week.

title: FACTS Forward Simulation
text:
2.4 Patient Data File
This format is identical to that of the patientsNNNNN.csv output files from simulation mode. Note that all columns should be present even if not used (e.g. baseline) in the particular design. It is recommended you supply the value -9999 in unused columns, this makes it clear to someone subsequently using the file that this is intended as an unused data column – the exception to this is the region id, here just supply the value “1”.

The subject data in a file named patients.dat should be provided in the directory in which the executable is run (or some other file name may be specified with the --fsimdata option).
It is a text file with comma separated fields. Empty lines and lines beginning with ‘#’ will be ignored.
Each subject’s data appears on a single line with comma separated values. For continuous and dichotomous these are:

Subject ID: An integer value that is not used other than to identify a subject’s data records.
Region ID: The subject’s region ID (1…R).
Enrollment Date: A non-negative number of days.
Dose Index: Subject’s dose arm (1...D)
Last Visit #: Last observed visit. Zero to number of visits.
Dropout indicator: 1=dropped out, 0 otherwise
Baseline: Not used if no baseline (supply -9999)



For each scheduled visit:


Response at visit. Ignored if after Last Visit # (supply -9999). For dichotomous endpoints these are 0 or 1 (or -1 if restricted Markov). Note that in C/ME if the analysis is to be conducted on change from baseline and baseline is present, the Response column is expected to contain the original response and not difference from baseline.



The multiple endpoint format is identical except that columns are needed for each endpoint:

Subject ID
Region ID
Enrollment Date
Dose Index
Last Visit #: Zero to number of overall visits.
Dropout indicator



Then for each endpoint:


Last visit observed for the endpoint: 0 to the number of visits used for the endpoint.
Baseline: Not used if no baseline (supply -9999)


For each visit used by the endpoint:


Response



The time to event format is simpler in that there are no visits, but there are predictor columns:

Subject ID
Region ID
Enrollment Date:
Dose:
Dropout indicator: 1=dropped out, 0 otherwise
Duration: Duration until censoring (outcome=0) or time of event (outcome=1)
Outcome: 0=censored, 1=event observed, -1=event not yet observed/not yet censored (this will cause forward simulation to simulate the remainder of the subject’s observation time).
Predictor value: A continuous value for a continuous predictor. 0 or 1 for a dichotomous predictor. For either a continuous or dichotomous predictor, supply -9999 if not yet observed or censored by the primary endpoint. As per Duration for a time to event predictor. Unused if there is no predictor (supply -9999).
Pred Outcome: 1 if the predictor value/event has been observed. 0 if censored (the subject dropped out before the predictor value was observed, or censored by the primary endpoint if either a continuous or dichotomous predictor). -1 if the predictor value/event not yet observed/not yet censored. Unused if there is no predictor (supply -9999).


The subject data provided must be compatible with the trial setup specified in the ‘param’ file.
Where fields are unused, a numeric value still needs to be supplied but the exact value supplied is immaterial (though It is recommended that the value supplied is an integer).

title: FACTS Forward Simulation
text:
2.5 Forward Simulation Mode
The engine executables can be run with the following command line parameters:

p : Required. Invokes forward simulation mode
n <NNN> : Specifies how many trials to simulate forward. NNN patients files will be produced at the end of the run giving dose and region allocation for the existing and simulated subjects. (Default is NNN=5)
f <paramfilename> : Specify the ‘param’ file. Default is nuk1_e.param (C/ME), bin1_e.param (D), or tte1_e.param (TTE).
--interim <I> : Where I is the interim number, an integer number should be supplied, there is no check that the value supplied is an integer, and the design engine behaviour is undefined if that is not the case.
--current-week <W> : Where <W> is the current time in weeks (this parameter is required and should be correct with respect to the data submitted; if the specified date and the data supplied are not in alignment, the design engine’s behaviour is undefined).
--fsimparam <forwardsimspecsfilename> : Default is contin_fsim.param (C), dichot_fsim.param (D), me_fsim.param (ME), or tte_fsim.param (TTE).
--fsimdata <subjectdatafilename> : Default is patients.dat
--noadapt : If this is specified, then adaptive features of the trial are turned off in the forward simulation.

title: FACTS Forward Simulation
text:
2.6 Output Files

patientsNNNNN.csv, the complete subjects data for each of the forward simulations (i.e including the input subjects plus the simulated forward data. The format of the file is the same as the standard patientsNNNNN.csv FACTS outputs when simulating from scratch.

title: FACTS Forward Simulation
text:
2.7 Forward Simulation Implementation note
In order to create a complete internal history of the current trial, the forward sim engine always performs an interim analysis using the data supplied invoke it and the time of the analysis is taken from the “–current-week” parameter. FACTS then proceeds to do the forward simulation according to the interim schedule from fsim_start_week onwards. The engine does not have detailed history of the trial conduct until the current time so it needs to do an interim right away to internally generate things like blocks and randomization probs., etc. It would be almost impossible to recreate the exact history of the trial internally. Hence, the ideal usage pattern is to invoke the forward simulation engine right at the time of an interim analysis. There are several implications of this:

Any of the decisions (trial stopping, arm dropping, etc.) that could be taken at an interim can be triggered at this initial interim. In particular there may be no simulation forward because the decision is to stop the trial straight away.
Since detailed history of the blocking used in the randomization lists up to the current time is not known to the engine, a fresh set of blocks is always generated following the first interim.

Forward simulation has been implemented to provide estimates of likely recruitment, not a prediction of the outcome of the trial. The forward simulation is based on the simulation profiles of the user specified dose response, longitudinal response, accrual rate and dropout rates in the parameter file, not on estimates based on what has been observed so far.

title: Frequentist Analysis
text:
On the Frequentist Analysis tab the user can specify that some standard frequentist analyses be performed at trial analyses. The frequentist analysis tab is completely separate from, and independent of, any p-value QOIs that have been defined. The analyses specified on this tab cannot be used for simulated trial decisions - they are for storing in output only.
Each specified analysis can be conducted using a variety of ways of handling missingness. Select all ways of handling missingness that are desired:

Missing data replaced by last observation carried forward (LOCF)
Missing data replaced by baseline observation carried forward (BOCF). This is only available if the endpoint is continuous and Baseline is being simulated.
Missing data is ignored (a “per-protocol” analysis).
Missing data is treated as a failure. This is only available if the endpoint is dichotomous.

If the trial has interim analyses, then for the simulations for which frequentist weeks files are to be output (specified on the Simulation tab) the standard frequentist analyses will be performed. If the trial has p-values QOIs, those QOIs are calculated every interim in all simulations.
Having the frequentist analysis include Dunnett’s adjusted p-values is a separate option (that applies to all the analysis type requested) because of the significant run-time overhead this can entail. Dunnett’s adjustment is available for continuous and dichotomous frequentist analyses.
The frequentist analysis tabs for the continuous and dichotomous engines also have trend tests, and allow the user to specify contrast coefficients to conduct those tests.
Note that the reported frequentist estimates of the treatment effect take the specified direction of response on the Study tab (whether a response indicates subject improving or worsening) into account. They are adjusted so that a treatment that is estimated to be better than the control always has a positive treatment effect.






Figure 1: The frequentist analysis tab for a continuous endpoint.




Continuous Endpoints
At the end of each simulated trial the following frequentist values will be calculated for each missingness handling method checked:

Using unadjusted dose-placebo comparisons based on a two-sample t-test calculate the:

test statistic,
(p-value)[## “1-sided p-value is reported in all the frequentist results. This is done in order to be consistent with comparisons with 1-sided α-values elsewhere.”],
confidence interval for the mean difference,
for each dose its marginal probabilities of significance (the number of times it was significantly separated from placebo independent of whether any other doses were) .

If selected, using Dunnett-adjusted dose-placebo comparisons based on a two-sample t-test calculate the:

test statistic,
p-value,
confidence interval for the mean difference
for each dose its marginal probabilities of significance (the number of times it was significantly separated from placebo independent of whether any other doses were) .

Using the general trend test calculate the t-test statistic and p-value using user supplied contrast coefficients.

If neither placebo nor an active comparator are simulated, a difference from 0 is assessed for each dose arm and Dunnett-adjusted calculations are not carried out.
If high values of the endpoint are good, P-values are calculated using a one-sided t-test testing \[H_0: \mu_T < \mu_C\] against \[H_1: \mu_T \ge \mu_C\] with \(\mu_T\) being the true treatment response mean and \(\mu_C\) being the true control response mean.
